118840.q: In what form is the fat in a fatty liver mainly stored?
118840.e: In fatty liver, mainly triglycerides collect in fat droplets of the liver cells. They form when more fatty acids arrive than are broken down or exported.
118840.m: A fatty liver mainly stores triglycerides.

118841.q: What is a fatty liver called when inflammation with cell damage is added?
118841.e: In steatohepatitis, liver cells die and inflammatory cells move in. It can progress to scarring of the liver.
118841.m: An inflamed fatty liver is called steatohepatitis.

118842.q: Which serious long-term consequence can a progressing fatty liver disease have?
118842.e: Over years, inflammation can turn into fibrosis and finally cirrhosis. This also increases the risk of liver cancer.
118842.m: An untreated fatty liver can turn into cirrhosis.

118843.q: What are the most important risk factors for non-alcoholic fatty liver?
a: Lack of vitamin C and sunburn
118843.e: Metabolic fatty liver is closely linked to being overweight, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. High blood pressure and raised blood fats also play a part.
118843.m: Being overweight and diabetes favour fatty liver.

118844.q: What is the most important treatment for metabolic fatty liver?
a: Losing weight through diet and exercise
118844.e: Even losing a few per cent of body weight can clearly lower liver fat. Exercise also improves sensitivity to insulin.
118844.m: Losing weight and exercise are the best therapy for fatty liver.

118845.q: Which organ does the hepatitis B virus mainly attack?
118845.e: Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver. The hepatitis B virus multiplies in the liver cells and can damage the liver permanently.
118845.m: The hepatitis B virus attacks the liver.

118846.q: What is the most effective protection against hepatitis B in Switzerland?
a: A vaccination, ideally as a baby or teenager
None, because there is no vaccine
118846.e: The FOPH recommends the hepatitis B vaccination for all babies and for teenagers who have not yet been vaccinated. It protects very reliably.
118846.m: A vaccination protects against hepatitis B.

118847.q: How do you check whether a hepatitis B vaccination has worked?
a: You measure the antibodies in the blood
You take an X-ray of the liver
118847.e: After the vaccination, the body makes antibodies against the virus. If their level in the blood is high enough, you are considered protected.
118847.m: Antibodies in the blood show vaccine protection.

118848.q: Why can you not get hepatitis B from the hepatitis B vaccination?
a: It contains only one part of the virus coat, not a whole virus
It only works after ten years
118848.e: The vaccine contains only one protein from the virus coat. The immune system learns from it to recognise the virus, but an infection is impossible.
118848.m: The hepatitis B vaccine contains no virus that can multiply.

118849.q: In whom does a hepatitis B infection especially often become chronic?
118849.e: The immune system of babies usually cannot get rid of the virus. In adults, on the other hand, the infection usually heals.
118849.m: In babies, hepatitis B especially often becomes chronic.

118850.q: Which serious long-term consequences can chronic hepatitis B have?
a: Cirrhosis of the liver and liver cell cancer
118850.e: The constant inflammation leads to scarring of the liver. In addition, the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma rises sharply.
118850.m: Chronic hepatitis B can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

118851.q: Through which route, among others, is the hepatitis B virus passed on?
a: Through blood, for example via shared syringes
118851.e: The virus is present in the blood in high concentration and is very contagious. Even tiny amounts of blood on needles can cause an infection.
118851.m: Hepatitis B is passed on mainly through blood and body fluids.

118852.q: Why do antibiotics not help against hepatitis B?
a: Because hepatitis B is caused by a virus
Because the liver breaks down antibiotics immediately
Because hepatitis B is an allergy
Because antibiotics only work in children
118852.e: Antibiotics only work against bacteria. Against viruses such as the hepatitis B virus, antiviral medicines are needed.
118852.m: Antibiotics do not work against viruses.

118853.q: Which organ can become scarred over years in chronic hepatitis C?
118853.e: The hepatitis C virus often inflames the liver unnoticed for years. This can lead to cirrhosis of the liver.
118853.m: Hepatitis C can scar the liver.

118854.q: Which statement about vaccination against hepatitis C is true (as of 2025)?
a: It is part of the measles vaccination
A single dose protects for life
118854.e: Because the virus changes so much, no vaccine has been approved so far. Protection comes mainly from avoiding contact with blood and treating infected people.
118854.m: There is no vaccine against hepatitis C yet.

118855.q: Which medicines are mostly used to cure hepatitis C today?
118855.e: Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) specifically block virus proteins. Treatment usually lasts 8 to 12 weeks.

118856.q: What is the cure rate for hepatitis C with modern direct-acting antivirals?
118856.e: With today's combination therapies, the virus is permanently removed in well over 90 per cent of patients. Earlier interferon therapies were much less effective.
118856.m: Hepatitis C can almost always be cured today.

118857.q: What did the discovery of the hepatitis C virus, honoured with the Nobel Prize in 2020, make possible?
a: Blood tests for blood donations and targeted medicines
118857.e: Since the virus has been known, blood donations can be tested for it. Medicines have also been developed that now almost always cure hepatitis C.
118857.m: The discovery of the hepatitis C virus made blood tests and cures possible.

118858.q: How does a hepatitis C infection often progress without treatment?
a: It becomes chronic in a large share of infected people
It always heals within a week
It always causes a high fever
118858.e: In most infected people, the virus stays in the body permanently. The infection often goes on for years with almost no complaints.
118858.m: Hepatitis C often becomes chronic without being noticed.

118859.q: What is the most important way the hepatitis C virus is passed on in Switzerland?
a: Blood contact, for example when sharing syringes
118859.e: Hepatitis C is passed on almost only through blood. Today this mainly concerns sharing injecting equipment when using drugs.
118859.m: Hepatitis C is passed on mainly through blood.

118860.q: How long does a modern treatment for hepatitis C usually last?
118860.e: Modern antiviral tablets are usually taken for 8 to 12 weeks. Afterwards the virus is gone in the vast majority of patients.
118860.m: Hepatitis C can be cured in a few weeks today.

118861.q: Which enzyme in the blood is most specific for damage to liver cells?
118861.e: Alanine aminotransferase is found mainly in the cytoplasm of liver cells. When the cells are damaged, it passes into the blood.
118861.m: ALT is the most typical liver cell value.

118862.q: For which causes is gamma-GT in the blood typically raised?
a: Drinking alcohol and blocked bile flow
118862.e: Gamma-glutamyl transferase reacts sensitively to alcohol and cholestasis. It is therefore a common screening value.
118862.m: A raised gamma-GT often points to alcohol or blocked bile flow.

118863.q: Which lab value typically rises together with gamma-GT when bile flow is blocked?
118863.e: In cholestasis, more alkaline phosphatase is made in the bile ducts. However, it can also come from bone.
118863.m: Alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT show blocked bile flow.

118864.q: Why should you not do hard sport before a blood test for liver values?
118864.e: Intense exercise releases enzymes from the muscles, including AST. A raised value could then wrongly be read as liver damage; the De Ritis ratio of AST to ALT helps to interpret it.
118864.m: Hard sport can distort liver values such as AST.

118865.q: Which clotting value quickly shows that the liver is producing less?
118865.e: Many clotting factors are made in the liver and have a short half-life. If the liver produces less, the Quick value falls and the INR rises.
118865.m: The prothrombin time shows how well the liver is producing.

118866.q: Which blood protein is made in the liver and falls in chronic liver failure?
118866.e: Albumin is the most common plasma protein and is made by the hepatocytes. Because of its long half-life, it only falls when the liver has been weak for a longer time.
118866.m: Low albumin can show chronic liver weakness.

118867.q: Why is AST less specific to the liver than ALT?
a: Because it is also plentiful in heart and skeletal muscle
Because it is made only in the brain
Because it never gets into the blood
118867.e: Aspartate aminotransferase is found in many tissues, especially in muscle cells. A raised AST can therefore also come from muscle damage.
118867.m: AST can also come from muscles.

118868.q: Why do low levels of albumin and clotting factors show a weakened liver?
a: The liver breaks these proteins down
These proteins are made in the kidney
118868.e: The liver makes many blood proteins, such as albumin, clotting factors and cholinesterase. If their levels fall, the liver's production is limited.
118868.m: Low liver-made blood proteins show weak liver production.

118869.q: What made liver transplantation a successful treatment from the 1980s onwards?
118869.e: Thomas Starzl attempted the first liver transplant in 1963, but many recipients rejected the organ. Only with ciclosporin from the early 1980s did many survive long-term.
118869.m: Medicines against rejection made transplants successful.

118870.q: Why can a living person also donate for a liver transplant?
a: Because part of the liver can be removed and grows back
Because the liver is not needed for life
Because only the gall bladder is transplanted
118870.e: The liver has a great ability to regenerate. After part of it is removed, the liver parts grow back considerably in both donor and recipient.
118870.m: The liver can grow back after part of it is removed.

118871.q: Which foundation runs the national allocation of donor organs in Switzerland?
118871.e: Swisstransplant runs the national allocation office on behalf of the Confederation. For the liver, urgency counts most, measured with the MELD score.
118871.m: Swisstransplant allocates donor organs in Switzerland.

118872.q: Which visible sign of liver disease goes with a high bilirubin level?
118872.e: Bilirubin is a yellow breakdown product of the red blood pigment, which the liver excretes. It is also one of the values in the MELD score, together with INR and creatinine.
118872.m: A high bilirubin level turns skin and eyes yellow.

118873.q: Where is a donor liver usually placed during a transplant?
a: In the place of the removed diseased liver
In the pelvis next to the bladder
Under the skin of the thigh
In the chest, next to the old liver
118873.e: The diseased liver is removed and the donor liver is put in its place. Experts call this orthotopic, meaning “in the right place”. Kidneys, on the other hand, are usually placed in the pelvis.
118873.m: The donor liver usually goes in the place of the old liver.

118874.q: Why is a liver transplant for liver cancer only an option in early stages?
a: Because otherwise the cancer keeps growing despite the new liver
Because otherwise the donor liver is too small
Because large tumours do not allow anaesthesia
118874.e: If the cancer has already spread, it keeps growing despite the new liver, especially as the medicines against rejection weaken the immune defences. The Milan criteria set how large and how many the tumours may be.
118874.m: For liver cancer, a transplant only helps early on.

118875.q: Which medicines do recipients of a donor liver usually have to take for life?
a: Blood pressure lowerers such as ramipril
118875.e: The immune system recognises the foreign organ and would reject it. Immunosuppressants damp down this reaction.
118875.m: After a transplant, immunosuppressants prevent rejection.

118876.q: What happens in newborn babies with blocked bile ducts (biliary atresia)?
a: Bile builds up and the liver scars
The stomach no longer makes acid
118876.e: In biliary atresia, bile cannot drain away. The children turn yellow and the liver scars quickly; this is the most common reason for liver transplants in children.
118876.m: Blocked bile ducts damage the liver of newborns.

118877.q: What is a transplant called in which a donor liver is divided and supplies two recipients?
118877.e: In a split liver, the organ is usually divided into a smaller left part for a child and a larger right part for an adult. That way one donor organ helps two people.
118877.m: A split liver supplies two recipients.

118878.q: What does ammonia in the human body mainly come from?
a: From the breakdown of amino acids
From the breakdown of fatty acids
118878.e: When amino acids are broken down, the amino group is released as ammonia. Gut bacteria also make ammonia from protein.
118878.m: Ammonia is produced when amino acids are broken down.

118879.q: Which condition arises when a lot of ammonia reaches the brain in liver failure?
118879.e: Ammonia is toxic to nerve cells and astrocytes. It causes confusion, drowsiness and, in the worst case, coma.
118879.m: Too much ammonia damages the brain.

118880.q: In which organ is poisonous ammonia turned into urea?
118880.e: The liver converts ammonia into harmless urea in the urea cycle. This is then excreted through the kidneys.
118880.m: The liver turns ammonia into urea.

118881.q: How does the urea made from ammonia mainly leave the body?
118881.e: Urea dissolves well in water and is filtered from the blood by the kidneys. It is the most important nitrogen-containing component of urine.

118882.q: Which amino acid is the most important harmless way to transport ammonia in the blood?
118882.e: Many tissues attach ammonia to glutamate and release glutamine into the blood. In the liver and kidney, the nitrogen is released again.
118882.m: Glutamine carries ammonia safely through the blood.

118883.q: Which enzyme attaches ammonia to glutamate?
118883.e: Glutamine synthetase uses ATP and makes glutamine from glutamate and ammonia.
118883.m: Glutamine synthetase detoxifies ammonia into glutamine.

118884.q: In what form is ammonia mainly found in the blood at normal pH?
118884.e: The pKa of ammonium is about 9.2. At a blood pH of 7.4, by far the largest part is therefore protonated.
118884.m: In the blood, ammonia is mostly present as ammonium.

118885.q: Which organ excretes ammonium and so helps remove acid from the body?
118885.e: The kidney tubules make ammonia from glutamine, which binds protons in the urine. In this way acids are excreted as ammonium.
118885.m: The kidney also excretes acid as ammonium.

119185.q: What is a glomerulus in the kidney?
a: A tangle of fine blood vessels
A hormone gland on the kidney
119185.e: The glomerulus is a tangle of capillaries at the start of each nephron. This is where primary urine is filtered out of the blood.
119185.m: The glomerulus is the filter tangle of the kidney.

119186.q: What is formed when fluid from the blood is filtered in the glomerulus?
119186.e: In the glomerulus, water and small dissolved substances are pressed out of the blood. This primary urine is then greatly concentrated in the kidney tubules.
119186.m: Primary urine is formed in the glomerulus.

119187.q: What are the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule called together?
119187.e: The glomerulus and Bowman's capsule together form the renal corpuscle, also called the Malpighian corpuscle. It is the start of every nephron.
119187.m: Every nephron begins with a renal corpuscle.

119188.q: What is the smallest working unit of the kidney, which begins with the glomerulus, called?
119188.e: Each kidney contains around a million nephrons. A nephron consists of the renal corpuscle and a long kidney tubule.
119188.m: The nephron is the working unit of the kidney.

119189.q: Why do red blood cells not normally get into the primary urine?
a: They are too big for the kidney filter
They are dissolved in the glomerulus
They get stuck in the bladder
119189.e: The filter in the glomerulus only lets water and small particles through. Blood cells and large proteins stay in the blood.
119189.m: The kidney filter holds back blood cells and large proteins.

119190.q: What mainly drives filtration in the glomerulus?
a: The blood pressure in the capillaries
The muscle work of Bowman's capsule
The pressure in the renal pelvis
119190.e: The hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries presses water and small particles into the inside of the capsule. The colloid osmotic pressure of the plasma proteins works against it.
119190.m: Blood pressure pushes the filtrate out of the glomerulus.

119191.q: Roughly how many glomeruli does a human kidney have?
119191.e: Each kidney has about a million nephrons, each with its own glomerulus. Together this gives a very large filter surface.
119191.m: Each kidney has around a million filter tangles.

119192.q: What is an inflammation of the glomeruli called?
119192.e: In glomerulonephritis, the filter tangles are inflamed, often because the immune system reacts wrongly. Blood and protein in the urine are typical.
119192.m: Glomerulonephritis is an inflammation of the kidney filters.

119193.q: A lot of protein is found in a urine sample. What can this point to?
a: You have drunk too much water
The liver is working especially well
119193.e: A healthy glomerulus keeps large proteins in the blood. A lot of protein in the urine therefore suggests a damaged kidney filter.
119193.m: Protein in the urine can be a sign of a damaged kidney filter.

119194.q: Roughly what percentage of primary urine is taken back into the blood?
119194.e: Of around 180 litres of primary urine, only about 1.5 litres of final urine remain. So about 99 per cent is reabsorbed.
119194.m: Almost all primary urine returns to the blood.

119195.q: What is primary urine most similar to in its make-up?
119195.e: Primary urine contains water, salts, glucose, amino acids and urea in almost the same concentration as plasma. Blood cells and large proteins are missing.
119195.m: Primary urine is blood plasma almost without protein.

119196.q: Which substance in primary urine is reabsorbed almost completely in healthy people?
119196.e: Glucose is taken back into the blood almost completely in the proximal tubule. Healthy final urine therefore contains hardly any sugar.
119196.m: Healthy urine contains practically no glucose.

119197.q: Why is sugar often found in the urine in untreated diabetes?
a: The kidneys can no longer take back all the glucose
The liver releases sugar directly into the bladder
Primary urine normally contains no sugar
119197.e: The transporters in the tubule can only take back a certain amount of glucose. If blood sugar is too high, they are overloaded and the rest ends up in the urine.
119197.m: When blood sugar is too high, sugar ends up in the urine.

119198.q: In which section of the nephron is most of the primary urine reabsorbed?
119198.e: The proximal tubule takes back about two thirds of the water and sodium. Its cells carry a brush border that enlarges the surface.
119198.m: The proximal tubule does the main work of reabsorption.

119199.q: What is the process called in which substances from primary urine return to the blood?
119199.e: In reabsorption, tubule cells take up substances from the urine and pass them to the blood. Secretion is the opposite route, from blood into urine.
119199.m: Reabsorption takes valuable substances back from the urine.

119200.q: How is glucose taken up from primary urine in the proximal tubule?
119200.e: Sodium-glucose cotransporters (SGLT) use the sodium gradient to take glucose along. The gradient is created by the sodium-potassium pump, which is why it is called secondary active transport.
119200.m: In the tubule, glucose travels together with sodium.

119201.q: How does primary urine compare osmotically with blood plasma?
a: It is four times more concentrated
119201.e: Water and small dissolved particles are filtered in the same proportion. That is why primary urine has almost the same osmolarity as plasma, around 290 mosmol/l.
119201.m: At first, primary urine is just as concentrated as plasma.

119202.q: Which principle does the loop of Henle use to concentrate urine?
119202.e: The descending and ascending limbs lie side by side and fluid flows through them in opposite directions. This builds up a strong concentration gradient in the kidney medulla.
119202.m: The loop of Henle works on the countercurrent principle.

119203.q: Which part of the loop of Henle is practically impermeable to water?
119203.e: The ascending limb pumps salt into the tissue but does not let water follow. This makes the kidney medulla salty.
119203.m: The ascending limb releases salt, but no water.

119204.q: What happens in the descending limb of the loop of Henle?
a: Water leaves into the kidney medulla by osmosis
Glucose is released into the urine
119204.e: The descending limb lets water through easily. Because the surrounding medulla is salty, water flows out and the urine becomes more concentrated.
119204.m: In the descending limb, water leaves the urine.

119205.q: What does the ascending limb of the loop of Henle release into the surrounding kidney medulla?
119205.e: The ascending limb actively transports salt out of the urine into the tissue. This creates a high salt concentration in the kidney medulla.
119205.m: The ascending limb makes the kidney medulla salty.

119206.q: What do water tablets that block salt transport in the loop of Henle do?
a: The amount of urine rises sharply
The amount of urine falls sharply
119206.e: If more salt stays in the urine, it pulls water with it. As a result, more urine is passed and the body loses water.
119206.m: Water tablets acting on the loop of Henle increase the amount of urine.

119207.q: In which part of the kidney are the loops of Henle mainly found?
119207.e: The loops dip from the cortex down into the medulla, especially deep in the nephrons close to the medulla. There they build up the concentration gradient.
119207.m: The loops of Henle reach deep into the kidney medulla.

119208.q: What use is the loop of Henle to the body?
a: It helps save water and make concentrated urine
It stores urine until it is passed
119208.e: Thanks to the loop of Henle, the kidney can remove a lot of water from the urine. That way the body loses little fluid even when you are thirsty.
119208.m: The loop of Henle helps the body save water.

119209.q: How is the loop of Henle in the kidney built?
a: As a U-shaped loop with a descending and an ascending limb
As a spiral around the renal artery
119209.e: The loop of Henle is a hairpin-shaped section of the kidney tubule. It dips down into the kidney medulla and comes back up again.
119209.m: The loop of Henle is a hairpin-shaped loop of the kidney tubule.

119210.q: At the end of the ascending limb, how does the tubular fluid compare with blood plasma?
a: The same as final urine when thirsty
119210.e: Because the ascending limb removes salt but not water, the fluid afterwards is more dilute than plasma. That is why it is also called the diluting segment.
119210.m: The ascending limb dilutes the urine.

119211.q: Which hormone makes the collecting ducts of the kidney more permeable to water?
119211.e: When water is short, the pituitary gland releases ADH. It makes water channels be built into the collecting duct cells, so more water returns to the body.
119211.m: ADH helps the kidney save water.

119212.q: Which hormone from the adrenal cortex promotes the recovery of sodium in the kidney?
119212.e: Aldosterone acts on the collecting duct. It lets more sodium return to the blood and more potassium be excreted. In this way it also affects blood pressure.
119212.m: Aldosterone keeps salt in the body.

119213.q: Besides water balance, what other job does the kidney have?
a: It helps set the pH of the blood
It makes the red blood cells
It stores glycogen for the muscles
119213.e: The kidney can excrete acid or hold back bases. Part of this fine regulation takes place in the collecting ducts.
119213.m: The kidney also regulates the acid-base balance.

119214.q: What happens to the urine in the collecting duct when the body needs to save water?
119214.e: When water is short, the collecting duct becomes permeable to water. Water flows into the salty medulla, and the urine becomes dark and concentrated.
119214.m: When you are thirsty, the collecting duct concentrates the urine.

119215.q: Where does urine flow after it has left the collecting ducts?
119215.e: The collecting ducts open into the renal pelvis. From there, urine flows through the ureter into the bladder.
119215.m: From the collecting ducts, urine reaches the renal pelvis.

119216.q: Which section passes into the collecting duct through a connecting tubule?
119216.e: After the loop of Henle comes the distal tubule. Through the connecting tubule, several nephrons open into a shared collecting duct.
119216.m: Several nephrons share one collecting duct.

119217.q: Roughly how many nephrons does a human kidney contain?
119217.e: Each kidney has about a million nephrons. Several of them open into a shared collecting duct.
119217.m: A kidney has around a million nephrons.

119218.q: How do medicines that make you pass more urine, so-called diuretics, work?
a: They make the kidney excrete more salt and water
119218.e: Diuretics block the recovery of sodium in the kidney. More water is excreted along with the salt. They are used, for example, for high blood pressure.
119218.m: Diuretics flush out salt and water.

119219.e: ADH is made by nerve cells in the hypothalamus. It travels along their nerve fibres into the pituitary gland.
119219.m: ADH is made in the hypothalamus.

119220.q: Where is ADH released into the blood?
119220.e: The posterior pituitary stores ADH and releases it into the blood when needed. It does not make the hormone itself.
119220.m: The posterior pituitary releases ADH into the blood.

119221.q: What is the second name of antidiuretic hormone?
119221.e: ADH is also called vasopressin because in high concentrations it narrows blood vessels. “Antidiuretic” means that it reduces the amount of urine.
119221.m: ADH and vasopressin are the same hormone.

119222.q: Which stimulus mainly triggers the release of ADH?
a: A drop in the potassium level
119222.e: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus report when the blood becomes too concentrated. A sharp fall in blood volume also promotes the release.
119222.m: Concentrated blood calls ADH into action.

119223.q: How does alcohol affect the release of ADH?
a: It blocks it, so you have to pass more urine
It increases it, so you pass less urine
It has no effect on it at all
119223.e: Alcohol slows the release of ADH. The kidneys then excrete more water, which can contribute to fluid loss and thirst.
119223.m: Alcohol blocks ADH and makes you pass more urine.

119224.q: Which disease arises when too little ADH is made?
119224.e: Without ADH, the kidney cannot concentrate urine; people affected pass many litres of dilute urine and are very thirsty. Since 2022, an international expert group has proposed a new name that directly names the hormone deficiency.
119224.m: If ADH is missing, a great deal of dilute urine flows.

119225.q: How does ADH make sure more water is recovered in the collecting ducts of the kidney?
a: It makes water channels be built into the cell walls
It turns urine into blood plasma
119225.e: ADH makes the cells of the collecting ducts build water channels, called aquaporins, into their membrane. As a result, more water flows from the urine back into the blood.
119225.m: ADH opens water channels in the kidney.

119226.q: Which class of substances does ADH belong to?
a: Peptide hormone made of nine amino acids
119226.e: ADH is a short peptide of nine amino acids. It is closely related to oxytocin, which also consists of nine amino acids.
119226.m: ADH is a small peptide hormone.

119227.q: Which group of hormones does aldosterone belong to?
119227.e: Aldosterone is a steroid hormone that controls the mineral balance. That is why it counts as a mineralocorticoid.
119227.m: Aldosterone is the most important mineralocorticoid.

119228.q: Which rise in the blood directly stimulates the adrenal gland to make aldosterone?
119228.e: Besides angiotensin II, a high potassium level is the strongest direct stimulus. Aldosterone then makes sure that more potassium is excreted.
119228.m: A lot of potassium in the blood increases aldosterone production.

119229.q: In which organ does aldosterone mainly act?
119229.e: In the kidney, aldosterone makes sure more sodium is recovered and more potassium is excreted. Water stays in the body along with the sodium.
119229.m: Aldosterone mainly acts in the kidney.

119230.q: Through which type of receptor does aldosterone act?
a: Through a receptor inside the cell
Through a G protein receptor in the membrane
119230.e: As a fat-soluble steroid, aldosterone enters the cell and binds to a receptor in the cytoplasm. This moves into the nucleus and acts there on reading the genes.
119230.m: Aldosterone changes how genes are read in the nucleus.

119231.q: Which gland makes the hormone aldosterone?
119231.e: Aldosterone is made in the outer layer of the adrenal gland, the cortex. Other steroid hormones such as cortisol are also made there.
119231.m: Aldosterone comes from the adrenal cortex.

119232.q: How does blood pressure typically change with too much aldosterone over a long time?
119232.e: Water stays in the body along with the retained sodium. Blood volume increases, and blood pressure rises.
119232.m: Too much aldosterone raises blood pressure.

119233.q: What happens to the aldosterone level if you eat a lot of table salt for a long time?
119233.e: A lot of salt increases blood volume, so less renin and angiotensin II is made. As a result, the adrenal gland releases less aldosterone.
119233.m: With a lot of salt, the body cuts back on aldosterone.

119234.q: Which blood values are typical of a lack of aldosterone, for example in Addison's disease?
a: Sodium too low, potassium too high
Sodium too high, potassium too low
Calcium too low, phosphate too high
Glucose too high, potassium too low
119234.e: Without aldosterone, the kidney loses sodium and holds on to potassium. People affected often have low blood pressure and crave salt.
119234.m: Without aldosterone, sodium is lost and potassium builds up.

119235.q: From which basic substance is aldosterone made, like all steroid hormones?
119235.e: All steroid hormones have the same ring framework and are made from cholesterol. In the adrenal cortex, aldosterone is formed from it in several enzyme steps.
119235.m: Steroid hormones are built from cholesterol.

119236.q: Why is creatinine well suited to estimating kidney function?
a: It is made at a steady rate and filtered freely
It is made only in the liver
119236.e: Creatinine is made at a fairly constant rate and is filtered freely in the glomerulus, but not reabsorbed. If its blood level rises, the kidney is filtering less.
119236.m: A high creatinine level points to weaker filtering.

119237.q: When does serum creatinine typically first rise above the normal range?
a: When filtering has fallen by about half
With just 5 per cent less filtering
119237.e: Because the blood level and filtering are not linked in a straight line, creatinine stays normal at first. This range is called the creatinine-blind range.
119237.m: Creatinine only reveals weak kidneys late.

119238.q: Apart from kidney function, what does the creatinine level in the blood strongly depend on?
119238.e: People with a lot of muscle make more creatinine. With very little muscle, a normal value can hide weak kidneys.
119238.m: Muscular people have more creatinine in their blood.

119239.q: In whom can a normal creatinine value hide weak kidneys?
a: In people with very little muscle mass
In people with high blood pressure
119239.e: People with little muscle make little creatinine. The value then stays normal despite weak kidneys; as an addition, cystatin C is measured, which hardly depends on muscle mass.
119239.m: With little muscle mass, creatinine can hide weak kidneys.

119240.q: Apart from the creatinine value, what information do you need to estimate kidney filtering (eGFR)?
119240.e: The CKD-EPI formula used most often today calculates an estimated glomerular filtration rate from creatinine, age and sex. Age and sex are linked to muscle mass.
119240.m: The eGFR is estimated from creatinine, age and sex.

119241.q: Urine creatinine 8000 µmol/l, urine flow 1 ml/min, plasma creatinine 80 µmol/l. What is the creatinine clearance?
119241.e: Clearance is urine concentration times urine flow divided by plasma concentration: 8000 times 1 divided by 80 gives 100 ml/min.
119241.m: Clearance is urine flow times urine concentration divided by plasma concentration.

119242.q: Why does creatinine clearance slightly overestimate the true filtration rate?
a: Part of the creatinine is also secreted
Creatinine is broken down in the urine
119242.e: A small share also reaches the urine through tubular secretion. As a result, more creatinine appears in the urine than was filtered.
119242.m: Tubular secretion makes creatinine clearance come out slightly too high.

119243.q: How can serum creatinine change after a big meal of cooked meat?
a: It can rise for a short time
It is sure to stay unchanged
119243.e: When meat is cooked, creatine in it already turns into creatinine. After eating, the blood level can therefore be raised for a short time.
119243.m: Do not eat a big meat meal before a creatinine test.

119244.q: Roughly how much primary urine do an adult's kidneys make per day?
119244.e: The kidneys filter about 180 litres of primary urine every day. About 99 per cent of it is recovered; only about 1.5 litres of urine is passed.
119244.m: About 180 litres of primary urine become only about 1.5 litres of urine.

119245.q: What does the glomerular filtration rate tell you?
a: How much fluid the kidneys filter from the blood per minute
How much urine is stored in the bladder per day
How fast the heart pumps blood to the kidneys
How much sugar the kidneys break down per day
119245.e: The glomerular filtration rate measures how much plasma all the glomeruli together filter per minute. It is the most important measure of kidney function.
119245.m: The filtration rate shows how well the kidneys filter.

119246.q: How does the kidneys' filtration rate normally change with increasing age?
a: It stays the same all your life
119246.e: Over the years, nephrons are lost and the filtration rate slowly falls. That is why some medicines have to be given in lower doses to older people.
119246.m: Kidney function slowly declines with age.

119247.q: What happens to most of the primary urine?
a: It is taken back into the blood
It is stored in the kidney
119247.e: The kidney tubules take water, salts and sugar back into the blood. So of about 180 litres of primary urine, only about 1 per cent is left as urine.
119247.m: Almost all primary urine is taken back into the blood.

119248.q: 600 ml of plasma flows through the kidneys per minute, and 120 ml of it is filtered. What share of the plasma is filtered?
119248.e: 120 divided by 600 gives 0.2, so 20 per cent. This share is called the filtration fraction.
119248.m: About a fifth of the kidney plasma is filtered.

119249.q: The blood pressure in the glomerulus pushes outwards with 50 mmHg. Two opposing forces push back with 40 mmHg together. What is the net pressure that filters?
119249.e: You subtract the opposing forces from the outward pressure: 50 minus 40 gives 10 mmHg. This small surplus drives filtration.
119249.m: The effective filtration pressure is only a small surplus.

119250.q: What happens to the filtration rate when the vessel leading into a glomerulus narrows?
119250.e: A narrowing before the glomerulus lowers the pressure in the capillaries. Less pressure means less filtration.
119250.m: Narrow before the filter means less filtrate.

119251.q: What does autoregulation of kidney blood flow achieve?
a: The filtration rate stays roughly constant when blood pressure varies
The filtration rate follows every blood pressure value exactly
The kidney stops filtering during exertion
The kidney greatly increases filtering at night
119251.e: The kidney's vessels narrow when pressure is high and widen when it is low. That way filtration stays stable over a wide range of blood pressure.
119251.m: The kidney keeps its filtering stable by itself.

119252.q: In which range is the normal pH of arterial blood?
119252.e: The pH of blood is kept tightly around 7.4, so blood is slightly alkaline. Lower values are called acidosis, higher ones alkalosis.
119252.m: Healthy blood has a pH of about 7.4.

119253.q: Which is the most important buffer in blood plasma?
119253.e: The bicarbonate buffer is especially effective because the lungs can control CO2 and the kidneys bicarbonate independently of each other. That is why it is called an open buffer system.
119253.m: Bicarbonate is the main buffer of the blood.

119254.q: Which two organs mainly regulate the body's acid-base balance?
119254.e: The lungs can quickly breathe out more or less CO2. The kidneys work more slowly, but excrete acid in a targeted way and hold on to bicarbonate.
119254.m: The lungs and kidneys keep blood pH stable.

119255.q: How do the lungs partly compensate for metabolic acidosis?
119255.e: Breathing more blows off more CO2, so the pH rises again. The deep breathing in severe acidosis is called Kussmaul breathing.
119255.m: When the body is too acidic, it breathes more deeply.

119256.q: Bicarbonate 24 mmol/l, CO2 partial pressure 40 mmHg (times 0.03 gives 1.2 mmol/l), pKa 6.1. What pH results?
119256.e: According to Henderson-Hasselbalch, pH equals 6.1 plus log(24 divided by 1.2). That is 6.1 plus log 20, so 6.1 plus 1.3, which is 7.4.
119256.m: In blood, a ratio of 20 to 1 gives a pH of 7.4.

119257.q: Which disorder is present in diabetic ketoacidosis?
119257.e: When insulin is lacking, many ketone bodies form, and they are acids. The acid comes from metabolism, hence metabolic.
119257.m: Ketone bodies make the blood acidic through metabolism.

119258.q: Which disorder arises when someone hyperventilates heavily in a panic?
119258.e: The heavy breathing breathes out too much CO2. The blood becomes more alkaline, which can cause tingling and muscle cramps.
119258.m: Breathing too much makes the blood alkaline.

119259.q: Which enzyme speeds up the formation of carbonic acid from CO2 and water?
119259.e: Carbonic anhydrase is found, for example, in red blood cells and in tubule cells. It makes the conversion many times faster.
119259.m: Carbonic anhydrase combines CO2 and water lightning fast.

119260.q: What is an electrolyte in the chemical sense?
a: A substance that breaks up into ions in solution
A substance that contains only electrons
A substance that always blocks electric current
119260.e: Electrolytes such as table salt break up into charged particles in water. That is why their solutions conduct electric current.

119261.q: Which cation is most common in the extracellular space?
119261.e: Sodium largely determines the osmolarity outside the cells. In this way it also controls how much water is held there.
119261.m: Sodium is the main cation outside the cells.

119262.q: Which cation is most common inside cells?
119262.e: In the cells, the potassium concentration is about 30 times higher than in the blood. This is important for the resting membrane potential.
119262.m: Potassium is the main cation inside cells.

119263.q: Why must the sodium level in the blood be regulated very tightly?
a: It determines how water is shared between cells and their surroundings
It provides most of the cells' energy
119263.e: Sodium holds water outside the cells. Too much or too little sodium makes cells shrink or swell, which harms the brain in particular.
119263.m: Sodium controls how water is spread around the body.

119264.q: Which organ is especially at risk when the potassium level in the blood is far off?
119264.e: Potassium is crucial for the electrical excitation of muscle and nerve cells. Even small deviations can trigger dangerous heart rhythm disorders.
119264.m: Too much or too little potassium endangers the heart rhythm.

119265.q: Which extracellular anion is the most important in terms of amount?
119265.e: Chloride accompanies sodium as its counter-ion and is present in plasma at about 100 mmol/l. Bicarbonate follows at about 24 mmol/l.
119265.m: Chloride is sodium's main partner in the blood.

119266.q: How many sodium and potassium ions does the sodium-potassium pump move per cycle?
119266.e: Per cycle, the pump uses one ATP and moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in. In this way it maintains the concentration differences.
119266.m: The sodium-potassium pump swaps three sodium for two potassium.

119267.q: What can happen if someone drinks an extreme amount of plain water in a short time?
a: The sodium level in the blood falls dangerously
The potassium level in the blood rises sharply
119267.e: A great deal of water without salt dilutes the blood. A sodium level that is too low makes brain cells swell and can be life-threatening, for example in marathon runners.
119267.m: Too much water at once can dangerously dilute the sodium in the blood.

119268.q: About 99 per cent of which electrolyte is stored in the skeleton?
119268.e: Calcium is found almost entirely as hydroxyapatite in bones and teeth. The small remainder in the blood is essential for clotting, muscles and nerves.
119268.m: Almost all the body's calcium is in the bones.

119269.q: Which diseases are the most common causes of chronic kidney failure?
119269.e: High blood sugar and high blood pressure damage the small kidney vessels and the glomeruli over years. In many countries they are the main reasons people need dialysis.
119269.m: Diabetes and high blood pressure harm the kidneys most.

119270.q: What does the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) tell you?
a: How much blood the kidneys filter per minute
How much urine you drink per day
How much sugar is in the blood
119270.e: The GFR measures the kidneys' filtering in millilitres per minute. If it falls sharply, this is called kidney failure.
119270.m: The GFR shows how well the kidneys filter.

119271.q: What does the term uraemia mean?
a: Waste substances that should be passed in urine build up in the blood
There is blood in the urine
There is sugar in the urine
119271.e: In uraemia, waste substances such as urea stay in the body. The results include nausea, itching and confusion.
119271.m: Uraemia is poisoning by the body's own waste substances.

119272.q: Why can heavy fluid loss, for example from severe diarrhoea, lead to acute kidney failure?
a: The kidneys get too little blood
The kidneys are attacked by bacteria
119272.e: When fluid is lacking, blood pressure falls and the kidneys get too little blood to filter. Doctors call this prerenal kidney failure.
119272.m: Too little blood for the kidneys can make them fail.

119273.q: Which mineral rises in the blood in advanced kidney failure and can trigger dangerous heart rhythm disorders?
119273.e: The diseased kidney no longer excretes enough potassium. A potassium level that is too high disturbs the electrical excitation of the heart.
119273.m: In kidney failure, potassium in the blood rises.

119274.q: What does permanently raised albumin in the urine show?
a: A harmless, meaningless effect of sport
119274.e: Healthy glomeruli let hardly any albumin through. If it can be detected in the urine permanently, this is considered an early sign of kidney damage.
119274.m: Albumin in the urine is a warning sign for the kidney.

119275.q: Which treatments replace the function of the kidneys in the final stage?
a: A blood transfusion or a plaster cast
119275.e: In end-stage kidney failure, kidney replacement therapy is needed. The best long-term solution is usually a transplant.
119275.m: Without kidney function, only dialysis or a new kidney can help.

119276.q: Why does chronic kidney disease often damage the bones too?
a: The kidney activates too little vitamin D
The kidney makes too much bone marrow
The kidney burns the calcium in the bones
119276.e: The diseased kidney activates too little vitamin D and excretes too little phosphate. The calcium-phosphate balance is thrown off, and the bone is damaged.
119276.m: Diseased kidneys also weaken the bones.

119277.q: Which physical principle does haemodialysis mainly use to remove toxins?
119277.e: Blood and dialysis fluid are separated by a semi-permeable membrane. Small substances such as urea move along their concentration gradient into the dialysate.
119277.m: In dialysis, toxins pass through a membrane.

119278.q: How often is haemodialysis typically carried out for kidney failure?
119278.e: Three sessions a week of about four to five hours each are usual. In between, patients have to be careful with drinking and with foods rich in potassium.
119278.m: Haemodialysis usually takes place three times a week.

119279.q: Which vascular access is often created by surgery on the arm for haemodialysis?
a: An access into the spinal cord
119279.e: In an arteriovenous fistula, often called a Cimino shunt, an artery is joined to a vein. This makes the vein strong and easy to puncture.
119279.m: The shunt vein in the arm is the lifeline of dialysis patients.

119280.q: How is excess water removed during haemodialysis?
a: By ultrafiltration with a pressure gradient
119280.e: A pressure difference across the membrane presses water out of the blood into the dialysate. This ultrafiltration replaces the missing urine production.
119280.m: Ultrafiltration removes excess water from the blood.

119281.q: Which substance usually stops the blood from clotting in the dialysis machine?
119281.e: Heparin blocks clotting while the blood flows outside the body through tubes and filters. Vitamin K, fibrinogen and thrombin, on the other hand, promote clotting.
119281.m: Heparin keeps the blood liquid in the dialysis circuit.

119282.q: Which dialysis method uses the patient's own peritoneum as the membrane?
119282.e: In peritoneal dialysis, dialysis solution is filled into the abdominal cavity and changed after a few hours. It can be done at home.
119282.m: In peritoneal dialysis, your own peritoneum does the filtering.

119283.q: How do blood and dialysis fluid usually flow relative to each other in the dialyser?
a: Not at all, they stand still
119283.e: With countercurrent flow, the concentration gradient is kept along the whole length of the filter. That way more waste substances are removed.
119283.m: In the dialyser, blood and dialysate flow against each other.

119284.q: Which waste product of protein breakdown is removed from the blood in large amounts during dialysis?
119284.e: Urea is produced when proteins are broken down and is normally excreted through the kidneys. How much it decreases is also used to measure how effective a dialysis is.
119284.m: The dialysis dose is measured by urea.

119583.q: What is the typical value of the resting membrane potential of a nerve cell?
119583.e: In most neurons the resting membrane potential is around -70 mV. So the inside of the cell is negatively charged compared with the outside.
119583.m: A resting neuron has a voltage of about minus 70 millivolts inside.

119584.q: Which ion mainly determines the resting membrane potential of a neuron?
119584.e: At rest, the membrane is mainly permeable to potassium ions. Their outflow along the concentration gradient charges the inside of the cell negatively.
119584.m: The resting potential is mainly a potassium potential.

119585.q: Which equation is used to calculate the equilibrium potential of a single type of ion?
119585.e: The Nernst equation links the ratio of an ion's concentration inside and outside with the voltage at which diffusion and electrical force balance out.
119585.m: The Nernst equation gives the equilibrium potential of a single ion.

119586.q: Which pump maintains the concentration differences of sodium and potassium at the nerve cell?
119586.e: Using ATP, the sodium-potassium pump moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in. Without it, the concentration differences would disappear.
119586.m: The sodium-potassium pump maintains the ion gradients.

119587.q: Where is the concentration of potassium ions higher in a resting nerve cell?
119587.e: Inside the cell, potassium is about 30 times more concentrated than outside. This gradient drives the outflow of potassium at rest.
119587.m: Potassium is plentiful inside and scarce outside.

119588.q: Where is the concentration of sodium ions higher in a resting nerve cell?
119588.e: Sodium is about ten times more concentrated outside the cell than inside. That is why it flows into the cell when sodium channels open.
119588.m: Sodium waits outside the cell membrane.

119589.q: Roughly what is the equilibrium potential of potassium in a neuron?
119589.e: The ratio of potassium inside and outside gives an equilibrium potential of around -90 mV. The resting potential is slightly more positive because a little sodium also flows in.
119589.m: The potassium equilibrium potential is more negative than the resting potential.

119590.q: Through which channels do potassium ions constantly flow out of the cell at the resting membrane potential?
119590.e: Potassium leak channels are open even at rest. They make the membrane at rest mainly permeable to potassium.
119590.m: Leak channels let potassium out even at rest.

119591.q: What happens during the action potential when the sodium channels open?
a: Sodium flows in and the inside of the cell becomes positive
Sodium flows out and the inside of the cell becomes more negative
Potassium flows in and the cell rests
119591.e: Sodium is much more concentrated outside than inside. When the channels open, it flows into the cell and briefly reverses the voltage.
119591.m: Sodium flowing in makes the inside of the cell positive.

119592.q: At what threshold is an action potential triggered in a typical neuron?
119592.e: If the membrane is depolarised from its resting value to about -50 mV, enough voltage-gated sodium channels open. The action potential then runs in a self-reinforcing way.
119592.m: Only when the threshold is reached does the action potential fire.

119593.q: Which ion flow causes depolarisation during an action potential?
119593.e: Voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium flows into the cell. This makes the inside of the cell briefly positive.
119593.m: Sodium flows in and reverses the voltage.

119594.q: Which ion flow is mainly responsible for repolarisation after the peak of an action potential?
119594.e: Voltage-gated potassium channels open with a delay. Potassium flows out and makes the inside of the cell negative again.
119594.m: Potassium flows out and restores the negative voltage.

119595.q: What is the phase called in which the membrane is briefly more negative than at rest after an action potential?
119595.e: The potassium channels close slowly, so briefly too much potassium flows out. The voltage drops below the resting potential.
119595.m: In hyperpolarisation, the voltage briefly dips below the resting value.

119596.q: Which principle describes that an action potential is either triggered completely or not at all?
119596.e: Below the threshold no action potential arises; above it, it always runs at the same height. Stronger stimuli do not produce a bigger action potential.
119596.m: An action potential comes completely or not at all.

119597.q: Why can no new action potential be triggered during the absolute refractory period?
a: The ATP is completely used up.
119597.e: After opening, the sodium channels go into an inactivated state. Only after repolarisation can they be opened again.
119597.m: Inactivated sodium channels make the neuron briefly unexcitable.

119598.q: Where on a neuron is an action potential normally triggered?
a: at the tips of the dendrites
at the membrane of the axon terminal
119598.e: At the axon hillock, the density of voltage-gated sodium channels is especially high. There the incoming signals are added up, and when the threshold is reached an action potential is started.
119598.m: The axon hillock decides whether a neuron fires.

119599.q: Which scientists explained the mechanism of the action potential using the giant axon of the squid?
119599.e: Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley measured the ion currents in the giant axon and described them mathematically. They received the Nobel Prize for it in 1963.
119599.m: Hodgkin and Huxley worked out the action potential.

119600.q: How does a neuron encode a stronger stimulus if all action potentials are the same height?
119600.e: Since the height of the action potential is fixed, the strength of the stimulus is passed on through the number of action potentials per second. This is called frequency coding.
119600.m: Strong stimuli show up as many action potentials per second.

119601.q: Which temporary chemical change does the protein of the sodium-potassium pump undergo during each transport cycle?
a: It is broken down into glucose.
It is moved into the nucleus.
119601.e: A phosphate group is briefly attached to the pump protein and later removed again. This changes its shape so that it opens alternately to one side of the membrane or the other.
119601.m: The pump changes its shape through phosphorylation.

119602.q: Where does the sodium-potassium pump get the energy for transport from?
119602.e: The pump is an ATPase. It works against the concentration gradients and therefore needs energy from ATP.
119602.m: The sodium-potassium pump runs on ATP.

119603.q: Why is the sodium-potassium pump described as electrogenic?
a: It moves one net positive charge out per cycle.
It conducts current along the axon.
119603.e: Three positive charges go out, only two come in. As a result, the pump directly contributes a little to the negative voltage inside the cell.
119603.m: The pump moves one positive charge outwards with each cycle.

119604.q: The sodium-potassium pump is a textbook example of which type of transport across the membrane?
119604.e: The pump moves ions against their concentration gradient and uses energy from ATP directly to do so. In diffusion and osmosis, by contrast, particles move without using energy.
119604.m: The sodium-potassium pump is an example of active transport.

119605.q: Which group of drugs blocks the sodium-potassium pump and is used for heart failure?
119605.e: Cardiac glycosides such as digoxin from foxglove block the pump in heart muscle cells. This indirectly raises the calcium in the cell, and the heart beats more strongly.
119605.m: Cardiac glycosides slow down the sodium-potassium pump.

119606.q: What happens in the long run if the sodium-potassium pump of a nerve cell is blocked?
a: The resting potential becomes more negative.
119606.e: Without the pump, leak currents gradually even out the concentrations inside and outside. This also removes the basis for resting and action potentials.
119606.m: Without the pump, nerve cells lose their ion gradients.

119607.q: In which structure of the cell is the sodium-potassium pump located?
119607.e: The pump is a transmembrane protein of the plasma membrane. Only there can it transport ions between the inside of the cell and the outside.
119607.m: The sodium-potassium pump sits in the cell membrane.

119609.q: Is the sodium-potassium pump directly needed for a single action potential to run quickly?
a: No, it only maintains the gradients.
Yes, it opens the sodium channels.
Yes, it creates the voltage peak.
No, it only works in muscles.
119609.e: During an action potential only very few ions flow, so the gradients hardly change. The pump restores the concentrations over a longer time.
119609.m: The pump keeps up the supply, not the single impulse.

119610.q: Into which space are neurotransmitters released at a chemical synapse?
119610.e: The vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release the transmitter into the narrow synaptic cleft. From there it diffuses to the receptors of the next cell.

119611.q: Which ion triggers the release of neurotransmitters when an action potential arrives?
119611.e: At the axon terminal, voltage-gated calcium channels open. The calcium flowing in makes vesicles fuse with the membrane.
119611.m: Calcium gives the starting signal for transmitter release.

119612.q: Which neurotransmitter is the most important excitatory messenger in the brain?
119612.e: Glutamate is released at most excitatory synapses in the central nervous system. It acts, among others, through AMPA and NMDA receptors.
119612.m: Glutamate is the brain's main driver.

119613.q: Which neurotransmitter is the most important inhibitory messenger in the brain?
119613.e: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) opens chloride channels and makes the next cell harder to excite. Many sedatives strengthen this effect.
119613.m: GABA is the brain's most important brake.

119614.q: How does the nerve poison botulinum toxin (Botox) act at the synapse between nerve and muscle?
a: It prevents the release of the messenger
It increases the release of the messenger
It makes the muscle twitch constantly
119614.e: Botulinum toxin cuts proteins that are needed to release acetylcholine. The muscle no longer receives a signal and stays paralysed.
119614.m: Botox blocks signals from nerve to muscle.

119615.q: Which messenger is released at most sympathetic nerve endings on the target organs?
119615.e: The postganglionic fibres of the sympathetic nervous system mainly release noradrenaline. It raises, for example, heart rate and blood pressure.
119615.m: The sympathetic nervous system mostly acts on organs through noradrenaline.

119616.q: What does an inhibitory neurotransmitter do to the next cell?
a: It makes it harder to excite
It triggers an action potential immediately
It passes the signal on faster
119616.e: Inhibitory messengers such as GABA or glycine usually open chloride channels. The next cell moves further away from the threshold for an action potential.
119616.m: Inhibitory messengers slow down the next cell.

119617.q: What is a small depolarisation of the next cell caused by an excitatory transmitter called?
119617.e: EPSP stands for excitatory postsynaptic potential. Several EPSPs can add up over time and space until the threshold for an action potential is reached.
119617.m: An EPSP brings the next cell closer to the threshold.

119618.q: Which gas acts as an unusual messenger in the nervous system and is not stored in vesicles?
119618.e: Nitric oxide (NO) is made when needed and diffuses freely through membranes. It can even act backwards, from the receiving cell to the sending cell.
119618.m: Nitric oxide is a gaseous messenger.

119619.q: From which amino acid is dopamine made in the body?
119619.e: Tyrosine is first hydroxylated by the enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase, then dopamine is formed in a second step. The body can also make tyrosine from phenylalanine.
119619.m: Dopamine is made from the amino acid tyrosine.

119620.q: In which brain structure do mainly dopamine-producing nerve cells die in Parkinson's disease?
119620.e: The dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra in the midbrain control movement through the striatum. When they die, tremor, muscle stiffness and slowness of movement develop.
119620.m: In Parkinson's, dopaminergic cells in the substantia nigra die.

119621.q: Where does dopamine act as a messenger in the nervous system?
a: At the synapses between nerve cells
119621.e: Dopamine is released at synapses and binds to receptors on the next nerve cell. In this way it passes on signals.
119621.m: Dopamine passes on signals at synapses.

119622.q: Why are Parkinson's patients given L-dopa instead of dopamine directly?
a: Dopamine does not pass the blood-brain barrier.
Dopamine is poisonous in the stomach.
119622.e: Dopamine itself hardly gets from the blood into the brain. L-dopa is taken up by a transporter and only converted into dopamine in the brain.
119622.m: L-dopa smuggles dopamine across the blood-brain barrier.

119623.q: Which brain system that uses dopamine is especially linked to reward and motivation?
119623.e: Dopaminergic neurons run from the midbrain to the nucleus accumbens. This reward system also plays an important role in addiction.
119623.m: The mesolimbic system is the brain's reward system.

119624.q: Which messenger is made in the body directly from dopamine?
119624.e: The enzyme dopamine beta-hydroxylase converts dopamine into noradrenaline. Adrenaline can in turn be made from noradrenaline.
119624.m: Dopamine is the precursor of noradrenaline.

119625.q: Which group of substances does dopamine belong to?
119625.e: Dopamine contains a catechol ring with two hydroxyl groups and an amino group. Like noradrenaline and adrenaline, it counts as a catecholamine.

119626.q: How do many drugs such as cocaine act on the brain's reward system?
a: They increase the amount of dopamine at the synapses
They immediately destroy all nerve cells
119626.e: Cocaine stops dopamine from being taken back up into the nerve cell. The reward system is strongly stimulated, which can contribute to addiction.
119626.m: Many drugs work through an excess of dopamine.

119627.q: From which amino acid is serotonin made?
119627.e: Tryptophan is converted into 5-hydroxytryptophan and then decarboxylated to serotonin. Tryptophan is an essential amino acid from food.

119628.q: What job does serotonin have in the brain?
a: It acts as a messenger between nerve cells
It forms the sheath of nerve fibres
119628.e: Serotonin is a neurotransmitter. It is released at synapses and influences mood, sleep and appetite, among other things.
119628.m: Serotonin is a messenger in the nervous system.

119629.q: Where is most of the serotonin in the human body?
119629.e: By far the largest part is made by enterochromaffin cells in the gut lining. There it stimulates gut movement.
119629.m: Most serotonin is in the gut.

119630.q: What does the drug group SSRI stand for?
119630.e: SSRIs block the transporter that takes serotonin back from the synaptic cleft. They are mainly used against depression.
119630.m: SSRIs make serotonin work longer in the synaptic cleft.

119631.q: Which mental illness is a lack of serotonin often linked with?
119631.e: Many medicines against depression increase the amount of serotonin in the synaptic cleft. However, the causes of depression are varied and not just a lack of serotonin.
119631.m: Serotonin plays a part in depression.

119632.q: Which hormone is made from serotonin in the pineal gland?
119632.e: In the pineal gland, serotonin is converted into melatonin, mainly at night. Melatonin influences the sleep-wake rhythm.
119632.m: The sleep hormone melatonin is made from serotonin.

119633.q: Why is serotonin often called the “happiness hormone”?
a: It is only made when you laugh
It is only made when you eat chocolate
119633.e: In the brain, serotonin affects mood, calmness and well-being. The term “happiness hormone” is, however, a big simplification.

119634.q: Why does serotonin from food hardly affect your mood?
a: It does not get through the blood-brain barrier
It is completely destroyed in the mouth
It is not found in any food
119634.e: The blood-brain barrier protects the brain and hardly lets serotonin from the blood through. The brain therefore has to make its own serotonin from tryptophan.
119634.m: The brain makes its own serotonin.

119635.q: What is a node of Ranvier?
a: a gap between two sections of myelin
a ring of synapses on the cell body
a bundle of glial cells in the cortex
119635.e: The myelin sheath does not cover the axon without gaps. At the nodes, the axon membrane is exposed.
119635.m: At the node, the axon membrane is exposed without myelin.

119636.q: Who is the node of Ranvier named after?
119636.e: The Frenchman Louis-Antoine Ranvier described the constrictions in the 1870s. He was a doctor and histologist in Paris.
119636.m: Louis-Antoine Ranvier gave the node its name.

119637.q: Which ion channels are found especially densely at the nodes of Ranvier?
119637.e: The high density of sodium channels allows a new action potential to be created at every node. Under the myelin, by contrast, there are hardly any such channels.
119637.m: Nodes are densely packed with sodium channels.

119638.q: How do the nodes of Ranvier affect the conduction of nerve signals?
a: The signal jumps from node to node and so becomes faster
The signal is stopped at every node
The signal becomes slower at the nodes
The signal runs backwards at the nodes
119638.e: New action potentials only form at the nodes; the myelin insulates in between. This jumping, saltatory conduction is much faster than in fibres without myelin.
119638.m: Thanks to the nodes, the signal jumps quickly along the axon.

119639.q: What is the myelinated section of an axon between two nodes of Ranvier called?
119639.e: Between every two nodes there is an internode. It is wrapped by a single myelin-forming cell.
119639.m: An internode lies between two nodes.

119640.q: In the peripheral nervous system, a node lies between two cells of which type?
119640.e: In the peripheral nervous system, each Schwann cell forms a piece of myelin around an axon. Where two Schwann cells meet, a node forms.
119640.m: In peripheral nerves, Schwann cells form the myelin between the nodes.

119641.q: In which group of animals are nodes of Ranvier typically found?
119641.e: Myelinated axons with nodes are a feature of vertebrates. Most invertebrates have no comparable myelin.

119642.q: Which disease destroys myelin sheaths in the brain and spinal cord and so disturbs conduction between the nodes?
119642.e: In multiple sclerosis, the immune system attacks the myelin. The signal can then no longer jump properly from node to node, causing paralysis or vision problems.
119642.m: In multiple sclerosis the myelin is damaged.

119643.q: What does the Latin word “saltare”, from which “saltatory” comes, mean?
119643.e: The signal seems to jump from node to node. Hence the name saltatory conduction.

119644.q: Roughly how fast can fast myelinated nerve fibres in humans conduct?
119644.e: Thick, well myelinated fibres reach around 100 metres per second. That is about 360 km/h.
119644.m: Myelinated fibres conduct at up to about 100 metres per second.

119645.q: What is conduction in axons without a myelin sheath called?
119645.e: Without myelin, a new action potential has to form at every point of the membrane. The signal therefore travels on without gaps and slowly.

119646.q: Roughly how fast do thin unmyelinated C fibres conduct in humans?
119646.e: Thin fibres without myelin only conduct at about 0.5 to 2 m/s. They carry, for example, dull, slow pain.
119646.m: Unmyelinated C fibres are slow lines.

119647.q: What energy advantage does saltatory conduction have?
a: Fewer ions have to be pumped back.
No ATP is needed at all any more.
The nerve cell needs no oxygen.
119647.e: Because ions only flow at the nodes, the overall ion exchange is much smaller. The sodium-potassium pump therefore has less work to do.

119648.q: What physical effect does the myelin sheath have on the axon?
a: It conducts current like a wire.
119648.e: Myelin consists of many layers of lipids and increases membrane resistance. At the same time it lowers capacitance, so the signal is passed on passively far and fast.
119648.m: Myelin works like the insulation on a cable.

119649.q: How do squid without myelin achieve fast conduction for their escape reaction?
a: through a very large axon diameter
119649.e: A thicker axon has a lower internal resistance, so current flows further. The squid's giant axon can be up to about one millimetre thick.
119649.m: Without myelin, only a thick axon helps for fast conduction.

119650.q: A signal travels at 100 m/s along a nerve fibre 1 m long. How long does it take?
119650.e: Time is distance divided by speed: 1 m / 100 m/s = 0.01 s. That is 10 milliseconds.
119650.m: At 100 metres per second, a signal takes ten milliseconds for one metre.

119651.q: Glial cells wrap many nerve fibres in a fatty sheath. What is this sheath called?
119651.e: The myelin sheath insulates the nerve fibre electrically. As a result, the signal jumps from node to node and is passed on much faster.
119651.m: The myelin sheath made by glial cells speeds up nerve conduction.

119652.q: What job do glial cells have in the nervous system in general?
a: They support, supply and protect the nerve cells
They carry all sensory signals to the brain on their own
They form the bones of the skull
They carry oxygen in the blood
119652.e: Glial cells hold the nerve cells in place, supply them with nutrients, insulate nerve fibres and fight off germs.
119652.m: Glial cells are the helper cells of the nerve cells.

119653.q: Glial cells called astrocytes help build a protective barrier of the brain. What is it called?
119653.e: The blood-brain barrier only lets certain substances from the blood into the brain. Astrocytes wrap the brain's blood vessels with their end feet.
119653.m: The blood-brain barrier protects the brain from many substances in the blood.

119654.q: Certain glial cells line the cavities of the brain and spinal cord. Which fluid fills these cavities?
119654.e: Cerebrospinal fluid fills the ventricles of the brain and surrounds the brain and spinal cord. It cushions knocks and transports substances.
119654.m: Cerebrospinal fluid fills the cavities of the brain.

119655.q: What does the Greek word “glia”, from which the name glial cell comes, mean?
119655.e: Glial cells used to be thought of as a kind of putty holding the neurons together. Today we know that they have many active jobs.

119656.q: Which scientist coined the term neuroglia as “nerve putty” in the 19th century?
119656.e: In the middle of the 19th century, the Berlin pathologist Rudolf Virchow described a connecting substance between the nerve cells. He called it neuroglia.
119656.m: Rudolf Virchow gave neuroglia its name.

119657.q: What is a brain tumour that starts from glial cells called?
119657.e: Gliomas arise from abnormal glial cells such as astrocytes or oligodendrocytes. Glioblastoma is an especially malignant form.
119657.m: A glioma is a tumour of glial cells.

119658.q: According to newer estimates, what is the ratio of glial cells to nerve cells in the human brain?
a: about ten times more glial cells
about a hundred times more glial cells
about ten times fewer glial cells
119658.e: For a long time it was assumed that there were ten times more glial cells than neurons. Newer counts give a ratio of roughly one to one for the whole brain.
119658.m: The brain has about as many glial cells as nerve cells.

119659.q: According to a well-known learning rule, what happens to the connection between two nerve cells that are often active at the same time?
119659.e: The psychologist Donald Hebb described this rule in 1949. In short: “cells that fire together, wire together”. This is how firm connections form when we learn.
119659.m: Nerve cells active together strengthen their connection.

119660.q: What happens to a synapse that is used often and strongly during learning?
119660.e: Frequently used synapses become more effective over hours to weeks. Experts call this long-term potentiation; it is considered the basis of learning.

119661.q: Which brain region is especially important for forming new memories?
119661.e: The hippocampus lies deep in the temporal lobe. If it is damaged on both sides, people can hardly store new memories any more.
119661.m: The hippocampus helps form new memories.

119662.q: What mainly changes in the brain when we learn something new?
119662.e: When we learn, synapses are strengthened, weakened or newly formed. This ability to change is called neuroplasticity.
119662.m: Learning changes the connections between nerve cells.

119663.q: According to current knowledge, can the adult brain still make new nerve cells?
a: Yes, but only in a few regions such as the hippocampus
Yes, everywhere and in large numbers
Only in the cerebellum during sleep
119663.e: Newly formed neurons have been found in adults in a part of the hippocampus. How much new formation there is in humans is still being researched.
119663.m: Even the adult brain makes new neurons in a few regions.

119664.q: What is a time window in development called in which the brain is especially easy to shape for certain experiences?
119664.e: Hubel and Wiesel showed that an eye covered during an early phase can later hardly use the visual cortex. Similar time windows exist, for example, for learning languages.
119664.m: In critical periods the brain is especially easy to shape.

119665.q: Can synapses also become weaker on purpose during learning?
119665.e: Besides strengthening, there is also a lasting weakening of synapses, called long-term depression. Together they allow networks to be fine-tuned.
119665.m: Synapses can also be weakened on purpose.

119666.q: Which phenomenon after an amputation is linked with a reorganisation of the cerebral cortex?
119666.e: After an amputation, neighbouring areas of the body map in the cortex take over the area that has become free. This reorganisation can cause sensations in the missing limb.
119666.m: Phantom pain shows how the cerebral cortex reorganises itself.

119667.q: Who first recorded an electroencephalogram of a human in Jena in 1924?
119667.e: The psychiatrist Hans Berger recorded brain waves in 1924 and published them in 1929. He also introduced the name electroencephalogram.
119667.m: Hans Berger is considered the inventor of the EEG.

119668.q: Which waves does the EEG typically show when you are relaxed and awake with your eyes closed?
119668.e: Alpha waves of about 8 to 13 Hz occur when you are calmly awake with your eyes closed. When you open your eyes, they usually become weaker.
119668.m: Relaxed with eyes closed, the EEG shows alpha waves.

119669.q: Which EEG waves below 4 Hz are typical of deep sleep?
119669.e: Delta waves are slow waves with a high amplitude. They mark the deepest stages of sleep.
119669.m: In deep sleep, slow delta waves dominate.

119670.q: Which EEG waves of about 13 to 30 Hz occur during focused mental activity?
119670.e: Beta waves have a higher frequency and a smaller amplitude. They show an active, attentive brain.
119670.m: Focused thinking produces fast beta waves.

119671.q: According to which international system are EEG electrodes arranged on the scalp?
119671.e: In the 10-20 system, the electrodes are placed at distances of 10 or 20 per cent of certain distances across the head. This makes measurements comparable for different head sizes.
119671.m: The 10-20 system sets the electrode positions.

119672.q: In which order of magnitude is the voltage of EEG signals measured on the scalp?
119672.e: The signals are only a few to about a hundred microvolts strong. That is why sensitive amplifiers are needed.
119672.m: EEG signals are tiny voltages in the microvolt range.

119673.q: For diagnosing which disease is the EEG especially important?
119673.e: In epilepsy, the EEG often shows typical spikes and sharp waves. This makes it possible to identify where seizures start and what kind they are.
119673.m: The EEG is a key tool in epilepsy.

119674.q: What does an EEG with electrodes on the scalp record?
a: The electrical activity of many nerve cells of the cerebral cortex
The blood flow in the brain's vessels
The oxygen content in the brain
The tension of the neck muscles
119674.e: Nerve cells of the cerebral cortex produce tiny electric currents when they work. When very many are active at the same time, their sum can be measured on the scalp as a brain wave curve.
119674.m: The EEG measures the brain waves of many nerve cells at once.

119675.q: What kind of disease is multiple sclerosis?
119675.e: In MS, the body's own immune system attacks the myelin sheaths. This creates areas of inflammation and scars.
119675.m: In MS, the immune system turns against the body's own nervous system.

119676.q: Which part of the nervous system is affected in multiple sclerosis?
a: only the nerves of the skin
119676.e: MS affects the central nervous system, meaning the brain, spinal cord and optic nerves. Peripheral nerves are usually spared.
119676.m: MS is a disease of the central nervous system.

119677.q: Roughly what is the ratio of women to men in multiple sclerosis?
a: Women are affected about 2 to 3 times more often.
Men are affected about 3 times more often.
Both are affected exactly equally often.
119677.e: Like many autoimmune diseases, MS affects women much more often. The reasons for this are not yet fully understood.
119677.m: MS affects far more women than men.

119678.q: Which course of multiple sclerosis is most common at the start?
119678.e: In most patients, relapses occur first, which clear up completely or partly. Later this can turn into a progressive course.

119679.q: Which imaging method shows MS lesions in the brain best?
119679.e: On MRI, the areas of inflammation in the white matter are clearly visible. It is therefore central to diagnosis and to checking how the disease develops.

119680.q: At what age does multiple sclerosis usually begin?
119680.e: The disease usually appears in young adulthood. It is a common cause of neurological disability in young adults.
119680.m: MS often begins in young adulthood.

119681.q: Why can MS symptoms temporarily get worse in the heat, for example in a hot bath?
a: Damaged nerve fibres conduct even worse when warm
Heat thins the blood in the brain
119681.e: In fibres with a damaged myelin sheath, conduction becomes less reliable at higher temperatures. When the body cools down, the symptoms improve again.
119681.m: In MS, heat can make symptoms worse for a short time.

119682.q: Which inflammation is a common first sign of multiple sclerosis?
119682.e: Optic neuritis causes blurred vision and pain when moving the eyes. In many patients it is the first symptom.
119682.m: Optic nerve inflammation can be the first sign of MS.

119980.q: In which lobe of the brain is the prefrontal cortex?
119980.e: The prefrontal cortex forms the very front part of the frontal lobe, directly behind the forehead.
119980.m: The prefrontal cortex is at the very front of the frontal lobe.

119981.q: Which abilities are mainly linked to the prefrontal cortex?
119981.e: The prefrontal cortex controls the so-called executive functions. These include planning actions, making decisions and holding back sudden impulses.
119981.m: The prefrontal cortex is the brain's planning and control centre.

119982.q: Which railway worker survived an iron rod through his frontal lobe in 1848 and afterwards changed a lot in personality?
119982.e: During a blast, an iron rod pierced Phineas Gage's skull. He survived, but was afterwards described as uncontrolled and erratic, which pointed to the role of the frontal lobe in social behaviour.
119982.m: The case of Phineas Gage showed that the frontal lobe helps shape personality.

119983.q: According to current knowledge, up to roughly what age does the prefrontal cortex mature?
