119983.e: The prefrontal cortex is one of the brain regions that mature last. The rebuilding processes last into young adulthood, until about the mid-20s.
119983.m: The prefrontal cortex is one of the last brain areas to finish developing.

119984.q: Which memory system, which holds and works on information for a short time, depends strongly on the prefrontal cortex?
119984.e: In working memory, information is kept active for seconds, for example during mental arithmetic. Imaging studies show strong activity in the prefrontal cortex at such times.
119984.m: During mental arithmetic, working memory is busy in the frontal lobe.

119985.q: Why is leucotomy, in which nerve pathways to the frontal lobe were cut, now seen as a dark chapter of medicine?
a: It often changed personality and drive severely and permanently
It was too expensive for hospitals
119985.e: The operation made many patients calmer, but often also listless and without drive. Despite a Nobel Prize for Egas Moniz in 1949, it is no longer used today.
119985.m: Leucotomy is now seen as a warning example in medical history.

119986.q: Which messenger is especially important for the prefrontal cortex and is boosted by ADHD medicines such as methylphenidate?
119986.e: Methylphenidate blocks the reuptake of dopamine and noradrenaline. This raises their concentration in the gap between the nerve cells, which can improve attention and impulse control.
119986.m: Methylphenidate increases the amount of dopamine between nerve cells.

119987.q: What is the part of the prefrontal cortex directly above the eye sockets that evaluates rewards called?
119987.e: Orbit is the technical term for the eye socket. The orbitofrontal cortex lies above it and is involved in decisions and in evaluating rewards.
119987.m: The orbitofrontal cortex lies above the eye sockets.

119988.q: Where does the hippocampus get its name from?
a: From the name of its discoverer
From the Latin word for memory
119988.e: Hippocampus is the Greek-Latin name for the seahorse. The curved part of the brain looks like this animal.
119988.m: The hippocampus looks like a seahorse.

119989.q: In which lobe of the brain is the hippocampus?
119989.e: The hippocampus lies on both sides in the inner part of the temporal lobe.
119989.m: The hippocampus sits deep in the temporal lobe.

119990.q: What did the famous patient “H. M.”, who had parts of both hippocampi removed in 1953, show?
a: The hippocampus is needed to form new memories
Without a hippocampus you can no longer see
119990.e: After the operation, H. M. could no longer remember new experiences permanently. Old memories and skills, however, were largely kept.
119990.m: The patient H. M. showed that the hippocampus stores new memories.

119991.q: Which technical term for part of the hippocampus recalls the ram's horns of an Egyptian god?
119991.e: The main part of the hippocampus is called cornu Ammonis, meaning Ammon's horn. Its curled shape recalls the ram's horn of the god Amun.
119991.m: Because of its shape, the hippocampus is also called Ammon's horn.

119992.q: Which cells in the hippocampus, whose discovery earned John O'Keefe the Nobel Prize in 2014, are active in particular places?
119992.e: Place cells fire when an animal is at a particular spot in space. They form a kind of inner map.
119992.m: Place cells in the hippocampus form an inner map.

119993.q: During which phase are memories transferred from the hippocampus to the cerebral cortex especially intensely?
119993.e: In deep sleep, content stored in the hippocampus during the day is replayed. This gradually consolidates it in the cerebral cortex.
119993.m: In deep sleep the brain consolidates what it has learnt.

119994.q: What is meant by adult neurogenesis, which is studied in the hippocampus?
a: The formation of new nerve cells in adulthood
The death of nerve cells in old age
The development of the brain in the embryo
The healing of bones after a fracture
119994.e: For a long time it was believed that no new nerve cells form in the adult brain. New formation has been found in the hippocampus, but how much happens in humans is disputed.
119994.m: New nerve cells can form in the hippocampus even in adulthood.

119995.q: Which sign is typical when the hippocampus is damaged early in Alzheimer's?
119995.e: In Alzheimer's, the hippocampus is one of the first brain regions affected. That is why gaps in short-term memory are noticed first.
119995.m: Alzheimer's damages the hippocampus early and with it remembering new things.

119996.q: What does the Greek name amygdala mean?
119996.e: Amygdala is the Greek word for almond. The structure is an almond-shaped group of nuclei in the temporal lobe.
119996.m: Because of its shape, the amygdala is named after the almond.

119997.q: Which feeling is the amygdala most closely linked with?
119997.e: The amygdala checks stimuli for danger in a flash and triggers fear and startle reactions. However, it is also involved in other feelings.
119997.m: The amygdala raises the alarm when there is danger.

119998.q: What did the patient “S. M.”, whose two amygdalae had been destroyed by a rare disease, show?
119998.e: S. M. had the rare Urbach-Wiethe syndrome. Even in dangerous situations she showed hardly any fear, which proves the role of the amygdala in fear.
119998.m: Without the amygdala, the feeling of fear is largely missing.

119999.q: Which functional system of the brain is the amygdala counted as part of?
119999.e: The limbic system processes feelings and is involved in memory. The amygdala and hippocampus, among others, are counted as part of it.
119999.m: The amygdala belongs to the limbic system of feelings.

120000.q: Which brain structure works closely with the amygdala in fear to store memories of dangerous experiences?
120000.e: The amygdala gives memories their emotional colour, the hippocampus stores the context. That is why frightening experiences are often remembered especially well.
120000.m: The amygdala and hippocampus store fear memories together.

120001.q: Why do you often get a fright even before you have consciously recognised a danger?
a: A fast nerve pathway reports stimuli directly to the amygdala
The cerebellum recognises dangers faster than the eyes
The muscles react entirely without the brain
The heart first sends a warning signal to the brain
120001.e: Some sensory stimuli reach the amygdala on a short, rough route, others more slowly through the cerebral cortex. That is why you flinch before you know exactly what is going on.
120001.m: The amygdala reacts to danger before we consciously recognise it.

120002.q: Which form of learning, in which a neutral stimulus is linked with an unpleasant event, depends especially on the amygdala?
120002.e: In fear conditioning, for example, a tone alone causes fear after being paired several times with a frightening stimulus. Without a working amygdala, this link can hardly be made.
120002.m: The amygdala learns which stimuli signal danger.

120003.q: Which stress hormone does the adrenal cortex release when the amygdala starts a hormone chain through the hypothalamus and pituitary during stress?
120003.e: The amygdala activates the hypothalamus, which stimulates the adrenal cortex through the pituitary. This then releases the stress hormone cortisol.
120003.m: Under stress, the amygdala starts a hormone chain that reaches the adrenal cortex.

120004.q: What is the main job of the thalamus?
a: To filter sensory information and pass it on to the cerebral cortex
To learn the fine-tuning of movements
120004.e: The thalamus is a relay station: almost all sensory signals pass through it to the cerebral cortex. That is why it is also called the “gateway to consciousness”.
120004.m: The thalamus is the gateway to consciousness.

120005.q: Which part of the brain does the thalamus belong to?
120005.e: The thalamus is the largest part of the diencephalon. It lies deep inside between the cerebrum and the brainstem.
120005.m: The thalamus is the largest part of the diencephalon.

120006.q: Which is the only sense that is not mainly passed to the cerebral cortex through the thalamus?
120006.e: Smell information goes from the olfactory bulb directly to the olfactory cortex without first being relayed in the thalamus. All other senses pass through the thalamus.
120006.m: Only smells take the direct route past the thalamus relay station.

120007.q: Through which brain structure do signals from the retina reach the visual cortex in the occipital lobe?
120007.e: The fibres of the optic nerve are relayed in a nucleus of the thalamus, the lateral geniculate body. From there the visual pathways run to the visual cortex.
120007.m: Visual information is also relayed in the thalamus.

120008.q: In a rare prion disease, mainly the thalamus is destroyed. Which ability do people affected increasingly lose?
120008.e: In fatal familial insomnia, misfolded prions mainly destroy nuclei of the thalamus. The people affected increasingly lose the ability to sleep.
120008.m: Without an intact thalamus, sleep can break down.

120009.q: What does the Greek word “thalamos” mean?
120009.e: In Ancient Greek, thalamos meant an inner room or a bedroom. The name suits its hidden position deep in the brain.
120009.m: The thalamus is named after an inner chamber.

120010.q: What can occur on the opposite side of the body after a stroke in the thalamus?
a: Severe pain that is hard to treat
A loss of the sense of smell
120010.e: In thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome), people suffer severe pain on the opposite side of the body after a thalamic stroke, because the thalamus processes sensory signals wrongly.
120010.m: Damage to the thalamus can cause agonising pain.

120011.q: Which method can reduce severe shaking of the hands by having an electrode in the thalamus influence nerve cells electrically?
120011.e: In deep brain stimulation, a thin electrode is placed in a nucleus of the thalamus. Weak electrical pulses can clearly reduce severe shaking, for example in essential tremor.
120011.m: Electrodes in the thalamus can reduce severe shaking.

120012.q: What are the basal ganglia mainly responsible for?
120012.e: The basal ganglia are groups of nuclei deep in the cerebrum. In loops with the cerebral cortex, they promote intended movements and hold back unwanted ones.
120012.m: The basal ganglia choose which movement is carried out.

120013.q: Where in the brain are the basal ganglia?
a: On the surface of the cerebellum
120013.e: The basal ganglia are clusters of nerve cells deep in the cerebrum, below the cortex. They are closely linked through loops with the cerebral cortex and the thalamus.
120013.m: The basal ganglia lie deep in the cerebrum.

120014.q: For which disease of the basal ganglia is deep brain stimulation with implanted electrodes often used?
120014.e: In deep brain stimulation, an electrode is placed permanently in a nucleus of the basal ganglia. In many people with Parkinson's, this eases stiffness and tremor.
120014.m: Deep brain stimulation helps many people with Parkinson's.

120015.q: In which inherited disease with involuntary, sweeping movements do mainly nerve cells in the striatum die?
120015.e: Huntington's disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant way. The loss of nerve cells in the striatum leads to excessive, dance-like movements.
120015.m: Huntington's disease damages the striatum and causes involuntary movements.

120016.q: Which system in the brain, which also includes parts of the basal ganglia, plays a central role in addiction?
120016.e: Part of the basal ganglia belongs to the reward system. Addictive substances activate this system especially strongly, which is why people want them again and again.
120016.m: Addiction is closely linked to the reward system in the brain.

120017.q: Which part of the basal ganglia is called “pale globe” in translation?
120017.e: Globus means globe, pallidus means pale. The globus pallidus looks lighter than its surroundings because of many myelinated fibres.
120017.m: The globus pallidus is the pale globe of the basal ganglia.

120018.q: Which form of learning is especially linked with the basal ganglia?
120018.e: When actions are repeated often, the basal ganglia increasingly take over their control. That is how routines such as brushing your teeth become automatic habits.
120018.m: Habits are anchored in the basal ganglia.

120019.q: Which disorder with motor and vocal tics is linked with a malfunction of the basal ganglia?
120019.e: In Tourette syndrome, involuntary movements and sounds occur. It is thought that disturbed inhibition in the loops of the basal ganglia contributes to this.
120019.m: In Tourette syndrome, the movement selection of the basal ganglia is disturbed.

120020.q: Which messenger is missing in Parkinson's because the cells that make it for the basal ganglia die?
120020.e: In Parkinson's, nerve cells in the substantia nigra that supply dopamine to the basal ganglia die. Without dopamine, movements become slow and stiff.
120020.m: In Parkinson's, the basal ganglia lack dopamine.

120021.q: What job does the corpus callosum have in the brain?
a: It connects the two halves of the brain
It protects the brain from knocks
120021.e: The corpus callosum is a thick bundle of nerve fibres. Through it, the left and right halves of the brain exchange information.
120021.m: The corpus callosum connects the two halves of the brain.

120022.q: Which syndrome, in which one hand seems to act on its own, can occur after damage to the corpus callosum?
120022.e: In alien hand syndrome, one hand carries out movements that the person does not intend. It can occur after the corpus callosum is cut or after other brain damage.
120022.m: After damage to the corpus callosum, a hand can seem controlled by someone else.

120023.q: Roughly how many nerve fibres make up the corpus callosum?
120023.e: The corpus callosum contains about 200 to 250 million nerve fibres. This makes it by far the largest fibre connection between the hemispheres.
120023.m: Hundreds of millions of fibres connect the two halves of the brain.

120024.q: For which condition is the corpus callosum sometimes cut by surgery?
120024.e: In a callosotomy, the corpus callosum is cut so that epileptic seizures can no longer spread from one half of the brain to the other. The operation is only considered in severe cases that cannot be treated otherwise.
120024.m: Cutting the corpus callosum can stop seizures from spreading.

120025.q: In which half of the brain are the most important language centres in most people?
120025.e: In most people, especially right-handers, language is processed mainly in the left half of the brain. Experiments with split-brain patients also showed this.
120025.m: Language is usually in the left half of the brain.

120026.q: A split-brain patient sees an object only in the left visual field. What typically happens?
a: He cannot name it, but can find it by touch with his left hand
He can name it, but cannot find it by touch
He does not see the object at all
120026.e: The left visual field is processed in the right hemisphere, while language is usually on the left. Without the corpus callosum, the information does not reach the language centre, but the right half of the brain can control the left hand.
120026.m: Without the corpus callosum, the speaking half of the brain does not know what the other half sees.

120027.q: What was special about the brain of Kim Peek, the real person behind the film “Rain Man”?
a: He had only one brain hemisphere
120027.e: Kim Peek was born with agenesis of the corpus callosum, meaning without a corpus callosum. He had an extraordinary memory for thousands of books.
120027.m: Kim Peek lived without a corpus callosum and had an enormous memory.

120028.q: What is the corpus callosum mainly made of?
120028.e: The corpus callosum is made of nerve fibres wrapped in a fatty myelin layer. This makes the tissue look white.
120028.m: The corpus callosum is a large bundle of white matter.

120029.q: Who is Broca's area named after?
120029.e: In 1861 the French doctor Paul Broca described a patient who had lost the ability to speak and had damage in the left frontal lobe. The region has carried his name ever since.
120029.m: In 1861 Paul Broca found a speech centre in the frontal lobe.

120030.q: In which brain hemisphere is Broca's area located in most right-handed people?
120030.e: In over 90 per cent of right-handed people, language is mainly based in the left hemisphere. Broca's area lies there in the lower frontal lobe.
120030.m: In most people, language sits on the left.

120031.q: What could Broca's famous patient still do fairly well despite losing his speech?
120031.e: The patient could hardly speak any more but understood much of what was said to him. From this Broca concluded that speaking is controlled by its own area of the brain.
120031.m: When Broca's area is damaged, understanding is often preserved.

120032.q: How does a person with Broca's aphasia typically speak?
120032.e: In Broca's aphasia, producing speech is a struggle and there is little grammar. Understanding language, on the other hand, is usually fairly well preserved.
120032.m: In Broca's aphasia, speaking is laborious and choppy.

120033.q: Which language centre is mainly responsible for understanding language?
120033.e: Broca's area in the frontal lobe mainly controls speaking. Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe is especially important for understanding language.

120034.q: Because of its main disorder, what is Broca's aphasia also called?
120034.e: Broca's aphasia mainly affects the production of speech. That is why it is also called motor or expressive aphasia.
120034.m: Broca's aphasia mainly disturbs speaking itself.

120035.q: What is the most common cause of a sudden loss of language (aphasia) in adults?
120035.e: In a stroke, part of the brain no longer receives blood. If it hits the language centres in the left hemisphere, aphasia can suddenly occur.
120035.m: A stroke can suddenly take away a person's language.

120036.q: What is the leaving out of function words and endings, typical of Broca's aphasia, called?
120036.e: In agrammatism, sentences consist mainly of content words, such as “Me hospital go”. Small words and grammatical endings are missing.
120036.m: Agrammatism is language without the building blocks of grammar.

120037.q: Which doctor described the language centre in the temporal lobe named after him in 1874?
120037.e: In 1874 the German neurologist Carl Wernicke described patients who spoke fluently but hardly understood language. He linked this to a region in the temporal lobe.
120037.m: Carl Wernicke discovered the centre for understanding language.

a: In the rear part of the upper temporal gyrus
In the occipital lobe near the visual cortex
120038.e: Wernicke's area usually lies in the left hemisphere in the rear section of the superior temporal gyrus, close to the auditory cortex.
120038.m: Wernicke's area lies near the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.

a: A language disorder after brain damage
120039.e: In aphasia, understanding, speaking, reading or writing are disturbed because language centres in the brain are damaged. The voice and hearing are usually fine.
120039.m: Aphasia is a language disorder caused by brain damage.

120040.q: How does a person with Wernicke's aphasia typically speak?
120040.e: In Wernicke's aphasia, speech flows but contains wrong or invented words. Those affected often do not notice their mistakes because their understanding is impaired.
120040.m: In Wernicke's aphasia, people say a lot but little of it makes sense.

120041.q: What is a common cause of Wernicke's aphasia?
120041.e: Usually a stroke damages the language centre in the temporal lobe. With a broken jaw or diseased vocal cords, only the mechanics of speaking are disturbed, not the understanding of language.
120041.m: Wernicke's aphasia is often caused by a stroke.

120042.q: Which second language centre is mainly responsible for speaking?
120042.e: Broca's area in the frontal lobe mainly controls the production of speech. Wernicke's area, by contrast, is important for understanding language.
120042.m: Broca stands for speaking, Wernicke for understanding.

120043.q: In which brain hemisphere are the language centres located in most people?
120043.e: In most right-handed people and also in many left-handed people, Broca's and Wernicke's areas lie in the left hemisphere.
120043.m: The language centres are usually in the left hemisphere.

120044.q: What does a person with Wernicke's aphasia find especially difficult?
120044.e: Wernicke's area is responsible for understanding language. If it is damaged, those affected understand poorly what they hear, even though their hearing is good.
120044.m: In Wernicke's aphasia, mainly understanding is impaired.

120045.q: Who is Alzheimer's disease named after?
120045.e: In 1906 the German psychiatrist Alois Alzheimer described the typical changes in the brain of a patient with severe forgetfulness.
120045.m: Alzheimer's disease bears the name of Alois Alzheimer.

120046.q: Which deposits outside the nerve cells are typical of Alzheimer's disease?
120046.e: Fragments of the protein beta-amyloid clump together between nerve cells to form plaques. Together with tau fibrils, they are considered a hallmark of the disease.
120046.m: In Alzheimer's, beta-amyloid clumps between the nerve cells.

120047.q: Which protein forms the typical fibre bundles inside nerve cells in Alzheimer's?
120047.e: Tau protein normally stabilises the cell skeleton. In Alzheimer's it is altered and clumps into neurofibrillary tangles that damage nerve cells.
120047.m: Clumped tau protein destroys nerve cells from the inside in Alzheimer's.

120048.q: According to the WHO, roughly what share of all cases of dementia is Alzheimer's disease?
120048.e: The World Health Organization estimates that Alzheimer's makes up 60 to 70 per cent of all dementia cases. This makes it the most common form of dementia.
120048.m: Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia.

120049.q: Which ability is usually affected first in Alzheimer's disease?
120049.e: The disease usually begins in brain regions around the hippocampus. That is why those affected first find it hard to remember recent events, while old memories last longer.
120049.m: Alzheimer's usually starts with forgetting new things.

120050.q: Which risk factor increases the likelihood of Alzheimer's disease the most?
120050.e: The risk rises considerably with every decade of life. Genes, high blood pressure and lack of exercise also play a role.
120050.m: Age is the biggest risk factor for Alzheimer's.

120051.q: Which group of drugs is used to treat the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease?
120051.e: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil slow the breakdown of the messenger substance acetylcholine. They can ease the symptoms for a while but do not cure the disease.
120051.m: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors ease Alzheimer's but do not cure it.

120052.q: Which brain structure, important for storing new memories, is damaged early in Alzheimer's?
120052.e: The hippocampus transfers new experiences into long-term memory. Because it is affected early, those affected forget new things first.
120052.m: In Alzheimer's, the hippocampus suffers early.

120053.q: Which English doctor described the “shaking palsy” in an essay in 1817?
120053.e: James Parkinson published “An Essay on the Shaking Palsy” in 1817. The disease was later named after him.
120053.m: James Parkinson described the shaking palsy in 1817.

120054.q: What are drugs called that directly imitate the effect of dopamine at its receptors in Parkinson's?
120054.e: An agonist activates a receptor just like the natural messenger substance. Dopamine agonists thus partly replace the missing dopamine.
120054.m: Dopamine agonists act on the receptors like dopamine.

120055.q: What is the main Parkinson's symptom of slowed movements called?
120055.e: Brady means slow, kinesia means movement. Those affected start movements with a delay, walk with small steps and have a quiet voice and small handwriting.
120055.m: Bradykinesia is the typical slowing of movement in Parkinson's.

120056.q: When does the typical tremor in Parkinson's disease mainly occur?
120056.e: The Parkinson's tremor is a resting tremor that often fades during purposeful movements. Because of the finger movement it is also called a pill-rolling tremor.
120056.m: Parkinson's tremor shows mainly when the hand is resting.

120057.q: Which actor founded one of the largest foundations for Parkinson's research after his diagnosis?
120057.e: Michael J. Fox was diagnosed in 1991 at a young age. In 2000 he founded the Michael J. Fox Foundation, which funds research into Parkinson's.
120057.m: Michael J. Fox campaigns for Parkinson's research.

120058.q: Which messenger substance is lacking in the brain in Parkinson's disease?
120058.e: In Parkinson's, nerve cells in the substantia nigra that produce dopamine die. The shortage disrupts the control of movement.
120058.m: In Parkinson's, the brain lacks dopamine.

120059.q: Which sensory disorder often appears years before the movement problems in Parkinson's?
120059.e: Many of those affected notice years before diagnosis that their sense of smell is getting worse. The smell disorder is considered an important early sign.
120059.m: A weaker sense of smell can be an early sign of Parkinson's.

120060.q: Which of these signs is one of the main symptoms of Parkinson's disease?
120060.e: Typical signs are slowed movements, a tremor at rest and muscle stiffness (rigidity). If the arm is moved passively, it often gives way in jerks, like a cogwheel.
120060.m: Muscle stiffness is a main sign of Parkinson's.

120061.q: Why is World Parkinson's Day held on 11 April?
a: Dopamine was discovered on that day
It is the day the WHO was founded
James Parkinson died on that day
120061.e: James Parkinson was born on 11 April 1755. In 1817 he was the first to describe the shaking palsy.
120061.m: World Parkinson's Day falls on James Parkinson's birthday.

120062.q: What is the Glasgow Coma Scale, used by emergency services for head injuries, for?
120062.e: The scale checks whether someone opens their eyes, speaks and moves. This allows the level of consciousness to be judged quickly and comparably.
120062.m: The Glasgow Coma Scale measures how awake a person is.

120063.q: Which sign after a fall on the head needs a doctor's examination immediately?
a: A small bump with no other symptoms
A slight scratch on the forehead
A brief headache that quickly goes away
120063.e: If someone becomes more and more drowsy after a head injury or vomits, there may be bleeding or swelling in the brain. Then you must call the emergency number at once.
120063.m: Drowsiness and vomiting after a head injury are warning signs.

120064.q: Which three areas does the Glasgow Coma Scale assess?
a: Eye opening, verbal and motor response
120064.e: It scores eye opening (1 to 4), the verbal response (1 to 5) and the best motor response (1 to 6).
120064.m: The Glasgow scale checks eyes, speech and movement.

120065.q: What is the mildest form of traumatic brain injury called?
120065.e: A concussion (commotio cerebri) is a short-term disturbance of function without detectable tissue damage. Typical symptoms are headache, nausea and gaps in memory.
120065.m: A concussion is the mildest traumatic brain injury.

120066.q: Why should someone be watched after a head injury, even if they feel well again after a short loss of consciousness?
a: Bleeding inside the skull may only show itself later
The brain no longer needs oxygen afterwards
Otherwise they might catch a cold
120066.e: With some bleeds inside the skull, those affected at first seem awake again. Only when more blood collects does their condition suddenly become worse and life-threatening.
120066.m: After a head injury, danger can still come later.

120067.q: What is bleeding beneath the tough outer membrane of the brain (dura) called?
120067.e: “Sub” means under, and a “haematoma” is a bruise or collection of blood. A subdural haematoma therefore lies under the dura, an epidural haematoma above it, right against the bone.
120067.m: A subdural haematoma is bleeding under the dura.

120068.q: What life-threatening consequence can a sharp rise in pressure inside the skull have?
a: Drying out of the cerebrospinal fluid
120068.e: Because the skull cannot give way, swelling pushes parts of the brain towards the opening at the base of the skull. If the brainstem is trapped, breathing and circulation fail.
120068.m: High pressure in the skull can trap the brainstem.

120069.q: Why is swelling of the brain particularly dangerous in adults?
a: The swelling moves into the spine
The brain then stops making nerve cells
120069.e: Because the bony skull is rigid, swelling makes the pressure inside rise sharply. This can crush brain tissue and damage vital centres.
120069.m: There is hardly any room for extra volume inside the rigid skull.

120070.q: Which progressive brain disease is seen in athletes who take many blows to the head, such as boxers?
120070.e: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy develops after repeated, often mild head injuries. In boxers it used to be called “dementia pugilistica”.
120070.m: Repeated blows to the head can damage the brain permanently.

120071.q: What was the main aim of the European Human Brain Project?
a: To research and simulate the brain with computers
To replace brain surgery with robots
120071.e: The Human Brain Project wanted to bring together knowledge about the brain and recreate it with supercomputers. This was also meant to lead to new approaches for medicine and computer science.
120071.m: The Human Brain Project wanted to understand the brain in the computer.

120072.q: Which Swiss university did the Human Brain Project start from?
120072.e: The project was coordinated from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (EPFL) and later brought together over a hundred partner institutions in Europe.
120072.m: The Human Brain Project had its origin at EPFL.

120073.q: Who mainly funded the Human Brain Project?
120073.e: The project was paid for mainly by the EU through its research programmes. The participating countries also contributed.
120073.m: The Human Brain Project was an EU research project.

120074.q: Why is a complete simulation of the human brain so difficult?
a: It has around 86 billion nerve cells with countless connections
It has only a few but huge cells
It works entirely without electrical signals
120074.e: Each nerve cell is connected to thousands of others. This enormous number of connections exceeds even the power of today's supercomputers.
120074.m: The brain is extremely complex because of its many connections.

120075.q: What total budget was originally planned for the Human Brain Project?
120075.e: The project was planned with about one billion euros over ten years, funded by the EU and the participating countries.
120075.m: The Human Brain Project was planned with around one billion euros.

120076.q: Which important result did the Human Brain Project deliver, among others?
120076.e: Researchers created digital maps of the brain showing where each brain region lies. These atlases remain available for research.
120076.m: The Human Brain Project created digital maps of the brain.

120077.q: Which earlier project at EPFL simulated parts of the rat cerebral cortex from 2005?
120077.e: The Blue Brain Project first reconstructed and simulated a cortical column of the rat on a supercomputer. It was the basis for the later Human Brain Project.
120077.m: The Blue Brain Project paved the way for the Human Brain Project.

120078.q: What happened in the Human Brain Project in 2014?
a: Hundreds of researchers criticised it in an open letter
120078.e: In an open letter to the European Commission, many neuroscientists criticised the leadership and aims of the project. Afterwards the management was reorganised.
120078.m: The Human Brain Project had to be restructured after strong criticism.

120079.q: What do neuromorphic computers, like those developed in the Human Brain Project, imitate?
120079.e: Neuromorphic chips process signals in a similar way to nerve cells, with short pulses. They use much less energy than normal computers.

120379.q: In which photoreceptors of the retina is rhodopsin the visual pigment?
120379.e: Rhodopsin is the visual pigment of the rods, which are responsible for seeing in dim light. The cones have other opsins for colour vision.
120379.m: Rhodopsin is the visual pigment of the rods.

120380.q: Which two components make up rhodopsin?
120380.e: Rhodopsin consists of the protein opsin and the light-sensitive molecule retinal bound to it. Only together can they absorb light and trigger a signal.
120380.m: Rhodopsin is made of the protein opsin and the pigment retinal.

120381.q: From which vitamin does the body make the retinal needed for vision?
120381.e: Retinal is the aldehyde form of vitamin A. A lack of vitamin A therefore leads to poor vision at dusk.
120381.m: The body needs vitamin A for the visual pigment.

120382.q: What happens to 11-cis-retinal when it absorbs a photon?
a: It is broken down into carbon dioxide
It splits into two amino acids
It binds a calcium ion tightly
120382.e: Absorbing light causes isomerisation from 11-cis to all-trans-retinal. This change of shape activates the opsin and starts the signalling cascade.

120383.q: What other name is commonly used for rhodopsin?
120383.e: In the dark, rhodopsin has a reddish purple colour and is therefore called visual purple. It bleaches in the light.
120383.m: Because of its colour, rhodopsin is also called visual purple.

120384.q: Why can we hardly see colours at night?
a: Because then almost only the rods work, and they cannot tell colours apart
Because the cones break down rhodopsin at night
Because the pupil closes at night
Because the lens becomes cloudy at night
120384.e: Cones need a lot of light. At dusk almost only the rods are working, with their single visual pigment rhodopsin. They only provide brightness, not colours.
120384.m: All cats are grey in the dark, because only the rods are working.

120385.q: Why does the eye need a few minutes to see well after going from light to dark?
a: The bleached rhodopsin first has to form again
The lens has to change shape
The cones first have to grow
The optic nerve has to cool down
120385.e: Bright light bleaches the rhodopsin of the rods. In the dark it is slowly rebuilt and the eyes become more sensitive. This is called dark adaptation.
120385.m: In the dark, the eye first has to rebuild visual purple.

120386.q: Why can you often see a faint star better at night if you look just to one side of it?
a: There are more rods at the edge of the retina
There are more rods in the centre of the retina
The lens is thicker at the edge of the retina
The star then shines more brightly
120386.e: In the centre of the retina, the yellow spot, there are almost only cones. The light-sensitive rods with rhodopsin sit mainly at the edge.
120386.m: The edge of the retina is more sensitive to faint light.

120387.q: How does the membrane potential of a rod change when exposed to light?
120387.e: When cGMP is broken down, sodium channels close and the cell becomes more negative. In the dark, by contrast, a dark current flows constantly.

120388.q: Which photoreceptors are found almost exclusively in the fovea centralis?
a: Rods and cones in equal parts
120388.e: In the fovea centralis the cones are packed most densely, and rods are largely absent. This makes it the place of the sharpest colour vision.
120388.m: The fovea centralis contains almost only cones.

120389.q: Why is visual acuity greatest in the fovea centralis?
a: Its cones are hardly linked together
Most of the blood vessels are there
The cornea is most strongly curved there
120389.e: In the fovea, almost every cone passes its signal along its own chain to a ganglion cell. This low convergence allows very fine resolution.
120389.m: Little linking of the cones makes the fovea especially sharp-sighted.

120391.q: In which area of the retina is the fovea centralis located?
a: In the macula, the yellow spot
120391.e: The fovea lies in the middle of the macula lutea, the yellow spot. The yellow colour comes from pigments stored there.
120391.m: The fovea centralis lies in the middle of the yellow spot.

120392.q: Which spot on the retina lies on the nose side of the fovea and contains no sensory cells at all?
120392.e: At the blind spot, the optic disc, the optic nerve leaves the eye. Because there are no photoreceptors there, a gap appears in the field of vision, which the brain fills in.
120392.m: The optic nerve leaves the eye at the blind spot.

120393.q: Roughly what is the diameter of the fovea centralis?
120393.e: The fovea centralis measures only around one and a half millimetres. Yet a large part of the visual information that the brain analyses comes from this small area.
120393.m: The fovea centralis is only about one and a half millimetres across.

120394.q: Why does light reach the sensory cells in the fovea particularly unhindered?
a: The inner layers of the retina are pushed to the side
The vitreous body is interrupted there
The sensory cells lie in front of the retina there
120394.e: Normally light has to pass through several layers of cells before it reaches the photoreceptors. In the fovea these layers are pushed aside, which creates a pit.
120394.m: In the fovea, the layers of the retina that get in the way are pushed aside.

120395.q: What are the quick jumps of the eye called that bring objects onto the fovea?
120395.e: Saccades are very fast, jerky eye movements. They direct a point of interest onto the spot of sharpest vision.
120395.m: With saccades, the gaze jumps from target to target.

120396.q: Which condition, common in old age, mainly affects central vision?
120396.e: In age-related macular degeneration, cells in the area of the yellow spot die. Reading and recognising faces become difficult, while side vision is usually preserved.
120396.m: Macular degeneration mainly destroys central vision.

120397.q: What is meant by accommodation of the eye?
a: Adjusting the lens's focusing power to the distance
Adjusting the pupil to the brightness
Moving both eyes towards the nose
120397.e: During accommodation, the lens of the eye changes its shape and therefore its focusing power. In this way near and distant objects are focused sharply on the retina.
120397.m: Accommodation is the eye focusing on different distances.

120398.q: Which muscle is responsible for accommodation?
120398.e: The ring-shaped ciliary muscle in the ciliary body changes the tension on the lens through the suspensory fibres. This changes the lens's curvature.
120398.m: The ciliary muscle focuses the eye.

120399.q: What happens when you look at something close up?
a: The ciliary muscle tightens and the lens becomes rounder
The ciliary muscle relaxes and the lens becomes flatter
The cornea becomes flatter and thinner
The lens moves back towards the retina
120399.e: When the ciliary muscle contracts, the suspensory fibres slacken. The elastic lens takes on a rounder shape and bends the light more strongly.
120399.m: For close vision, the ciliary muscle contracts and the lens becomes rounder.

120400.q: What are the fibres called from which the lens of the eye is suspended?
120400.e: The zonular fibres connect the ciliary body to the lens capsule. Their tension determines how flat the lens is.
120400.m: The lens of the eye hangs from the zonular fibres.

120401.q: What is the main cause of age-related long-sightedness?
120401.e: Over the years the lens becomes harder and can hardly become rounder any more. That is why many people need reading glasses from about the age of 45.
120401.m: Age-related long-sightedness happens because the lens becomes stiffer.

120402.q: What is the power of a lens with a focal length of 0.25 m?
120402.e: The power is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres: 1 / 0.25 m gives 4 dioptres.
120402.m: The power in dioptres is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres.

120403.q: An eye has its far point at infinity and its near point at 0.1 m. What is its range of accommodation?
120403.e: The range of accommodation is 1/near point minus 1/far point: 1 / 0.1 m minus 0 gives 10 dioptres.
120403.m: The range of accommodation shows by how many dioptres the lens can increase its power.

120404.q: Which two reactions accompany accommodation when you look at something close up?
a: Convergence and narrowing of the pupils
Divergence and widening of the pupils
Convergence and widening of the pupils
120404.e: When looking at something close, both eyes turn inwards and the pupils become narrower. Together with accommodation this is called the near response.
120404.m: In near vision, accommodation, convergence and narrowing of the pupils work together.

120405.q: Which part of the autonomic nervous system triggers accommodation for near vision?
120405.e: The ciliary muscle is supplied by parasympathetic fibres of the oculomotor nerve. Activating them leads to adjustment for near vision.
120405.m: The parasympathetic nervous system controls the ciliary muscle.

a: A clouding of the lens of the eye
120406.e: In a cataract, the normally clear lens becomes increasingly cloudy. The light is scattered and the image looks blurred.
120406.m: In a cataract, the lens of the eye becomes cloudy.

120407.q: The German everyday name for a cataract is “grey star”. What is the medical term?
120407.e: In medicine the “grey star” is called a cataract. The word comes from Greek and means something like waterfall.
120407.m: The “grey star” is called a cataract.

120408.q: Which form of cataract is by far the most common?
120408.e: Most cataracts develop in later life due to changes in the lens proteins. This is called age-related cataract.
120408.m: Cataracts usually appear in old age.

120409.q: How is a cataract treated today?
a: The cloudy lens is replaced by an artificial lens
Eye drops make the lens clear again
The cornea is removed with a laser
120409.e: Medicines cannot reverse the clouding. During the operation the lens is removed and an intraocular lens is inserted.
120409.m: A cataract is treated with an artificial lens.

120410.q: How is a cataract operation usually carried out today?
a: As a day patient with local anaesthetic
Under general anaesthetic for many hours
120410.e: Cataract surgery is one of the most common operations of all. It usually takes less than half an hour, and you can go home afterwards.
120410.m: Cataract surgery is usually a short procedure without a hospital stay.

120411.q: Which radiation is considered a risk factor for cataracts?
120411.e: Years of exposure to UV light damage the proteins of the lens. Sunglasses with UV protection lower the risk.
120411.m: UV protection for the eyes helps prevent cataracts.

a: A clouding of the lens capsule after the operation
A second cataract in the other eye
A cataract that only causes trouble at night
Bleeding in the retina after the operation
120412.e: After cataract surgery, the rear lens capsule that is left behind can become cloudy. It is usually opened with an Nd:YAG laser without a hospital stay.
120412.m: A secondary cataract is a later clouding of the lens capsule.

120413.q: Which complaints are typical of an early cataract?
a: Double vision only when looking up
120413.e: The clouding of the lens scatters the light. Those affected see as if through fog and are strongly dazzled by headlights, for example.
120413.m: A cataract makes vision foggy and sensitive to glare.

120414.q: The German everyday name for glaucoma is “green star”. What is the medical term?
120414.e: The “green star” is called glaucoma. It covers a group of diseases with progressive damage to the optic nerve.

120415.q: Which structure is damaged in glaucoma?
120415.e: In glaucoma, nerve fibres of the optic nerve die. This leads to permanent gaps in the field of vision.
120415.m: In glaucoma, the optic nerve suffers.

120416.q: What is the most important risk factor for glaucoma?
a: Blood sugar that is too low
Reading a lot under artificial light
120416.e: Pressure inside the eye that stays too high presses on the head of the optic nerve. But there are also glaucomas with normal pressure.
120416.m: Raised pressure inside the eye is the main risk factor for glaucoma.

120417.q: Which examination is usual from about the age of 40 for the early detection of glaucoma?
a: Measuring the pressure inside the eye
120417.e: Eye doctors measure the pressure inside the eye and look at the optic nerve. In this way glaucoma can be detected before you notice anything yourself.
120417.m: From 40, it is worth having the pressure inside your eyes checked.

120418.q: The draining of which fluid is often disturbed in glaucoma?
120418.e: Aqueous humour is constantly produced in the eye and drains away again. If the drainage is disturbed, the pressure inside the eye rises.
120418.m: Blocked drainage of aqueous humour raises the pressure inside the eye.

120419.q: Why is chronic glaucoma often noticed only late?
a: The gaps begin painlessly at the edge of the field of vision
It goes away again from time to time
120419.e: In the common open-angle glaucoma, the gaps first appear in the outer field of vision and do not hurt. That is why check-ups from middle age onwards are important.
120419.m: Glaucoma creeps in unnoticed from the edge.

120420.q: Which form of glaucoma is an eye emergency?
120420.e: In acute angle closure, the drainage angle suddenly closes and the pressure rises sharply. Typical signs are pain, a rock-hard eyeball, worsening vision and nausea.
120420.m: An acute glaucoma attack must be treated immediately.

120421.q: How is open-angle glaucoma usually treated first?
120421.e: Eye drops lower the pressure by reducing the production of aqueous humour or improving its drainage. Nerve fibres that have already been lost, however, cannot be recovered.
120421.m: Glaucoma is usually treated with pressure-lowering drops.

120422.q: How is the common red-green colour blindness inherited?
120422.e: The genes for the red and green opsins lie on the X chromosome. The condition is inherited recessively.
120422.m: Red-green colour blindness is inherited X-linked recessive.

120423.q: For which job is normal colour vision usually a requirement?
120423.e: In the cockpit, coloured signals, lights and displays must be recognised reliably. Colour vision is therefore tested in the aviation medical check.
120423.m: Pilots must be able to tell colours apart reliably.

120424.q: Roughly how many men in Central Europe have red-green colour blindness?
120424.e: In Central Europe, about one in every eleven or twelve men is affected, while among women it is less than one per cent. The reason is inheritance via the X chromosome.
120424.m: Red-green colour blindness affects many more men than women.

120425.q: What does not work properly in red-green colour blindness?
a: One type of cone in the retina
120425.e: There are three types of cone for colour vision. In red-green colour blindness, the red or the green cone is missing or altered.
120425.m: In red-green colour blindness, one type of cone is affected.

120426.q: Why do women have red-green colour blindness much less often than men?
a: They have no Y chromosome on which the gene lies
120426.e: The gene lies on the X chromosome. Women have two of them, so a healthy X makes up for the altered one. Men have only one X.
120426.m: A second X chromosome usually protects women from red-green colour blindness.

120427.q: Which picture plates are often used to test for red-green colour blindness?
120427.e: Ishihara plates show numbers made of coloured dots. People with red-green colour blindness cannot make out certain numbers or see different ones.

120428.q: How can you help people with red-green colour blindness when making charts and maps?
a: Show information with shapes, patterns or text as well
120428.e: Red and green are hard to tell apart for those affected. If shapes, patterns or labels add to the colour, the information is readable for everyone.
120428.m: Good charts do not rely on colour alone.

120429.q: After which scientist is colour blindness also called Daltonism?
120429.e: In 1794 the English chemist John Dalton described his own colour vision deficiency. It is often called Daltonism after him.
120429.m: John Dalton was the first to describe his own colour blindness.

120430.q: Where is the organ of Corti?
a: In the cochlea of the inner ear
120430.e: The organ of Corti lies in the cochlea on the basilar membrane. It converts sound vibrations into nerve signals.
120430.m: The organ of Corti is the hearing organ in the cochlea.

120431.q: What job does the organ of Corti do in the inner ear?
a: It converts sound vibrations into nerve signals
It balances the pressure in the middle ear
120431.e: The hair cells sit in the organ of Corti. They are moved by sound vibrations and turn them into nerve signals for the auditory nerve.
120431.m: The organ of Corti turns sound into nerve signals.

120432.q: What are the sensory cells in the organ of Corti called?
120432.e: The hair cells carry fine sensory hairs. When these are bent by sound, a nerve signal is produced.
120432.m: The sensory cells for hearing are hair cells.

120433.q: Roughly how many turns does the human cochlea have?
120433.e: The human cochlea is a bony passage with around two and a half turns. Unrolled, it would be about three centimetres long.
120433.m: The human cochlea has about two and a half turns.

120434.q: Why can very loud noise lead to permanent hearing loss?
a: It damages the hair cells, which do not grow back
It makes the ear bones melt
120434.e: The hair cells in the inner ear are overloaded by noise and can die. In humans they do not grow back, so the hearing loss remains.
120434.m: Destroyed hair cells do not grow back in humans.

120435.q: Through which nerve do the signals from the organ of Corti reach the brain?
120435.e: The cochlear nerve is part of the eighth cranial nerve. It passes the hearing information on to the brainstem.
120435.m: The cochlear nerve carries the signals of the organ of Corti.

120437.q: Roughly what range of frequencies can a young person hear?
120437.e: Human hearing picks up about 20 to 20,000 vibrations per second. With age, mainly the upper limit drops.
120437.m: Young people hear from about 20 hertz to 20 kilohertz.

120438.q: In which part of the ear are the hair cells for hearing?
120438.e: The hair cells sit in the organ of Corti in the cochlea of the inner ear. There, sound waves are converted into nerve signals.
120438.m: The sensory cells for hearing sit in the cochlea.

120439.q: What do the hair cells in the inner ear convert?
120439.e: Sound makes the fluid in the cochlea vibrate. The tiny hairs of the hair cells are bent, and the cells produce an electrical signal.
120439.m: Hair cells turn vibrations into nerve signals.

120440.q: Which sounds are picked up by the hair cells at the start of the cochlea, near the oval window?
120440.e: Each section of the cochlea is tuned to certain frequencies. High sounds are picked up at the start, low sounds at the tip of the cochlea.
120440.m: High sounds are heard at the start of the cochlea.

120441.q: What are the fine projections on the top of hair cells called?
120441.e: The stereocilia are arranged like steps and linked by fine tip links. When they are bent, ion channels open.
120441.m: The tiny hairs of hair cells are called stereocilia.

120442.q: How does the age-related loss of hair cells usually show itself first?
a: You hear high sounds less well
You hear low sounds less well
120442.e: The hair cells for high sounds are the first to be lost with age. That is why older people find it hard to hear high voices or birdsong.
120442.m: In old age, high sounds are the first to become harder to hear.

120443.q: Why does noise-induced hearing loss usually remain permanent in humans?
a: Destroyed hair cells do not grow back
120443.e: In mammals, destroyed hair cells of the cochlea are not replaced. Birds, on the other hand, can regenerate them, which is being researched intensively.
120443.m: Lost hair cells cannot be replaced in humans.

120444.q: Why is a hearing screening done for newborn babies?
a: So that a hearing problem is detected early
To check the shape of the ears
So that the child learns to speak faster
120444.e: If a hearing problem is discovered early, help can come quickly, for example with hearing aids. This is important for language development.
120444.m: Hearing problems detected early can be treated better.

120445.q: Which device can directly stimulate the auditory nerve in deafness caused by destroyed hair cells?
120445.e: A cochlear implant is placed in the cochlea. It converts sound into electrical pulses and uses them to stimulate the auditory nerve directly.
120445.m: A cochlear implant takes over the job of destroyed hair cells.

120446.q: How does a cochlear implant work?
a: It stimulates the auditory nerve directly with electrical pulses
It amplifies sound in the ear canal
It mechanically replaces the ear bones
It transmits sound through the skull bone
120446.e: A cochlear implant converts sound into electrical signals, which stimulate the auditory nerve through electrodes in the cochlea. In this way the damaged hair cells are bypassed.
120446.m: A cochlear implant stimulates the auditory nerve electrically.

120447.q: Which condition must be met for a cochlear implant?
a: The hair cells must be healthy
The middle ear must be inflamed
120447.e: The implant takes over the work of the hair cells, not that of the nerve. Without a working auditory nerve, it cannot bring signals to the brain.
120447.m: A cochlear implant needs a working auditory nerve.

120448.q: Where is the electrode array of a cochlear implant inserted?
120448.e: During the operation, the thin electrode array is pushed into the cochlea. Its contacts lie along the fibres of the auditory nerve.
120448.m: The implant's electrodes lie in the cochlea.

120449.q: Who developed the multi-channel cochlear implant in Australia?
120449.e: In 1978 the Australian surgeon Graeme Clark fitted a multi-channel cochlear implant in Melbourne. This development shaped today's devices.
120449.m: Graeme Clark developed the multi-channel cochlear implant.

120450.q: How do the signals of a cochlear implant pass through the skin to the implant?
a: By induction through a coil held by a magnet
Through sound waves in the ear canal
Through light signals through the skull
120450.e: A transmitter coil behind the ear is held in place by a magnet over the implant. Data and energy pass through the skin by electromagnetic induction.
120450.m: In a cochlear implant, a coil transmits the signals through the skin.

120451.q: What makes a cochlear implant different from a hearing aid?
a: It bypasses the hair cells instead of amplifying sound
It is always set more quietly
120451.e: A hearing aid makes sound louder and still needs working hair cells. The implant stimulates the nerve directly and is suitable for severe hearing loss.
120451.m: Hearing aids amplify, cochlear implants replace the hair cells.

120452.q: Why are children born deaf given a cochlear implant as early as possible?
a: The hearing pathway matures in the first years of life
The operation is banned for adults
The cochlea closes up after birth
120452.e: In the first years of life the brain is especially good at learning to process sounds. If they are missing for too long, the hearing pathway develops less well.
120452.m: Early fitting makes use of the sensitive phase of hearing development.

120453.q: What job does the speech processor of a cochlear implant do?
a: It splits sound into frequency bands
It measures the pressure inside the eye
It creates sound in the middle ear
120453.e: The speech processor picks up sound with a microphone and divides it into frequency channels. Each channel controls a particular electrode.
120453.m: The speech processor shares the sound out among individual electrodes.

120454.e: The organ of balance lies in the labyrinth of the inner ear, right next to the cochlea. Both are filled with endolymph.
120454.m: The organ of balance is in the inner ear.

120455.q: How many semicircular canals does the vestibular organ have on each side?
120455.e: Each inner ear has three semicircular canals that are roughly at right angles to each other. In this way rotations in all directions can be detected.
120455.m: Each organ of balance has three semicircular canals.

120456.q: What do the semicircular canals in the inner ear detect?
a: The air pressure in the middle ear
120456.e: When you turn, the fluid in the semicircular canals lags behind a little and bends fine sensory hairs. In this way the organ of balance reports rotations to the brain.
120456.m: The semicircular canals report rotating movements of the head.

120457.q: Which parts of the vestibular organ detect gravity and straight-line acceleration?
120457.e: The macula organs in the utricle and saccule carry a membrane with tiny crystals. It shifts with linear acceleration or tilting.
120457.m: The utricle and saccule measure gravity and linear acceleration.

120458.q: What are the otoliths in the organ of balance made of?
120458.e: The ear stones are tiny crystals of calcium carbonate. Because they are heavier than their surroundings, they react to gravity.
120458.m: The ear stones are made of calcium carbonate.

120459.q: Why do you still feel dizzy for a moment after spinning quickly in a circle, even though you are already standing still?
a: The fluid in the semicircular canals keeps flowing
Blood briefly drains from the head
The eyes are dazzled by the light
120459.e: The fluid in the semicircular canals is sluggish. When you stop turning, it keeps moving for a moment and tricks the brain into sensing a rotation.
120459.m: After spinning, the fluid in the semicircular canals keeps flowing.

120460.q: According to current thinking, what causes travel sickness?
a: Conflicting signals from the eyes and the organ of balance
Lack of oxygen in the vehicle
An inflammation of the middle ear
120460.e: If you read in a car, for example, your eyes report stillness but your organ of balance reports movement. This sensory conflict can cause nausea and dizziness.
120460.m: Travel sickness comes from a conflict between sight and balance.

a: Loose otoliths get into a semicircular canal
A clouding of the lens in the eye
120461.e: Loose ear stones move in the semicircular canal when you change position and trick the brain into sensing a rotation. With special positioning manoeuvres they can be moved back.
120461.m: In positional vertigo, stray ear stones disturb the semicircular canals.

120462.q: Which reflex keeps your gaze steady on a target when you move your head?
120462.e: When the organ of balance reports a head turn, the eyes immediately move just as fast in the opposite direction. This keeps the image on the retina stable.
120462.m: The vestibulo-ocular reflex stabilises the gaze.

120463.q: What does adaptation mean in sensory physiology?
a: Adjusting sensitivity to the strength of a stimulus
Passing a stimulus on to the brain
120463.e: In adaptation, sensory systems change their sensitivity depending on how strong a lasting stimulus is. This keeps them useful in very different surroundings.
120463.m: Adaptation is a sense adjusting to the strength of a stimulus.

120464.q: Why are you dazzled when you step out of a dark room into sunlight?
a: The retina is still set for darkness
The lens of the eye briefly clouds over
The optic nerve is temporarily interrupted
120464.e: In the dark the retina is very sensitive and the pupil is wide. Until light adaptation is complete, the light seems unpleasantly glaring.
120464.m: After darkness the eye needs a moment for light adaptation.

120465.q: Which sensory cells of the retina allow you to see at dusk after a while?
120465.e: The rods are much more sensitive to light than the cones but cannot tell colours apart. During dark adaptation they take over after a few minutes.
120465.m: In the dark we see mainly with the rods.

120466.q: Which of the eye's ways of adapting to brightness happens fastest?
120466.e: The pupil narrows or widens within fractions of a second to seconds. Biochemical adjustments in the retina take much longer.
120466.m: The pupil is the fastest to adjust how much light gets in.

120467.q: Why do you hardly feel the clothes you are wearing after a short time?
a: The spinal cord blocks all stimuli
120467.e: Fast-adapting mechanoreceptors mainly report changes. When the pressure stays the same, their signals quickly become weaker.
120467.m: Fast-adapting touch cells mainly report changes.

120468.q: Which sensory receptors hardly adapt at all, which is seen as a protective function?
120468.e: Nociceptors keep reporting tissue damage even when it lasts a long time. In this way the warning stays until the cause is removed.

120469.q: Why can you no longer smell the scent in a room after a while?
a: The scent substances break down at once
120469.e: Olfactory cells and the smell pathway reduce their sensitivity when a smell lasts. Someone entering the room fresh, however, notices the smell clearly.
120469.m: The nose quickly gets used to smells that stay the same.

120470.q: What colour is the afterimage after you have stared at a red surface for a long time?
120470.e: The red-sensitive cones adapt while you stare and become less sensitive. On a white surface, the opposite colour then dominates.
120470.m: An afterimage appears in the opposite colour.

120471.q: What is corrected with a LASIK operation?
120471.e: LASIK stands for laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis. The laser reshapes the cornea so that you can see sharply without glasses; a cataract, by contrast, affects the lens.

120472.q: Which tissue is reshaped in LASIK?
120472.e: The cornea provides most of the eye's focusing power. If its curvature is changed, the focusing power changes permanently.
120472.m: In LASIK, the cornea is reshaped.

120473.q: Which laser is used to remove corneal tissue in LASIK?
120473.e: The excimer laser emits ultraviolet light that removes tissue very precisely and with almost no heat. This allows the cornea to be shaped to within fractions of a micrometre.
120473.m: In LASIK, the excimer laser removes corneal tissue.

120474.q: What is the femtosecond laser used for in femto-LASIK?
a: It measures the pressure inside the eye
120474.e: The femtosecond laser makes a precise cut in the cornea with extremely short pulses. This creates the lid (flap), which is folded back for the reshaping.
120474.m: In femto-LASIK, the femtosecond laser cuts the flap.

120475.q: In PRK the laser is used without a corneal flap. What disadvantage does it have compared with LASIK?
a: Healing takes longer and is more painful
It changes the colour of the eyes
It only works for a few weeks
120475.e: In PRK, the top layer of cells of the cornea is removed and first has to grow back. In return there is no flap, which is an advantage if the cornea is thin.
120475.m: With PRK the eye heals more slowly, but without a corneal flap.

120476.q: How is the cornea changed when short-sightedness is corrected by laser?
a: It is flattened in the middle
It is curved more strongly in the middle
120476.e: A short-sighted eye bends light too strongly. If the cornea becomes flatter in the centre, the focusing power falls and the image lands on the retina.
120476.m: For short-sightedness, the laser flattens the centre of the cornea.

a: A cornea that is too thin
120477.e: For LASIK, enough corneal tissue must remain so that the cornea stays stable. If the cornea is too thin or bulges forward in a cone shape, doctors advise against it.
120477.m: A cornea that is too thin rules out LASIK.

120478.q: What is laser coagulation of the retina often used for?
a: Removing the lens of the eye
120478.e: In diabetic retinopathy, abnormal blood vessels grow in the retina. Targeted laser spots can slow this growth and help prevent bleeding.
120478.m: Laser coagulation protects the retina in diabetes.

120555.q: How does the siren of an ambulance coming towards you sound?
a: Higher than when it is still
Lower than when it is still
120555.e: As it approaches, the wave crests arrive at shorter intervals. So the listener hears a higher frequency.
120555.m: An approaching sound source sounds higher.

120560.q: Which animals use the frequency shift of their ultrasound echoes to locate prey?
120560.e: Some bats, such as horseshoe bats, analyse the Doppler shift of their calls. This lets them detect things like fluttering insect wings.
120560.m: Bats also locate prey with the help of the Doppler effect.

120773.q: Which co-receptor marks T helper cells on their surface?
120773.e: Because of their surface molecule CD4, T helper cells are also called CD4-positive T cells. The co-receptor stabilises the binding to the antigen-presenting cell.
120773.m: T helper cells are CD4-positive lymphocytes.

120774.q: Which cells show T helper cells fragments of germs so that they become active?
120774.e: Phagocytes take in germs, break them up and present fragments on their surface. When a T helper cell recognises such a fragment, it is activated.
120774.m: T helper cells are activated by antigen-presenting cells.

120775.q: Which virus specifically attacks T helper cells and, if untreated, leads to AIDS?
120775.e: HIV uses the CD4 molecule as a way in and gradually destroys the T helper cells. Without treatment, the immune defence therefore collapses.
120775.m: HIV weakens the immune system by destroying T helper cells.

120776.q: What role do T helper cells play in making antibodies?
a: They activate B cells, which then make antibodies
They have nothing to do with it
120776.e: B cells usually need the help of T helper cells to develop into plasma cells. Only these then produce large amounts of antibodies.
120776.m: T helper cells help B cells to make antibodies.

120777.q: Why are T helper cells also called the “conductors” of the immune system?
a: They coordinate other defence cells with messenger substances
They carry nerve signals to the brain
120777.e: T helper cells release messenger substances that activate phagocytes, B cells and killer cells. In this way they control the whole defence response.
120777.m: T helper cells control the immune defence.

120778.q: Where do T cells mature, which is also what the “T” in their name refers to?
120778.e: T cells are formed in the bone marrow and then mature in the thymus behind the breastbone. There they learn to tell the body's own substances from foreign ones.
120778.m: T cells mature in the thymus.

120779.q: What is the main job of regulatory T cells?
120779.e: Regulatory T cells slow down immune responses that go too far. In this way they help to prevent autoimmune diseases.
120779.m: Regulatory T cells protect the body from excessive immune reactions.

120780.q: Why do people with untreated AIDS fall ill with infections that are harmless for healthy people?
a: They lack the T helper cells that coordinate the defence
They have too many red blood cells
120780.e: HIV gradually destroys the T helper cells. Without them, the control of the defence collapses, and even otherwise harmless germs become dangerous.
120780.m: Without T helper cells, the defence collapses.

120781.q: What are the messenger substances called that immune cells use to communicate with each other?
120781.e: Cytokines such as the interleukins are released by immune cells. They activate other cells, make them multiply or damp down reactions.

120782.q: To which group of white blood cells do cytotoxic T cells belong?
120782.e: T cells and B cells are lymphocytes and form the specific defence. Granulocytes and monocytes belong to the innate defence.

120784.q: What does a cytotoxic T cell trigger in a cell infected with a virus?
a: Healing of the cell through repair
120784.e: The T cell releases substances that start apoptosis in the target cell. The cell dies in an orderly way, and the viruses inside cannot multiply any further.
120784.m: Cytotoxic T cells make diseased cells destroy themselves.

120785.q: Unlike T cells, which immune cells make antibodies?
120785.e: Activated B cells become plasma cells and release antibodies into the blood. Cytotoxic T cells, on the other hand, kill infected cells directly.

120786.q: Which cells are typically killed by cytotoxic T cells?
a: Cells infected with viruses and tumour cells
120786.e: Cytotoxic T cells recognise foreign peptides on the surface of the body's own cells. In this way they get rid of cells in which viruses are multiplying or that have become abnormal.
120786.m: Cytotoxic T cells remove infected and abnormal body cells.

120787.q: What is the aim of immunotherapy against cancer?
a: To activate the body's own immune system against the tumour
To destroy the tumour with radiation
To remove the tumour by surgery
To switch the immune system off completely
120787.e: Tumours can put the brakes on the defence. Immunotherapies release these brakes or prime T cells specifically so that they attack cancer cells.
120787.m: Immunotherapy turns the body's own defence into a cancer fighter.

120788.q: What is CAR T-cell therapy mainly used for?
a: Against certain types of blood cancer
120788.e: In CAR T-cell therapy, the patient's own T cells are genetically fitted with an artificial receptor. Afterwards they specifically recognise cancer cells, for example in certain leukaemias and lymphomas.
120788.m: CAR T-cell therapy turns your own T cells into targeted cancer hunters.

120789.q: How does a cytotoxic T cell recognise a body cell infected with a virus?
a: By foreign protein fragments on its surface
120789.e: Infected cells show fragments of viral proteins on their surface. The T cell recognises these foreign pieces with its receptor.
120789.m: T cells recognise infected cells by foreign protein fragments.

120790.q: Where do B lymphocytes mature in humans?
120790.e: B lymphocytes form and mature in the bone marrow. T lymphocytes, by contrast, mature in the thymus gland.
120790.m: B cells mature in the bone marrow.

120791.q: Where does the “B” in the name of B lymphocytes originally come from?
a: From the bursa of Fabricius in birds
120791.e: B cells were first discovered in chickens, where they mature in an organ called the bursa of Fabricius. The letter stayed, even though mammals do not have this organ.
120791.m: The “B” of B cells is a reminder of the bursa of Fabricius in birds.

120792.e: The B-cell receptor consists of an antibody anchored in the cell membrane. When it binds its antigen, the B cell is activated.
120792.m: The B-cell receptor is an antibody sitting in the membrane.

120793.q: What does a B cell become after it has recognised its antigen and been activated by a T helper cell?
120793.e: The activated B cell multiplies strongly. Some become plasma cells that make antibodies, others become long-lived memory cells.
120793.m: Activated B cells become plasma cells and memory cells.

120794.q: Why do people usually catch measles only once in their life?
a: The virus dies out after an illness
Afterwards the body makes no more mucous membranes
120794.e: After an infection, memory B cells and memory T cells stay in the body. At the next contact they react so quickly that you no longer fall ill.
120794.m: Memory cells often protect for life.

120795.q: What is the process called in which a B cell switches from making IgM to another antibody class such as IgA or IgE?
120795.e: In class switching, the constant part of the heavy chain is exchanged while the variable part stays the same. So the specificity is kept, but the function of the antibody changes.
120795.m: In class switching, an antibody keeps its target but changes its function.

120796.q: Which antibody class do B cells make first at the first contact with a germ?
120796.e: The early response to a new germ consists mainly of IgM. It is a large pentamer with ten binding sites and is good at clumping germs together.
120796.m: IgM is the first antibody of a new immune response.

120797.q: According to the clonal selection theory, how many different antigen structures is a single naive B cell specific for?
120797.e: Each B cell carries receptors with only one specificity. When it meets its antigen, it multiplies into a clone of identical cells.
120797.m: Each naive B cell recognises only one single antigen structure.

120798.q: Which mechanism creates the enormous variety of antibodies by recombining gene segments?
120798.e: As B cells mature, V, D and J gene segments are randomly put together in new ways. Susumu Tonegawa received the Nobel Prize in 1987 for this discovery.
120798.m: V(D)J recombination creates millions of different antibodies.

120799.q: From which cells do plasma cells develop?
120799.e: Activated B cells divide and develop into plasma cells. These are specialised in producing antibodies.
120799.m: Plasma cells are fully developed B cells.

120800.q: What is the main job of plasma cells?
a: They release large amounts of antibodies
120800.e: Plasma cells are real antibody factories. They release the antibodies into the blood and tissue fluids.
120800.m: Plasma cells produce antibodies in large amounts.

120801.q: Which cell organelle is especially well developed in plasma cells?
120801.e: Antibodies are proteins made for export on the ribosomes of the rough ER. Plasma cells therefore have an extensive rough ER and a large Golgi apparatus.
120801.m: The rough ER is where antibodies are produced in the plasma cell.

120802.q: Besides plasma cells, which cells develop from activated B cells and provide long-lasting immune protection?
120802.e: Some of the activated B cells become memory cells. At a new contact with the germ they react much faster, and this is also how vaccines work.

120803.q: Which cancer starts from abnormal plasma cells in the bone marrow?
120803.e: In multiple myeloma, a single clone of plasma cells multiplies out of control. It often produces large amounts of one uniform antibody and damages the bones.
120803.m: Multiple myeloma is a cancer of the plasma cells.

120804.q: Where are long-lived plasma cells mainly found in adults?
a: In the lens of the eye
120804.e: Long-lived plasma cells find special niches with survival signals in the bone marrow. From there they constantly release antibodies into the blood.
120804.m: Long-lived plasma cells live mainly in the bone marrow.

120805.q: What typical shape do the antibodies made by plasma cells have?
120805.e: An antibody consists of four protein chains that together form a Y. With its two arms it binds antigens, for example on germs.

120806.q: Roughly what share of the cells in the bone marrow are plasma cells in healthy adults?
120806.e: Plasma cells are only a small minority in healthy bone marrow. A clearly increased share is a sign of abnormal multiplication.
120806.m: Plasma cells are rare in healthy bone marrow.

120807.q: From which blood cells do macrophages develop?
120807.e: Monocytes circulate in the blood and move into tissues. There they mature into macrophages.
120807.m: Macrophages develop from monocytes in the blood.

120808.q: What does the Greek word “macrophage” mean?
120808.e: The word comes from the Greek “makros” for big and “phagein” for to eat. It describes the ability to take in large particles.
120808.m: Macrophages are the body's big eating cells.

120810.q: Which structure do macrophages form in tuberculosis to wall in germs?
120810.e: In tuberculosis, macrophages, giant cells and lymphocytes gather in small nodules around the bacteria. In this way the germs are walled in, but often not completely killed.
120810.m: Macrophages wall in tuberculosis bacteria in granulomas.

120811.q: How do macrophages recognise bacteria without having met them before?
a: By typical molecular patterns on the bacterial surface
By antibodies that they make themselves
120811.e: Receptors such as the Toll-like receptors recognise building blocks common to many germs, such as lipopolysaccharide. This is part of the innate defence.
120811.m: Macrophages recognise typical molecular patterns of germs.

120812.q: Apart from eating germs, what job do macrophages have?
a: They clear away cell debris and help wounds heal
120812.e: Depending on the signals, macrophages act more to promote inflammation (M1) or more to heal (M2). M2 macrophages clean up and promote the building of tissue.
120812.m: Macrophages fight germs and help with healing.

120813.q: Which macrophages clear away inhaled dust particles in the air sacs of the lungs?
120813.e: Alveolar macrophages move along the inner surface of the air sacs. They take in dust, soot and germs and are therefore also called dust cells.
120813.m: Alveolar macrophages keep the air sacs of the lungs clean.

120814.q: Which cells in the spleen mainly break down old red blood cells?
120814.e: Red blood cells live for about 120 days and then become less flexible. Macrophages in the spleen recognise and digest them, and the iron is recycled.
120814.m: Macrophages in the spleen dispose of old red blood cells.

120815.q: What, among other things, do macrophages use to kill bacteria they have taken in, inside the phagolysosome?
120815.e: An enzyme complex in the membrane produces superoxide and other aggressive oxygen compounds in the so-called respiratory burst. Together with enzymes and acid, they destroy the bacteria.
120815.m: Macrophages kill bacteria with aggressive oxygen compounds.

120816.q: Which part of the immune system does the complement system mainly belong to?
120816.e: The complement system consists of over 30 proteins in the blood plasma that can be activated without prior learning. But it works closely with antibodies.
120816.m: The complement system is part of the innate defence.

120817.q: With which part of the acquired defence does the complement system work closely?
120817.e: When antibodies stick to a germ, they can activate the complement system. This so-called classical pathway links the acquired defence with the innate defence.
120817.m: Antibodies can switch on the complement system.

120818.q: What does the complement system mainly consist of?
120818.e: The complement system includes over 30 proteins dissolved in the blood. They activate each other as in a cascade; one central protein is called C3.
120818.m: The complement system is a cascade of blood proteins.

120819.q: How does the complement system directly kill bacteria at the end of its cascade?
a: It makes holes in their membrane
It breaks them down with stomach acid
120819.e: Several complement proteins join together to form the membrane attack complex. Water flows in through this pore, and the bacterial cell bursts.
120819.m: The membrane attack complex punches holes in bacteria.

120820.q: What is it called when germs are marked with proteins such as C3b so that phagocytes can take them in more easily?
120820.e: C3b sticks to the surface of the germ. Phagocytes have receptors for it and therefore recognise marked germs much better.

120821.q: What effect do small fragments of the complement system such as C3a and C5a have?
120821.e: C3a and C5a widen blood vessels and attract immune cells. They are called anaphylatoxins; in large amounts they can contribute to shock.

120822.q: Why does the complement system have this name?
a: Because it complements the effect of antibodies
