121648.e: The term blood poisoning is widespread but inaccurate, as there is no poison in the strict sense. Lockjaw is an everyday name for tetanus.
121648.m: In everyday language, sepsis is called blood poisoning.

121649.q: Which signs during an infection can point to the start of sepsis?
121649.e: If a sick person breathes noticeably fast, seems confused or has low blood pressure, sepsis may be present. Then medical help is needed immediately.
121649.m: Fast breathing and confusion during an infection are warning signs.

121650.q: What is typical of septic shock?
a: A drop in blood pressure that needs circulation-supporting drugs despite fluids
High fever with no other symptoms
121650.e: In septic shock, the circulation is so badly disturbed that vasopressors are needed despite drips. The death rate is then especially high.
121650.m: Septic shock is the most severe form of sepsis.

121651.q: According to guidelines, within what time should antibiotics be given if septic shock is suspected?
a: Only after all lab results are in
121651.e: With every hour of delay, the risk of death rises considerably. That is why international guidelines recommend giving antibiotics within the first hour if possible.

121652.q: According to a large study in “The Lancet”, roughly how many deaths worldwide in 2017 were due to sepsis?
121652.e: The study estimated around 49 million cases of sepsis and about 11 million deaths for 2017. That was around one fifth of all deaths worldwide.
121652.m: Sepsis is one of the most common causes of death worldwide.

121653.q: Which people have an especially high risk of developing sepsis?
a: Babies, older people and people with weak immune systems
121653.e: In very young, old or immunocompromised people, the defence system is less able to contain an infection. Sepsis is therefore more common in them.
121653.m: Very young, old and immunocompromised people are especially at risk.

121654.q: Which blood value is measured in sepsis as a sign that the tissues are not getting enough oxygen?
121654.e: When cells lack oxygen, they get energy anaerobically and produce lactate. A raised lactate level shows a dangerous circulatory disorder.
121654.m: A high lactate level warns of a lack of oxygen in the tissues.

121655.q: If sepsis is suspected, what should be taken if possible before the first dose of antibiotics?
a: A saliva sample for a genetic test
121655.e: In blood cultures, the germs can be grown and tested for resistance. After antibiotics have been given, they often no longer grow, so the blood is taken beforehand.
121655.m: Blood cultures help to find the germ causing sepsis.

121656.q: In which year did the WHO declare the spread of COVID-19 a pandemic?
121656.e: On 11 March 2020, the WHO classified the worldwide spread of the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 as a pandemic. The first cases had appeared in China at the end of 2019.
121656.m: The WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic in March 2020.

121657.q: On which day did the WHO constitution come into force in 1948, a day now marked as World Health Day?
121657.e: The WHO constitution came into force on 7 April 1948. Since then, World Health Day has been held every year on this day with a focus theme.
121657.m: World Health Day is on 7 April.

121658.q: Which list has the WHO published regularly since 1977 as a guide for healthcare?
a: The Model List of Essential Medicines
The list of World Heritage Sites
The Red List of Threatened Species
The list of banned doping substances
121658.e: The model list names medicines that are important for basic healthcare in every country. It is revised about every two years.
121658.m: The WHO keeps a list of essential medicines.

121659.q: Who is Director-General of the WHO (as of 2026)?
121659.e: The Ethiopian Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has led the WHO since 2017 and was re-elected in 2022. Margaret Chan was his predecessor, and António Guterres is UN Secretary-General.
121659.m: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus leads the WHO.

121660.q: What is the highest decision-making body of the WHO, in which all member states are represented, called?
121660.e: The World Health Assembly meets every year in Geneva and sets the WHO's policy and budget. The Security Council is a body of the UN.
121660.m: The World Health Assembly is the highest body of the WHO.

121661.q: What status does the WHO have in the United Nations system?
a: It is a specialised agency of the UN
It is an authority of the European Union
121661.e: The WHO is a legally independent specialised agency of the United Nations with its own member states. It coordinates international health work.
121661.m: The WHO belongs to the UN as a specialised agency.

121662.q: Why does the WHO call for antibiotics to be used only in a targeted and sparing way?
a: So that fewer resistant bacteria develop
Because antibiotics only work in winter
Because there are hardly any antibiotics left worldwide
121662.e: Every use of antibiotics favours bacteria that are not affected by them. If resistance becomes more common, the medicines no longer work for dangerous infections.
121662.m: Using antibiotics sparingly slows down resistance.

121663.q: How does the WHO constitution define health?
a: As a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being
As simply the absence of illness
As the ability to work fully
As the result of regular visits to the doctor
121663.e: The definition in the constitution stresses that health is more than the absence of disease or infirmity. It includes mental and social well-being.
121663.m: For the WHO, health is more than the absence of illness.

121963.q: Which antibody class drives the classic immediate-type allergy?
121963.e: Allergen-specific immunoglobulin E sits on mast cells and, at renewed contact with the allergen, triggers the release of messenger substances.
121963.m: IgE plays the main role in immediate-type allergy.

121964.q: Against which invaders is immunoglobulin E originally mainly directed?
121964.e: Together with mast cells and eosinophil granulocytes, IgE helps to fight worms and other parasites. In allergies, this defence is directed against harmless substances.
121964.m: Originally, IgE serves to fight parasites.

121965.q: Which antibody was discovered in the 1960s and explained how allergic reactions are triggered?
121965.e: The married couple Ishizaka in the USA and Johansson and Bennich in Sweden described IgE in 1966 and 1967. This identified the antibody that drives immediate-type allergies.
121965.m: IgE was discovered in the 1960s as the allergy antibody.

121966.q: Why is IgE found only in very small amounts in the blood, even though it is so important in allergies?
a: Most of it is attached firmly to mast cells
It is excreted through the kidneys at once
It is only found in the gut
It breaks down when blood is taken
121966.e: IgE is the rarest antibody class in serum. Most of it is bound to mast cells and basophil granulocytes and waits there for the allergen.
121966.m: IgE is the rarest antibody class in the blood.

121967.q: Which messenger substance is released from mast cells during an allergic reaction and causes itching and swelling?
121967.e: When an allergen binds to IgE on mast cells, they release histamine. Antihistamines block its effect.
121967.m: Histamine from mast cells causes allergic symptoms.

121968.q: What is an allergy treatment called in which you receive increasing amounts of the allergen over years?
121968.e: In desensitisation, also called specific immunotherapy, the immune system slowly gets used to the allergen. The IgE-driven reaction becomes weaker as a result.
121968.m: Desensitisation gets the immune system used to an allergen.

121969.q: Which cells make IgE and other antibodies?
121969.e: Activated B cells mature into plasma cells and produce antibodies. Messenger substances from T helper cells, such as interleukin-4, get them to make IgE.
121969.m: Plasma cells produce antibodies, including IgE.

121970.q: Which medicine is injected first in a severe allergic shock?
121970.e: In anaphylaxis, triggered by IgE and mast cells, adrenaline narrows the blood vessels and widens the airways. People with allergies often carry an emergency auto-injector for this.
121970.m: In an allergic shock, adrenaline helps first.

121971.q: Which messenger substance is stored in the granules of mast cells and causes itching and swelling?
121971.e: Histamine widens blood vessels, makes them leakier and irritates nerve endings. This leads to redness, weals and itching.
121971.m: Mast cells store large amounts of histamine.

121972.q: In which kind of reaction do mast cells play a central role?
121972.e: Mast cells carry antibodies of the IgE type on their surface. When an allergen such as pollen binds to them, they release histamine within minutes.
121972.m: Mast cells trigger immediate allergic reactions.

121973.q: Where does the name “mast cell” come from?
a: They were thought to be well-fed cells
They are found mainly in the gut
They were first found in animals being fattened
They are shaped like a ship's mast
121973.e: Their discoverer believed that the cells, packed with granules, were “fattened” (German “gemästet”) and served to nourish the tissue. The name stayed, even though the idea was wrong.
121973.m: The mast cell's name comes from its fattened appearance.

121974.q: What is it called when an activated mast cell releases its stored granules?
121974.e: In degranulation, the storage granules merge with the cell membrane and release histamine and other mediators. This happens within seconds to minutes.
121974.m: An activated mast cell empties its granules by degranulation.

121975.q: Where do the precursors of mast cells develop?
121975.e: Mast cells come from blood-forming stem cells in the bone marrow. Their precursors move into the tissue and only mature there.
121975.m: The precursors of mast cells come from the bone marrow.

121976.q: What is a disease called in which mast cells multiply abnormally and build up in the tissue?
121976.e: In mastocytosis, mast cells build up in the skin, bone marrow or other organs. Those affected have a higher risk of severe allergic reactions.
121976.m: In mastocytosis there are too many mast cells.

121977.q: Which medicines block the effect of histamine from mast cells, for example in hay fever?
121977.e: Antihistamines occupy the histamine receptors so that the released histamine has less effect. Sneezing, itching and watery eyes ease off.
121977.m: Antihistamines damp down the effect of histamine.

121978.q: Which life-threatening reaction can occur when very many mast cells throughout the body release histamine at the same time?
121978.e: In anaphylaxis, the blood vessels throughout the body widen, blood pressure falls and the airways can swell shut. It is treated immediately with adrenaline.
121978.m: A massive release of histamine can trigger anaphylactic shock.

121979.q: What is hyposensitisation also called in technical language?
121979.e: In specific immunotherapy, the body receives the allergen that causes the problem in increasing doses. The aim is for the immune system to tolerate the substance again.

121980.q: How long does hyposensitisation usually last?
121980.e: So that the immune system changes for the long term, specialist societies recommend treatment for about three to five years. Shorter treatments work for less long.
121980.m: Hyposensitisation needs several years of patience.

121981.q: How is the allergen given in sublingual immunotherapy?
121981.e: Sublingual means “under the tongue”. Drops or tablets with the allergen are absorbed there instead of being injected.
121981.m: In sublingual therapy, the allergen goes under the tongue.

121982.q: For which allergy is hyposensitisation carried out especially often?
121982.e: Hay fever caused by grass or tree pollen is one of the most common allergies. Hyposensitisation can clearly ease the symptoms for years.
121982.m: Hay fever is often treated with hyposensitisation.

121983.q: Which messenger substance causes itching, sneezing and swelling in an allergic reaction?
121983.e: On contact with the allergen, mast cells release histamine. It widens vessels and irritates nerves, which causes the typical symptoms.
121983.m: Histamine causes the typical allergy symptoms.

121984.q: Why do patients usually have to stay at the surgery for about 30 minutes after a hyposensitisation injection?
a: Because of the risk of anaphylaxis
Because the allergen first has to take effect
So that the doctor can lower the blood pressure
Because the injection is removed again
121984.e: The injection contains the allergen and can rarely trigger a severe allergic reaction. Such reactions usually happen early and can then be treated immediately.
121984.m: After the injection, you wait at the surgery because of possible anaphylaxis.

121985.q: For which allergy is hyposensitisation especially effective and can even save lives?
121985.e: In insect venom allergies, the treatment protects most of those treated from severe reactions if they are stung again. It is not suitable for the other complaints named.
121985.m: Hyposensitisation works especially well against insect venom allergy.

121986.q: What is the first phase of hyposensitisation called, in which the dose of allergen is gradually increased?
121986.e: First the dose is increased up to the maximum dose. Then comes the maintenance phase with a constant dose at longer intervals.
121986.m: Hyposensitisation starts with the build-up phase.

a: An inherited tendency to make IgE against substances in the environment
An allergy that only occurs in adults
An inflammation of the joints caused by autoantibodies
An inborn inability to make antibodies
121987.e: People with atopy make IgE more easily against harmless substances such as pollen or house dust mites. This can lead to hay fever, asthma or eczema.
121987.m: Atopy is an inherited readiness for IgE-driven allergies.

121988.q: Which condition usually comes first in the so-called “atopic march”?
121988.e: The atopic march often begins in infancy with atopic eczema. Later, food allergies, hay fever and asthma can follow.
121988.m: The atopic march usually starts with atopic eczema.

121989.q: What does the Greek word “atopia”, from which the term atopy comes, mean?
a: Being out of place or unusual
121989.e: Atopia literally means “without a place” and referred to something unusual. In 1923 Coca and Cooke chose the word for the strange oversensitivity to harmless substances.

121990.q: What does the hygiene hypothesis say about how allergies develop?
a: Little contact with microbes in childhood increases the risk of allergy
Allergies are passed on by bacteria
121990.e: The hypothesis assumes that the immune system must get to know many microbes early on. If this contact is missing, it is later more likely to react to harmless substances.
121990.m: Early contact with microbes probably protects against allergies.

121991.q: According to studies from Switzerland, Austria and Germany, which children have allergies less often?
a: Children from traditional farms with livestock
Children from flats in big cities
Children who have never had pets
121991.e: Studies such as the ALEX study showed that early contact with cowsheds and raw milk lowers the risk of allergy. This is explained by the variety of microbes in the surroundings.
121991.m: Farm children get allergies less often.

121992.q: Against which substances do people with atopy typically develop allergies?
121992.e: In atopy, the immune system reacts with IgE to substances in the environment that are actually harmless, such as pollen, animal hair or house dust mites.
121992.m: People with atopy react to harmless substances in the environment.

121993.q: Which skin test is often used to check which allergens someone reacts to?
121993.e: In the skin prick test, drops containing allergens are put on the forearm and the skin is pricked lightly. If a weal forms, the person is sensitised.
121993.m: The skin prick test shows allergies on the skin.

121994.q: Which term describes the rise in allergies in industrialised countries since the middle of the 20th century?
121994.e: In many industrialised countries, the share of people with hay fever and asthma has risen sharply. Experts therefore speak of an allergy epidemic.
121994.m: Allergies have risen sharply in industrialised countries.

121995.q: Which feature typically distinguishes bronchial asthma from COPD?
a: The narrowing of the airways is largely reversible
Asthma only affects the air sacs
Asthma is always caused by smoking
There is no inflammation at all in asthma
121995.e: In asthma, the narrowing of the bronchi improves clearly on its own or with medicines. In COPD it largely remains.
121995.m: In asthma, the narrowing of the airways is reversible.

121996.q: Which spirometry value shows how much air you can breathe out forcefully in the first second?
121996.e: FEV1 stands for forced expiratory volume in one second. During an asthma attack this value drops considerably.

121997.q: Which simple device can people with asthma use to monitor their breathing at home?
121997.e: The peak flow meter measures the highest speed at which you can breathe out. Falling values give early warning of things getting worse.
121997.m: A peak flow meter is used to check asthma at home.

121998.q: Which substance is a typical short-acting reliever inhaler that quickly widens the bronchi during an asthma attack?
121998.e: Salbutamol is a beta-2 agonist and relaxes the muscles of the bronchi within a few minutes. It eases the attack but does not treat the inflammation.
121998.m: Salbutamol quickly widens the bronchi when you are short of breath.

121999.q: Which group of medicines treats the inflammation of the airways in asthma in the long term?
121999.e: Inhaled corticosteroids damp down the chronic inflammation directly in the bronchi. They are taken regularly, even when there are no symptoms.
121999.m: Inhaled steroids fight the inflammation in asthma.

122000.q: What is a severe asthma attack called that does not ease despite the usual emergency medicines?
122000.e: In status asthmaticus, the severe breathlessness continues and can become life-threatening. It must be treated in hospital.
122000.m: A severe asthma attack that does not end is called status asthmaticus.

122001.q: Which whistling breathing sound when breathing out is typical of an asthma attack?
122001.e: Wheezing happens when air is forced through narrowed small bronchi. It is heard mainly when breathing out.
122001.m: Whistling wheezing when breathing out is typical of asthma.

122002.q: Why should you rinse your mouth after inhaling a steroid spray for asthma?
a: To prevent a fungal infection in the mouth
So that the spray works more strongly
To prevent tooth decay from sugar
So that the bronchi widen faster
122002.e: Some of the steroid stays in the mouth and throat and weakens the local defence there. Rinsing prevents fungal infections and hoarseness.
122002.m: Rinse your mouth after using a steroid spray.

122003.q: Which white blood cells are typically found in greater numbers in the phlegm in allergic asthma?
122003.e: In allergic asthma, eosinophil granulocytes move into the wall of the bronchi and keep the inflammation going. Their number is raised in the sputum and often in the blood too.
122003.m: In allergic asthma, eosinophils are increased.

122004.q: Which antibody class triggers immediate-type allergy?
122004.e: In immediate-type allergy, IgE antibodies sit on mast cells. When the allergen meets them, the mast cells release histamine.
122004.m: Immediate-type allergies are triggered by IgE.

122005.q: How quickly does an immediate-type allergy typically start after contact with the allergen?
a: After about one to two days
122005.e: Because the IgE is already waiting on the mast cells, histamine is released almost at once. That is why this form is called the immediate type.

122006.q: What is the most severe form of immediate-type allergy, affecting the whole body, called?
122006.e: In anaphylactic shock, blood pressure and circulation drop, and the airways can swell shut. Without quick treatment it can be fatal.
122006.m: Anaphylactic shock is the most severe immediate-type reaction.

122007.q: Which medicine is the most important emergency treatment for anaphylactic shock?
122007.e: Adrenaline narrows the blood vessels, stabilises the circulation and widens the bronchi. People at risk therefore often carry an adrenaline auto-injector.

122008.q: Which skin test is most often used to check for an immediate-type allergy?
122008.e: In the skin prick test, a drop of allergen solution is put on the skin and the skin is pricked lightly. A weal after about 15 to 20 minutes points to sensitisation.
122008.m: The skin prick test shows immediate-type allergies on the skin.

122009.q: Why can someone with a birch pollen allergy get a tingling in the mouth when eating a raw apple?
a: Because of a cross-allergy caused by similar proteins
Because apples produce a lot of histamine
Because of poisoning from fruit acid
122009.e: The main birch allergen resembles a protein in apples, so the IgE recognises both. Cooking usually destroys this apple protein.
122009.m: Birch pollen allergy and apple allergy are often cross-allergies.

122010.q: What is the inflammation called that can appear again a few hours after the first immediate-type reaction?
122010.e: Besides histamine, mast cells also make substances that attract inflammatory cells. These cause a second wave of symptoms hours later.
122010.m: A late-phase reaction can follow the immediate reaction.

122011.q: Why does an allergy usually only show itself at repeated contact with the allergen?
a: At the first contact, the body first has to make the matching antibodies
At the first contact, the allergen is still too small
The body does not notice the first contact at all
Allergens are excreted at once the first time
122011.e: At the first contact, the immune system is sensitised and makes IgE. Only at a later contact does the allergic reaction happen.

122012.q: What does the word “allergy” literally mean in Greek?
122012.e: Allergy comes from the Greek allos for “other” and ergon for “activity”. It means a changed reaction of the body to substances that are actually harmless.
122012.m: Allergy literally means a different reaction.

122013.q: Which joints are typically affected first, and on both sides, in rheumatoid arthritis?
a: The knuckles and middle finger joints
The joints of the lower spine
122013.e: The inflammation usually begins symmetrically in the small joints of the hands. The joints nearest the fingertips, by contrast, are typically spared.
122013.m: Rheumatoid arthritis first affects the knuckles and middle finger joints.

122014.q: Which pattern of complaints in the morning is typical of rheumatoid arthritis?
a: Long-lasting morning stiffness of the joints
122014.e: The inflamed joints are often stiff for more than half an hour in the morning. In osteoarthritis, stiffness when getting going usually lasts only a few minutes.
122014.m: Long morning stiffness points to rheumatoid arthritis.

122015.q: To which kind of disease does rheumatoid arthritis belong?
a: Inherited diseases caused by a single gene
122015.e: In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system wrongly attacks the body's own tissue in the joints. This leads to lasting inflammation.
122015.m: In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system attacks the body's own joints.

122016.q: What fundamentally distinguishes rheumatoid arthritis from osteoarthritis?
a: It is an inflammation, not wear and tear
It is caused by an accident
It only affects the bones, never the joints
122016.e: Osteoarthritis develops through wear of the cartilage. Rheumatoid arthritis, on the other hand, is an inflammatory disease of the immune system.
122016.m: Arthritis means inflammation, osteoarthritis means wear and tear.

122017.q: Why should rheumatoid arthritis be treated as early as possible?
a: So that the joints are not permanently destroyed
Because otherwise it turns into osteoarthritis
Because medicines are banned later on
122017.e: The inflammation gradually attacks cartilage and bone. Early treatment slows this process and keeps the joints moving.
122017.m: If treated early, the joints stay healthy for longer.

122018.q: What do most medicines against rheumatoid arthritis do?
a: They damp down the overactive immune system
They kill bacteria in the joint
122018.e: Because the immune system attacks the joints, the medicines slow down the defence in a targeted way. As a result, inflammation, pain and swelling ease.
122018.m: Medicines for rheumatism slow down the immune system.

122019.q: Which tissue layer in the joint is inflamed first in rheumatoid arthritis?
a: The inner lining of the joint
The outer lining of the bone
The tendon sheath of the calf
122019.e: The inflamed inner lining of the joint (synovium) grows excessively and forms what is known as pannus. This gradually destroys cartilage and bone.
122019.m: Rheumatoid arthritis starts in the inner lining of the joint.

122020.q: Who gets rheumatoid arthritis more often?
122020.e: Women are affected about two to three times more often than men. The disease usually starts in middle adulthood.
122020.m: More women than men get rheumatoid arthritis.

122021.q: What are the firm lumps under the skin called that appear in some people with rheumatoid arthritis on outer surfaces such as the elbow?
122021.e: Rheumatoid nodules are inflamed lumps of tissue at places under pressure. Heberden's nodes, by contrast, belong to osteoarthritis of the joints nearest the fingertips.
122021.m: Rheumatoid nodules often sit on the elbows.

122022.q: Which skin sign on the face is typical of systemic lupus erythematosus?
122022.e: The redness stretches across the cheeks and the bridge of the nose and looks like a butterfly. It often gets worse after exposure to the sun.
122022.m: A butterfly rash on the face is typical of lupus.

122023.q: What are many autoantibodies directed against in systemic lupus erythematosus?
a: Parts of the cell nucleus such as DNA
122023.e: In lupus, the immune system makes antibodies against parts of the body's own cell nuclei. Antibodies against double-stranded DNA are especially typical.
122023.m: In lupus, antibodies attack parts of the body's own cell nuclei.

122024.q: Which screening test for autoantibodies against cell nuclei is almost always positive in lupus?
122024.e: Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are found in almost all patients with systemic lupus. A negative test therefore makes the diagnosis very unlikely.
122024.m: In lupus, antinuclear antibodies can almost always be detected.

122025.q: What does the Latin word “lupus” in the name of the disease mean?
122025.e: The name dates back to the Middle Ages, when skin ulcers were compared to wolf bites. Erythematosus means “reddened”.
122025.m: Lupus is the Latin word for wolf.

122026.q: Roughly how many out of ten people with systemic lupus erythematosus are women?
122026.e: Lupus affects women around nine times more often than men. It usually starts in young adulthood.

122027.q: How do most medicines against lupus work?
a: They damp down the immune system
122027.e: Because the immune system turns against the body itself, it is slowed down with drugs such as hydroxychloroquine, cortisone or other immunosuppressants.
122027.m: In lupus, the immune system is damped down.

122028.q: What is the dangerous organ involvement called in which lupus attacks the kidneys?
122028.e: In lupus nephritis, immune complexes are deposited in the filtering units of the kidneys and inflame them. Without treatment, kidney function can fail.

122029.q: Which environmental factor can trigger skin rashes and flare-ups in lupus?
122029.e: Many people with lupus are sensitive to light. UV light damages skin cells, whose parts then stimulate the misguided immune system.
122029.m: In lupus, consistent sun protection is important.

122030.q: How does lupus caused by medicines usually develop?
a: It fades after the drug is stopped
It gets worse and worse over time
It is passed on to the children
122030.e: Substances such as hydralazine or procainamide can cause lupus symptoms. After the drug is stopped, these usually disappear.
122030.m: Drug-induced lupus usually fades after the drug is stopped.

122031.q: What kind of disease is Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
a: An autoimmune disease of the thyroid
A viral infection of the liver
An iodine deficiency of the adrenal gland
A bacterial infection of the lungs
122031.e: In Hashimoto's thyroiditis, the body's own immune system attacks the thyroid. It becomes chronically inflamed and is gradually destroyed.
122031.m: Hashimoto's is an autoimmune inflammation of the thyroid.

122032.q: Against which thyroid enzyme are the typical antibodies in Hashimoto's thyroiditis directed?
122032.e: Anti-TPO antibodies are directed against thyroid peroxidase, which builds iodine into the thyroid hormones. They are raised in most of those affected.
122032.m: In Hashimoto's, antibodies against thyroid peroxidase are found.

122033.q: Which disorder of function does Hashimoto's thyroiditis usually lead to in the long run?
122033.e: The immune system gradually destroys the thyroid tissue. As a result, too few hormones are made.
122033.m: Hashimoto's usually leads to an underactive thyroid.

122034.q: How is an underactive thyroid caused by Hashimoto's thyroiditis treated?
122034.e: The missing hormone T4 is replaced with a tablet. The treatment usually lasts for life.
122034.m: In Hashimoto's, the missing thyroid hormone is replaced.

122035.q: How does the TSH level in the blood change when Hashimoto's thyroiditis has led to an underactive thyroid?
a: It drops to zero every day
122035.e: The pituitary gland notices the lack of hormone and releases more TSH to drive the thyroid. A raised TSH is therefore an early sign.
122035.m: With an underactive thyroid, TSH is raised.

122036.q: Which cells are found in huge numbers in the thyroid tissue in Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
122036.e: The tissue is densely filled with lymphocytes, some of which form real lymph follicles. That is why the disease is also called chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis.
122036.m: In Hashimoto's, lymphocytes move into the thyroid.

122037.q: Which complaint typically fits an underactive thyroid in Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
122037.e: Without enough thyroid hormone, the metabolism runs more slowly; you feel cold easily, are tired and put on weight. A racing heart and trembling fit an overactive thyroid better.
122037.m: With an underactive thyroid, you feel cold easily.

122038.q: In countries with enough iodine, such as Switzerland, what is the most common cause of an underactive thyroid?
122038.e: Because table salt in Switzerland is iodised, iodine deficiency hardly plays a role any more. The most common cause is then Hashimoto's autoimmune inflammation.
122038.m: Where there is enough iodine, Hashimoto's is the most common cause of an underactive thyroid.

a: The body's own antibodies constantly stimulate the thyroid
A lack of iodine makes the thyroid shrink
A tumour of the pituitary gland makes too much TSH
122039.e: Graves' disease is an autoimmune disease. Antibodies imitate the control hormone TSH and drive the thyroid constantly, so that it becomes overactive.
122039.m: In Graves' disease, antibodies constantly stimulate the thyroid.

122040.q: Which three signs are typical of Graves' disease (known in German as Basedow's disease)?
a: Goitre, bulging eyes and a racing heart
Thirst, needing to pass urine and weight gain
122040.e: In 1840 Carl von Basedow described the enlarged thyroid, the bulging eyes and the fast pulse. Not all patients show all three signs.
122040.m: Goitre, bulging eyes and a racing heart are typical of Graves' disease.

122041.q: Which trace element does the thyroid need to make its hormones?
122041.e: Thyroid hormones such as thyroxine contain iodine atoms. That is why iodine is added to table salt in Switzerland.
122041.m: Without iodine, the thyroid cannot make hormones.

122042.q: What makes the eye involvement in Graves' disease clearly worse?
122042.e: In Graves' disease, tissue and muscles behind the eye swell and push it forward. Smoking makes this inflammation clearly worse.
122042.m: Smoking worsens the eye involvement in Graves' disease.

122043.q: What are medicines called that slow down hormone production by the thyroid in Graves' disease?
122043.e: Antithyroid drugs such as thiamazole block the building of iodine into the thyroid hormones. As a result, hormone production falls.
122043.m: Antithyroid drugs slow down the overactive thyroid.

122044.q: Which treatment for Graves' disease destroys thyroid tissue in a targeted way using a radioactive substance?
122044.e: The thyroid takes up the radioactive iodine-131, which irradiates it from the inside. In this way the overactivity is ended permanently.
122044.m: Radioiodine therapy makes use of the thyroid's uptake of iodine.

122045.q: What is the TSH level like in an overactive thyroid caused by Graves' disease?
a: It is raised but cannot be measured
122045.e: The large amounts of thyroid hormones inhibit the pituitary gland, which therefore releases hardly any TSH. The antibodies still keep driving the thyroid.
122045.m: In Graves' disease, TSH is suppressed.

122046.q: Which complaint typically fits the overactive thyroid in Graves' disease?
122046.e: The metabolism runs at full speed, so those affected lose weight despite a good appetite. Restlessness, sweating and trembling often come on top.
122046.m: With an overactive thyroid, you lose weight despite your appetite.

122047.q: Which defence cells trigger a contact allergy?
122047.e: Contact allergy is driven by T cells, not by antibodies. It therefore belongs to the delayed-type allergies (type IV).
122047.m: In contact allergy, T cells are at work.

122048.q: Which substance is one of the most common causes of contact allergy in Europe?
122048.e: Nickel is found in costume jewellery, belt buckles and buttons. That is why European law limits how much nickel such objects may release.
122048.m: Nickel is a very common cause of contact allergy.

122049.q: Which test is used to detect a contact allergy?
122049.e: In the patch test, test substances are stuck onto the back with plasters. The result is read after about two to three days.
122049.m: Contact allergies are detected with the patch test.

122050.q: How long after contact does it usually take for allergic contact eczema to become visible?
122050.e: T cells first have to move to the spot and release messenger substances. That is why the eczema appears with a delay.
122050.m: Contact eczema only shows after days.

122051.q: What are small molecules called that only become a complete allergen by binding to the body's own proteins?
122051.e: Haptens such as nickel ions are too small on their own to trigger an immune response. Bound to skin proteins, they are recognised by T cells.
122051.m: Haptens only become allergens together with proteins.

122052.q: Which component of cement used to cause “bricklayer's itch” (cement eczema) very often?
122052.e: Hexavalent chromium in cement is a strong contact allergen. Since cement has been made low in chromate, bricklayer's itch has become rarer.
122052.m: Chromate in cement causes bricklayer's itch.

122053.q: Why do experts warn against “black henna” for temporary tattoos?
a: It can cause a strong contact allergy
It colours the skin for ever
It makes the skin sensitive to light as with sunburn
122053.e: The dye p-phenylenediamine (PPD) is often added to black henna. It can cause severe eczema and a lifelong allergy, for example to hair dyes.
122053.m: Black henna can cause a lifelong contact allergy.

122054.q: Apart from preservatives, which group of substances in cosmetics causes contact allergies especially often?
122054.e: Fragrances are among the most common contact allergens. In the patch test, several of them are tested together as a fragrance mix.
122054.m: Fragrances are among the common contact allergens.

122055.q: At which receptor do the classic antihistamines against allergies act?
122055.e: Anti-allergy antihistamines occupy the H1 receptor so that histamine has less effect there. Itching, sneezing and weals ease.
122055.m: Anti-allergy antihistamines act at the H1 receptor.

122056.q: Which side effect is especially common with first-generation antihistamines?
122056.e: Older antihistamines easily reach the brain and reduce alertness there. Newer substances hardly cross the blood-brain barrier.
122056.m: Old antihistamines often make you drowsy.

122057.q: Which substance is a second-generation antihistamine?
122057.e: Cetirizine makes you much less drowsy than older first-generation substances. It is often used for hay fever.
122057.m: Cetirizine is a modern antihistamine that causes little drowsiness.

122058.q: What are H2 antihistamines such as famotidine used for?
122058.e: H2 receptors are found, among other places, on the acid-producing cells of the stomach. If they are blocked, less acid is made.

122059.q: Which Swiss-born pharmacologist received the Nobel Prize in 1957, partly for developing the first antihistamines?
122059.e: Daniel Bovet was born in 1907 in Fleurier in the canton of Neuchâtel. He researched the first antihistamines in Paris and received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1957.
122059.m: Daniel Bovet from Neuchâtel was a pioneer of antihistamines.

122060.q: What is the antihistamine dimenhydrinate often taken for?
122060.e: Dimenhydrinate damps down the vomiting centre and the organ of balance. It is therefore taken before car or boat journeys.

122061.q: Which first-generation antihistamine is contained in many over-the-counter sleeping pills because of its sedating effect?
122061.e: Diphenhydramine easily reaches the brain and blocks H1 receptors there, which promote alertness. This side effect is used on purpose in sleeping pills.
122061.m: Diphenhydramine is used as a sleeping aid because it makes you drowsy.

122062.q: In an allergy, which cells release the histamine whose effect antihistamines slow down?
122062.e: Mast cells sit in the skin and mucous membranes and store histamine in granules. When an allergen binds to their IgE antibodies, they release the histamine.
122062.m: Mast cells release histamine in allergies.

122359.q: Which part of the brain does the hypothalamus belong to?
122359.e: The hypothalamus lies below the thalamus and is part of the diencephalon (interbrain).
122359.m: The hypothalamus is part of the diencephalon.

122360.q: Which hormone from fat tissue tells the hypothalamus how big the fat reserves are?
122360.e: The more fat is stored, the more leptin fat cells release. In the hypothalamus, leptin damps down the feeling of hunger.
122360.m: Leptin from fat tissue damps down hunger in the hypothalamus.

122361.q: Where is the pituitary gland, which is controlled by the hypothalamus?
a: Directly below the hypothalamus at the base of the brain
In the neck in front of the larynx
In the chest behind the breastbone
122361.e: The pituitary gland hangs on a short stalk below the hypothalamus and sits in a bony hollow at the base of the skull.
122361.m: The pituitary gland hangs directly below the hypothalamus.

122362.q: Which body quantity is mainly regulated by the hypothalamus to a set point of around 37 °C?
122362.e: The centre for temperature control lies in the hypothalamus. It compares the measured temperature with the set point and triggers sweating or shivering.
122362.m: The hypothalamus is the body's thermostat.

122363.q: Which sensory cells in the hypothalamus register whether the blood is too concentrated and trigger thirst?
122363.e: Osmoreceptors measure the osmolarity of the blood. If it rises, thirst develops and more ADH is released.
122363.m: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus report blood that is too salty.

122364.q: Which stimulus resets the internal clock in the hypothalamus every day?
122364.e: The retina tells the hypothalamus whether it is light or dark. In this way the day-night rhythm is adjusted to the surroundings every day.

122365.q: What is the hormonal stress axis called that starts from the hypothalamus and ends with the release of cortisol?
122365.e: Under stress, the hypothalamus stimulates the adrenal cortex to make cortisol through several hormone stages. This chain is also called the HPA axis.
122365.m: The HPA axis links the hypothalamus, the pituitary gland and the adrenal cortex.

122366.q: Which two hormones are made in the hypothalamus and stored and released in the posterior pituitary?
122366.e: ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin are made in nerve cells of the hypothalamus. They travel along the cells' extensions to the posterior pituitary and are released into the blood there.
122366.m: ADH and oxytocin come from the hypothalamus and are released in the posterior pituitary.

122367.q: Why is the hypothalamus called the link between the nervous system and the hormone system?
a: Its nerve cells make hormones themselves
It consists only of gland cells
It makes all the body's hormones
122367.e: The hypothalamus has neurosecretory cells: nerve cells that make hormones and release them into the blood. In this way it turns nerve signals into hormone signals.
122367.m: Neurosecretory cells make the hypothalamus the link between nerves and hormones.

122368.q: Which pituitary hormone is released by TRH from the hypothalamus?
122368.e: TRH (thyrotropin-releasing hormone) stimulates the anterior pituitary to release TSH. TSH then stimulates the thyroid.
122368.m: TRH releases TSH, and TSH drives the thyroid.

122369.q: Which pituitary hormone is released by CRH?
122369.e: CRH (corticotropin-releasing hormone) stimulates the production of ACTH in the pituitary gland. ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to make cortisol.
122369.m: CRH leads to the release of cortisol via ACTH.

122370.q: Which releasing hormone promotes the release of growth hormone?
122370.e: GHRH (growth hormone-releasing hormone) from the hypothalamus stimulates the release of somatotropin in the anterior pituitary.
122370.m: GHRH gives the signal for growth hormone.

122371.q: Which hormone of the hypothalamus inhibits the release of growth hormone?
122371.e: Somatostatin is an inhibiting hormone: in the pituitary gland it slows down the release of somatotropin and also of TSH.
122371.m: Somatostatin is the brake for growth hormone.

122372.q: Which messenger substance from the hypothalamus inhibits the release of prolactin from the pituitary gland?
122372.e: The release of prolactin is mainly held back by the hypothalamus. The inhibiting factor is dopamine, which is therefore also called prolactin-inhibiting hormone.
122372.m: Dopamine from the hypothalamus slows down the release of prolactin.

122373.q: By which route do the releasing hormones travel from the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary?
a: Through small blood vessels in the pituitary stalk
Through the cerebrospinal fluid in the spinal cord
122373.e: The hypothalamus and the pituitary gland are linked by their own small system of blood vessels in the pituitary stalk. In this way the releasing hormones reach their target quickly and in high concentration.
122373.m: Releasing hormones reach the pituitary gland through blood vessels in the pituitary stalk.

122374.q: To which class of substances do most releasing hormones of the hypothalamus belong?
122374.e: Releasing hormones such as TRH, CRH and GHRH are short chains of amino acids, in other words peptide hormones. They act through receptors on the cell membrane.
122374.m: Releasing hormones are mostly peptide hormones.

122375.q: What prevents the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland from releasing too much CRH and ACTH?
122375.e: When the cortisol level rises, cortisol inhibits the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland. As a result, CRH and ACTH fall, and the control loop stays in balance.
122375.m: Cortisol slows down its own release through negative feedback.

122376.q: What does a low TSH together with a raised thyroxine in the blood indicate?
122376.e: If the thyroid itself makes too much hormone, the large amount of thyroxine inhibits the pituitary gland through feedback. That is why TSH is low even though thyroxine is high.
122376.m: With an overactive thyroid, TSH is low and thyroxine is high.

122377.q: How does a high thyroxine level affect the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland?
a: It inhibits the release of TRH and TSH
It increases the release of TRH and TSH
It only increases the release of ACTH
122377.e: Through negative feedback, thyroxine reports that there is enough thyroid hormone. TRH and TSH then fall, and the thyroid is stimulated less.
122377.m: A lot of thyroxine slows down TRH and TSH.

122378.q: Why must long-term cortisone treatment be reduced slowly rather than stopped suddenly?
a: The body's own cortisol production is suppressed by feedback
The liver needs time to detoxify
122378.e: Cortisone taken as a medicine inhibits CRH and ACTH through negative feedback, so the adrenal cortex then makes little cortisol. If the medicine is stopped suddenly, cortisol is missing, which can be dangerous.
122378.m: After long cortisone treatment, the adrenal gland has to start up again slowly.

122379.q: In a control loop, what is an outside influence called that moves the actual value away from the set point?
122379.e: A disturbance variable changes the controlled value from outside, for example cold changing body temperature. The control loop then evens out this deviation.
122379.m: A disturbance variable pushes the actual value away from the set point.

122380.q: Which process in the body is an example of positive rather than negative feedback?
122380.e: In blood clotting, clotting factors that have formed activate further factors, so the process reinforces itself. That is positive feedback.
122380.m: Positive feedback reinforces a process instead of slowing it down.

122381.q: How does the pituitary gland's release of ACTH react when the adrenal cortex is destroyed and hardly makes any cortisol?
122381.e: Without cortisol, the inhibiting feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary gland is missing, and ACTH rises sharply. Because ACTH also stimulates the pigment cells, the skin of those affected often becomes darker.
122381.m: If the end hormone is missing, the controlling pituitary hormone rises.

122382.q: What happens in the pancreas when blood sugar rises, and how does this feed back?
a: More insulin lowers blood sugar, and then insulin release falls
More glucagon lowers blood sugar permanently
Less insulin makes blood sugar rise further
Cortisol is released and lowers the sugar
122382.e: High blood sugar stimulates the release of insulin. Insulin lowers blood sugar, and the falling sugar in turn reduces insulin release: a negative feedback.
122382.m: Blood sugar regulates its own lowering through insulin.

122383.q: Which part of a control loop measures the current actual value?
122383.e: The sensor measures the actual value and reports it to the controller. In the hormone system, these are for example receptors for hormones or glucose.
122383.m: The sensor measures, the controller compares, the actuator acts.

122384.q: How many iodine atoms does a thyroxine molecule (T4) contain?
122384.e: The number in the abbreviation T4 stands for the four iodine atoms in the molecule. Triiodothyronine (T3) has three iodine atoms.
122384.m: T4 has four iodine atoms and T3 has three.

122385.q: Which thyroid hormone is the biologically more active form in the target cells?
122385.e: In the tissues, thyroxine is mostly converted into T3 by removing one iodine atom. T3 binds much more strongly to the nuclear receptor.
122385.m: T3 is the active form of thyroid hormone.

122386.q: What effect does thyroxine have on the body's basal metabolic rate?
a: It has no effect on it
122386.e: Thyroid hormones increase energy use and heat production in almost all tissues. With an overactive thyroid, the basal metabolic rate rises clearly.

122387.q: In which protein is thyroxine stored in the follicles of the thyroid?
122387.e: The thyroid hormones are formed on a large protein, thyroglobulin, and stored in the colloid of the follicles. When needed, they are split off.
122387.m: Thyroxine is stored on thyroglobulin in the follicle.

122388.q: Which autoimmune disease leads to an overactive thyroid through antibodies against the TSH receptor?
122388.e: In Graves' disease, antibodies activate the TSH receptor permanently, and the thyroid makes too much hormone. Typical signs are a racing heart, weight loss and sometimes bulging eyes.
122388.m: In Graves' disease, antibodies stimulate the thyroid.

122389.q: Which substance is usually taken as hormone replacement for an underactive thyroid?
122389.e: Levothyroxine is artificially made T4. It is taken daily as a tablet and partly converted into T3 in the body.
122389.m: With an underactive thyroid, levothyroxine replaces the missing thyroid hormone.

122390.q: Since which year has iodised table salt been used in Switzerland against goitre and iodine deficiency?
122390.e: In 1922 Switzerland was one of the first countries to introduce iodised salt. Goitre and cretinism then declined sharply.
122390.m: Switzerland has been fighting iodine deficiency with iodised salt since 1922.

122391.q: What is the consequence of an untreated congenital lack of thyroid hormone?
122391.e: Thyroid hormones are essential for the brain to mature. Without treatment, intellectual disability and short stature result, which is why newborn babies are tested for it.
122391.m: Newborns are tested for a lack of thyroid hormone because the brain needs thyroxine.

122392.q: Why does iodine deficiency cause a goitre?
a: Raised TSH makes the thyroid grow
Iodine builds up in the neck
Thyroxine piles up in the tissue
122392.e: Without iodine, too little thyroxine is made, the inhibition of the pituitary gland disappears and TSH rises. TSH stimulates the thyroid to grow.
122392.m: Iodine deficiency leads to a goitre through a lot of TSH.

122393.q: What is the most important natural glucocorticoid in humans?
122393.e: Cortisol (hydrocortisone) is the most important glucocorticoid in humans. It is made in the adrenal cortex.
122393.m: Cortisol is the most important glucocorticoid.

122394.q: In which hormone gland is cortisol made?
122394.e: Cortisol is made in the cortex of the adrenal glands, which sit on the kidneys. Its release is controlled through the pituitary gland.
122394.m: Cortisol comes from the adrenal cortex.

122395.q: How does cortisol affect the blood sugar level?
a: It only lowers it at night
122395.e: Cortisol promotes the making of new glucose in the liver (gluconeogenesis) and reduces glucose uptake in some tissues. As a result, blood sugar rises.

122396.q: What are synthetic glucocorticoids such as prednisone mainly used for in medicine?
a: To build muscle in healthy people
122396.e: Glucocorticoids suppress inflammatory and immune reactions. They help, for example, with asthma, rheumatism or allergic reactions.
122396.m: Glucocorticoids have a strong anti-inflammatory effect.

122397.q: What is a typical side effect of taking cortisone in high doses for a long time?
122397.e: Too much cortisone changes the metabolism: fat builds up on the trunk and face, the skin becomes thin, and blood sugar and bone loss increase.
122397.m: High-dose cortisone over a long time has clear side effects.

122398.q: From which starting substance are glucocorticoids made in the body?
122398.e: Glucocorticoids are steroid hormones. All steroid hormones are built from cholesterol.
122398.m: Steroid hormones such as cortisol are made from cholesterol.

122399.q: At what time of day is the cortisol level normally highest in a healthy person?
122399.e: Cortisol follows a daily rhythm: it rises in the second half of the night and peaks in the morning. In the evening the levels are lowest.
122399.m: Cortisol is highest in the morning and lowest in the evening.

122400.q: Where is the receptor that cortisol binds to in the target cell?
122400.e: Cortisol is fat-soluble and passes through the cell membrane. It binds to a receptor in the cytoplasm, which then changes gene expression in the nucleus.
122400.m: Steroid hormones act through receptors inside the cell.

122401.q: What is the most important mineralocorticoid in humans?
122401.e: Aldosterone is the most important mineralocorticoid. It regulates the balance of sodium and potassium.
122401.m: Aldosterone is the most important mineralocorticoid.

122402.q: Where in the body is the hormone aldosterone made?
122402.e: Aldosterone is made in the outer layer of the adrenal gland, the cortex. The adrenal medulla, by contrast, makes adrenaline.
122402.m: Aldosterone comes from the adrenal cortex.

122403.q: What effect does aldosterone have in the kidney?
a: Sodium is taken back and potassium is excreted
Sodium and potassium are both excreted
Calcium is taken back and phosphate is excreted
122403.e: In the distal tubule and the collecting duct, aldosterone promotes the reabsorption of sodium. In exchange, potassium is excreted, and water is kept back along with the sodium.
122403.m: Aldosterone keeps sodium and gets rid of potassium.

122404.q: Which enzyme from the kidney starts the chain that leads to the release of aldosterone?
122404.e: When blood pressure in the kidney falls, renin is released. It starts the production of angiotensin II, which stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone.
122404.m: Renin from the kidney starts the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

122405.q: How does aldosterone affect blood pressure?
a: It raises it, because more salt and water stay in the body
It lowers it, because more water is excreted
It has no influence on it
It lowers it, because the heart beats more slowly
122405.e: Aldosterone makes the kidney take back sodium, and water stays in the body along with the sodium. The blood volume rises and with it the blood pressure.
122405.m: Aldosterone raises blood pressure through salt and water.

122406.q: Why are hormones such as aldosterone called “mineralocorticoids”?
a: They regulate the salt balance and come from the adrenal cortex
They are taken in from mineral water
122406.e: “Mineral” stands for salts such as sodium and potassium, “corticoid” for their origin in the cortex of the adrenal gland.

122407.q: What happens if the adrenal cortex makes too little aldosterone?
a: The body loses salt and blood pressure falls
122407.e: Without aldosterone, the kidney excretes too much sodium and water. Those affected have low blood pressure and often crave salt, as in Addison's disease.
122407.m: Without aldosterone, the body loses salt and blood pressure.

122408.q: What does a medicine that blocks the effect of aldosterone do?
a: The kidney excretes more sodium and water
The kidney keeps back more sodium
122408.e: If aldosterone cannot work, the kidney takes back less sodium. Water is lost along with the sodium, while potassium tends to stay in the body.
122408.m: If aldosterone is blocked, the kidney excretes more salt and water.

122409.e: Somatotropin is made by the somatotropic cells of the anterior pituitary and released into the blood.
122409.m: Growth hormone comes from the anterior pituitary.

122410.q: Which organ does somatotropin stimulate to make growth factors for bones and tissues?
122410.e: Growth hormone works largely indirectly: it makes the liver release growth factors into the blood, which then promote growth.
122410.m: Many effects of growth hormone work through the liver.

122411.q: What results from too much somatotropin in childhood, while the growth plates are still open?
122411.e: As long as the growth plates are open, too much growth hormone leads to excessive growth in height. This is called pituitary gigantism.
122411.m: Too much growth hormone in childhood makes you very tall.

122412.q: What is the condition called when too much somatotropin is made after the growth plates have closed?
122412.e: In adults, the long bones no longer grow in length; instead the hands, feet, chin and nose get bigger. The most common cause is a benign tumour of the pituitary gland.
122412.m: In adults, acromegaly enlarges the hands, feet and facial features.

122413.q: During which phase is somatotropin released especially strongly?
122413.e: The biggest release of growth hormone happens shortly after falling asleep, in the deep sleep phases. Enough sleep is therefore important for growth.
122413.m: Growth hormone is released mainly during deep sleep.

122414.q: How does somatotropin affect the blood sugar level?
a: It has no effect at all
122414.e: Somatotropin acts as an opponent of insulin: it promotes the production of glucose and reduces glucose uptake. That is why it counts as one of the hormones that raise blood sugar.
122414.m: Somatotropin works against insulin and raises blood sugar.

122415.q: Where does the somatotropin used today to treat short stature come from?
a: From the pituitary glands of deceased people
122415.e: Growth hormone used to be obtained from the pituitary glands of deceased people, which transmitted cases of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Today it is produced by genetic engineering in bacteria or cell cultures.
122415.m: Growth hormone is now produced safely by genetic engineering.

122416.q: Why does growth hormone have to be injected rather than swallowed as a tablet?
a: As a protein, it would be broken down in the digestive tract
The tablets would be too large
It only works directly in the muscle
122416.e: Somatotropin is a large peptide hormone made of amino acids. In the stomach and intestines it would be digested like protein from food and would not reach the blood in an effective form.
122416.m: Protein hormones such as somatotropin must be injected.

122417.q: Where do the cells of the islets of Langerhans release their hormones?
a: Into the lymph of the intestine
122417.e: The islet cells are endocrine: they release insulin and glucagon directly into the blood vessels. The rest of the pancreas releases digestive juice into the intestine.
122417.m: The islets of Langerhans release their hormones directly into the blood.

122418.q: Which cells of the islets of Langerhans produce insulin?
122418.e: Beta cells make up most of the islet cells and produce insulin.

122419.q: Which hormone do the alpha cells of the islets of Langerhans produce?
122419.e: Alpha cells produce glucagon, the opponent of insulin. Glucagon raises blood sugar.

122420.q: Which hormone is produced by the delta cells of the islets of Langerhans?
122420.e: Delta cells produce somatostatin, which inhibits the release of insulin and glucagon in the surrounding area.
122420.m: Delta cells produce the inhibiting hormone somatostatin.

122421.q: Roughly what share of the mass of the pancreas do the islets of Langerhans make up?
122421.e: By far the largest part of the pancreas produces digestive enzymes. The islets make up only around 1 to 2 per cent of the organ's mass.
122421.m: The islets of Langerhans are only a small part of the pancreas.

122422.q: Why are the islets of Langerhans called “islets”?
a: They lie scattered as small clusters of cells in the rest of the gland tissue
They float freely in the abdomen
122422.e: The hormone-producing clusters of cells lie like islands in the tissue that produces digestive juice. Paul Langerhans described them in 1869 as a student without knowing their function.
122422.m: The islets of Langerhans lie scattered throughout the pancreas.

122423.q: What happens to the beta cells in type 1 diabetes mellitus?
a: They are destroyed by the body's own immune system
122423.e: In type 1 diabetes, immune cells attack the beta cells. Once a large proportion has been destroyed, the missing hormone has to be supplied from outside for life.
122423.m: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune destruction of the beta cells.

122424.q: How does glucagon act in the liver?
a: It promotes the breakdown of glycogen
It promotes the build-up of glycogen
It inhibits the release of glucose
It promotes the production of bile
122424.e: In the liver, glucagon stimulates the breakdown of glycogen and the production of new glucose. The glucose is released into the blood and blood sugar rises.
122424.m: Glucagon releases sugar from the liver's stores.

122425.q: Which researchers succeeded in isolating insulin in Toronto in 1921?
122425.e: In 1921 Banting and Best obtained insulin from the pancreases of dogs. As early as 1922 a patient was treated with it for the first time.
122425.m: Insulin was isolated by Banting and Best in 1921.

122426.q: What is the central disorder at the start of type 2 diabetes mellitus?
a: Too much glucagon because of a tumour
122426.e: In type 2 diabetes, muscle, fat and liver cells respond less well to insulin. At first the pancreas even produces more insulin; later it becomes exhausted.
122426.m: Type 2 diabetes usually begins with insulin resistance.

122427.q: Which medicine in tablet form is usually considered the first choice for type 2 diabetes?
122427.e: Metformin mainly inhibits the production of new glucose in the liver and improves sensitivity to insulin. On its own it hardly ever causes low blood sugar.
122427.m: Metformin is the standard medicine for type 2 diabetes.

122428.q: Roughly what share of all cases of diabetes is type 2?
122428.e: With around 90 per cent of all cases, type 2 diabetes is by far the most common form of diabetes.
122428.m: Most people with diabetes have type 2.

122429.q: What is measured in a fasting blood sugar test?
a: The sugar level in the blood after several hours without food
The sugar in the urine after breakfast
The amount of sugar in food
The store of insulin in the pancreas
122429.e: For the test you must not eat anything for at least eight hours. If the blood sugar is then clearly raised on repeated occasions, this points to diabetes.
122429.m: Fasting blood sugar is measured without eating beforehand.

122430.q: What does a glucose tolerance test check?
a: How well the body processes a large amount of sugar
How much sugar someone eats each day
Whether someone can taste sugar well
How much sugar the muscles store
122430.e: You drink a sugar solution and the blood sugar is measured afterwards. If it is still too high after two hours, the body is processing sugar poorly.
122430.m: The glucose tolerance test shows how well the body processes sugar.

122431.q: Which eye disease is a typical long-term consequence of poorly controlled diabetes?
122431.e: Permanently high blood sugar damages the small blood vessels of the retina. This diabetic retinopathy can even lead to blindness.
122431.m: Diabetes can damage the blood vessels of the retina.

122432.q: What does the word “mellitus” in diabetes mellitus mean?
122432.e: “Mellitus” comes from Latin and means sweet as honey. In the past, diabetes was recognised by the sweet taste of the urine.
122432.m: Diabetes mellitus literally means a flow as sweet as honey.

122433.q: Which measure has been shown to improve insulin sensitivity in type 2 diabetes without medicine?
122433.e: Working muscles take up glucose even independently of insulin and become more sensitive to insulin. Exercise and weight loss are cornerstones of treatment.
122433.m: Exercise makes the muscles more sensitive to insulin again.

122434.q: What does the HbA1c value measure?
a: The proportion of haemoglobin with glucose attached
The number of red blood cells
The amount of insulin in the blood
The current blood sugar in real time
122434.e: HbA1c is glycated haemoglobin. The value shows what percentage of the haemoglobin is bound to glucose.
122434.m: HbA1c shows how much haemoglobin has sugar attached.

122435.q: Over what period does the HbA1c value reflect the average blood sugar?
122435.e: Red blood cells live for around 120 days. That is why HbA1c shows the average blood sugar of the last two to three months.
122435.m: HbA1c is the blood sugar memory of the last two to three months.

122436.q: For which disease is the HbA1c value checked regularly?
122436.e: HbA1c shows the average blood sugar of the past few months. That is why it is the most important control value in diabetes.
122436.m: HbA1c is the most important long-term value in diabetes.

122437.q: In which blood cells is the haemoglobin found that sugar binds to in HbA1c?
122437.e: Haemoglobin is the red pigment in the red blood cells. Part of it combines with glucose from the blood.
122437.m: HbA1c forms in the red blood cells.

122438.q: What happens to the HbA1c value if blood sugar is too high for weeks?
122438.e: The more glucose there is in the blood, the more of it binds to haemoglobin. Permanently high blood sugar therefore makes the HbA1c rise.
122438.m: High blood sugar over weeks raises the HbA1c.

122439.q: Why does HbA1c show the blood sugar of the last two to three months?
a: Because red blood cells live for around 120 days
Because the liver stores sugar for three months
Because insulin works for three months
Because the kidneys only filter every three months
122439.e: Haemoglobin collects glucose throughout the whole lifespan of a red blood cell. This is around 120 days.
122439.m: The lifespan of the red blood cells determines the memory of HbA1c.

122440.q: Why do you not need to fast before an HbA1c measurement?
a: The value hardly depends on short-term fluctuations
Because eating always lowers the value
Because the measurement is done in urine
Because the glucose is filtered out
122440.e: HbA1c reflects an average over weeks. A single meal hardly changes it at all.
122440.m: HbA1c does not require a fasting blood sample.

122441.q: What advantage does HbA1c have for monitoring diabetes over time?
a: It shows long-term blood sugar control
It shows acute low blood sugar immediately
122441.e: Because HbA1c reflects the average of the past few months, it is well suited for assessing treatment. However, it does not detect short episodes of low blood sugar.
122441.m: HbA1c is used to assess treatment over months.

122442.q: What is the steady release of insulin by an insulin pump throughout the day called?
122442.e: The basal rate covers the basic need for insulin around the clock. It can be programmed differently for each hour.
122442.m: The basal rate covers the basic need for insulin.

122443.q: What is the extra amount of insulin released by the pump for a meal called?
122443.e: For the carbohydrates in a meal or to correct high values, you release a bolus at the press of a button.
122443.m: For meals, the pump releases a bolus.

122444.q: Which type of insulin is normally used in an insulin pump?
122444.e: The pump continuously releases small amounts of fast-acting insulin. Because it acts quickly, the dose can be finely adjusted hour by hour.
122444.m: An insulin pump works with fast-acting insulin.

122445.q: Into which tissue does an insulin pump release the insulin?
a: Into the fatty tissue under the skin
122445.e: The insulin flows through a fine cannula into the fatty tissue under the skin (subcutaneously). The cannula is changed every few days.
122445.m: The pump releases insulin under the skin.

122446.q: Why does ketoacidosis quickly threaten if the insulin supply from the pump is interrupted?
a: There is no depot of long-acting insulin
The pump then releases too much insulin
The insulin becomes toxic in the pump
The body immediately produces too much glucagon and insulin
122446.e: With a pump, there is only a little fast-acting insulin in the body. If the supply fails, insulin runs out after a few hours and the body breaks down fat into ketone bodies.
122446.m: If the pump fails, insulin runs out quickly.

122447.q: What are systems called in which a glucose sensor and an insulin pump adjust the dose automatically?
122447.e: In automated insulin delivery, an algorithm continuously calculates the amount of insulin from the sensor values. Meals usually still have to be entered by the user (hybrid closed loop).
122447.m: A closed-loop system connects sensor and pump automatically.

122448.q: What does a continuous glucose monitoring system (CGM), often combined with an insulin pump, measure?
a: The sugar in the tissue fluid under the skin
The insulin level in the blood
The blood pressure on the upper arm
122448.e: A small sensor under the skin continuously measures the glucose level of the tissue fluid. The values appear on the mobile phone or the pump.
122448.m: A CGM sensor measures sugar continuously under the skin.

122449.q: What is an insulin pump called that sticks directly onto the skin without a tube?
122449.e: Patch pumps contain the insulin reservoir and cannula in a small housing that is stuck directly onto the skin and controlled by a device.
122449.m: A patch pump sticks onto the skin without a tube.

122450.q: Which molecule is the best-known second messenger?
122450.e: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) carries the signal from hormones such as adrenaline or glucagon into the inside of many cells.
122450.m: cAMP is the classic second messenger.

122451.q: Which enzyme makes cAMP from ATP?
122451.e: After being activated by a G protein, adenylate cyclase converts ATP into cAMP.
122451.m: Adenylate cyclase turns ATP into cAMP.

122452.q: How is a hormone signal passed on after cAMP has been formed in the cell?
a: cAMP activates enzymes that pass on the signal
cAMP leaves the cell again as a hormone
cAMP is immediately built into the DNA
cAMP destroys the receptor on the membrane
122452.e: cAMP switches on enzymes in the cell. These change other proteins and so trigger the actual response of the cell.
122452.m: cAMP switches on enzymes in the cell.

122453.q: Why do peptide hormones such as glucagon need a second messenger?
a: They cannot cross the cell membrane
They only act in the cell nucleus
They are destroyed in the blood immediately
122453.e: Peptide hormones are water-soluble and cannot pass through the lipid bilayer. They bind to a receptor on the outside, and a second messenger carries the signal inside.
122453.m: Water-soluble hormones need a second messenger.

122454.q: Which molecule links a hormone receptor to adenylate cyclase?
122454.e: When a hormone binds to a G protein-coupled receptor, a G protein is activated. This switches on adenylate cyclase.
122454.m: A G protein connects the receptor and adenylate cyclase.

122455.q: Which ion also serves as a second messenger in many cells, for example in muscle contraction?
122455.e: When the calcium concentration inside the cell rises, this triggers reactions, for example the contraction of muscle fibres or the release of messenger substances.
122455.m: Calcium is an important messenger inside the cell.

122456.q: Why is a molecule such as cAMP called a “second messenger”?
a: The hormone is the first messenger, the molecule in the cell the second
It is always formed only at the second contact with a hormone
It only works for one second
It was the second hormone ever discovered
122456.e: The hormone brings the message as far as the cell membrane. Inside the cell, a second messenger such as cAMP carries the message on.
122456.m: The second messenger carries the hormone's signal into the cell.

122457.q: Why must a second messenger signal be broken down again quickly in the cell?
a: So that the cell can respond to new signals
Because otherwise the hormone flows back into the blood
So that the cell produces more hormones
122457.e: If cAMP were not broken down, the cell would stay switched on permanently. Enzymes break down the messenger so that the signal ends and the cell is ready to receive again.
122457.m: A signal must also be switched off again.

122458.q: What is the advantage of a signalling cascade with a second messenger?
a: The hormone reaches the cell nucleus
122458.e: A single hormone molecule activates many enzyme molecules, each of which forms many cAMP molecules. In this way a small stimulus produces a large response.
122458.m: A signalling cascade strongly amplifies a weak hormone signal.

122757.q: Which organelle is found in plant cells but is missing in animal cells?
122757.e: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis; animal cells have no chloroplasts.
122757.m: Only plant cells and algae have chloroplasts.

122758.q: Which small organelle breaks down long-chain fatty acids and splits toxic hydrogen peroxide with the enzyme catalase?
122758.e: Peroxisomes contain oxidative enzymes; the hydrogen peroxide produced is broken down by catalase into water and oxygen.
122758.m: Peroxisomes detoxify hydrogen peroxide with catalase.

122759.q: Which structure separates the contents of the nucleus from the cytoplasm?
122759.e: The nuclear envelope consists of two membranes and is pierced by nuclear pores through which substances are exchanged.
122759.m: The nuclear envelope with its nuclear pores surrounds the genetic material.

122760.q: What is the membrane called that surrounds the large central vacuole of a plant cell?
122760.e: The tonoplast separates the cell sap of the vacuole from the cytoplasm and regulates the exchange of substances.
122760.m: The vacuole of the plant cell is surrounded by the tonoplast.

122762.q: Why is part of the endoplasmic reticulum called the “rough ER”?
a: It is surrounded by a cell wall
122762.e: Under the electron microscope the rough ER looks grainy because many ribosomes are attached to the outside of its membranes.
122762.m: The rough ER is studded with ribosomes.

122763.q: What is the main task of the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
a: Making membrane proteins and proteins for secretion
122763.e: Proteins are made at the rough ER that are built into membranes or exported from the cell; in the process they enter the inside of the ER.
122763.m: Proteins for membranes and for export are made at the rough ER.

122764.q: Which substances are mainly made at the smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
a: Lipids such as phospholipids and steroids
122764.e: The smooth ER has no ribosomes; it synthesises lipids, including membrane phospholipids and steroid hormones.
122764.m: The smooth ER is the lipid factory of the cell.

122765.q: Which structure is the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum directly connected to?
122765.e: The ER emerges directly from the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope; its interior is connected to the space between the two nuclear membranes.
122765.m: The ER and the nuclear envelope form one continuous membrane system.

122766.q: What task does the especially extensive smooth ER perform in liver cells?
122766.e: In liver cells, the smooth ER contains enzymes that chemically convert medicines and toxins so that they can be excreted.
122766.m: The smooth ER of the liver helps with detoxification.

122767.q: How do newly made proteins get from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus?
a: In membrane vesicles that bud off
122767.e: Transport vesicles bud off from the ER, fuse with the membranes of the Golgi apparatus and release their cargo.
122767.m: Vesicles transport proteins from the ER to the Golgi apparatus.

122768.q: What causes a ribosome to bind to the ER during protein synthesis?
a: A signal peptide on the new protein
A start codon on the mRNA
A poly-A tail on the mRNA
122768.e: A signal sequence at the start of the growing chain is bound by a recognition particle (SRP), which guides the ribosome to the ER membrane.
122768.m: A signal peptide sends proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum.

122769.q: What is a single stack of flattened membrane cisternae of the Golgi apparatus called?
122769.e: The Golgi apparatus of a cell consists of one or more dictyosomes, that is, stacks of flat membrane sacs.
122769.m: A Golgi stack is called a dictyosome.

122770.q: In which cells did Camillo Golgi discover the organelle named after him in 1898?
122770.e: Camillo Golgi stained nerve cells with silver salts and discovered a fine network inside the cell. In 1906 he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine.
122770.m: Golgi discovered his organelle in nerve cells.

122771.q: Which side of the Golgi apparatus receives the vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum?
122771.e: The cis side faces the ER and serves as the receiving side; vesicles are sent off from the opposite trans side.
122771.m: The Golgi apparatus receives on the cis side and dispatches on the trans side.

122772.q: What is the main task of the Golgi apparatus?
a: Storing and reading the genetic material
122772.e: In the Golgi apparatus, proteins from the ER are processed further, given address labels and packed into vesicles for their destination.
122772.m: The Golgi apparatus is the post office and packing station of the cell.

122773.q: Which chemical change do many proteins undergo in the Golgi apparatus?
a: They are split into amino acids
They are reduced to fatty acids
122773.e: In the Golgi apparatus, the sugar chains attached in the ER (glycosylation) are modified and extended; this produces glycoproteins.
122773.m: In the Golgi apparatus, many proteins receive their final sugar chains.

122774.q: How are secretory proteins packed by the Golgi apparatus released from the cell?
122774.e: Secretory vesicles move to the cell membrane, fuse with it and empty their contents outside.
122774.m: In exocytosis, vesicles fuse with the cell membrane.

122775.q: Which organelle is formed when vesicles bud off from the Golgi apparatus?
122775.e: Vesicles containing digestive enzymes bud off from the trans side of the Golgi apparatus and become lysosomes.
122775.m: Lysosomes come from the Golgi apparatus.

122776.q: What task do Golgi vesicles perform in plant cells after nuclear division?
122776.e: The vesicles supply material for the new cell wall and fuse in the middle of the cell to form the cell plate, which separates the daughter cells.
122776.m: Plant cells form a cell plate between the daughter cells.

122777.q: In which cells is the Golgi apparatus particularly well developed?
a: In gland cells with a lot of secretion
122777.e: Cells that release many substances, such as goblet cells or cells of the pancreas, need a lot of packing and dispatch capacity.
122777.m: Cells that secrete a lot have a large Golgi apparatus.

122778.e: Ribosomes are complexes of ribosomal RNA and numerous proteins, made up of a large and a small subunit.
122778.m: Ribosomes consist of RNA and proteins.

122779.q: What sedimentation coefficient do the ribosomes in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells have?
122779.e: Eukaryotic ribosomes in the cytoplasm sediment at 80 Svedberg; their subunits are 60S and 40S.
122779.m: 80S ribosomes work in the cytoplasm of eukaryotes.

122780.q: Which step of protein biosynthesis do ribosomes carry out?
122780.e: At the ribosome, the base sequence of the mRNA is translated into a chain of amino acids.
122780.m: Ribosomes translate the mRNA into proteins.

122781.q: What is a group of ribosomes called that read the same mRNA at the same time?
122781.e: Several ribosomes can work one after another on one mRNA; in this way many copies of a protein are made at once.
122781.m: A polysome consists of several ribosomes on one mRNA.

122782.q: Which RNA brings the amino acids to the ribosome?
122782.e: Transfer RNA carries an amino acid and uses its anticodon to recognise the matching codon of the mRNA.
122782.m: The tRNA delivers the amino acids to the ribosome.

122783.q: Why can antibiotics such as tetracycline harm bacteria without seriously disturbing protein synthesis in the human cytoplasm?
