122783.e: The ribosomes of bacteria differ in size and structure from the cytoplasmic ribosomes of humans, so some drugs bind specifically only to the bacterial ones.
122783.m: Many antibiotics specifically attack the ribosomes of bacteria.

122784.q: What distinguishes ribosomes from organelles such as lysosomes or mitochondria?
a: They are larger than the nucleus
122784.e: Ribosomes are molecular complexes without a surrounding membrane and are found in all cells, including bacteria.
122784.m: Ribosomes are not surrounded by a membrane.

122785.q: Roughly what pH is found inside a lysosome?
122785.e: Lysosomes are acidic; their digestive enzymes work best at a pH of around 4.5 to 5.
122785.m: The inside of a lysosome is acidic.

122786.q: What kind of enzymes do lysosomes contain?
122786.e: Lysosomes contain dozens of hydrolytic enzymes that split proteins, nucleic acids, fats and carbohydrates.
122786.m: Lysosomes digest substances with acid hydrolases.

122787.q: Why are lysosomes sometimes called the “stomach” of the cell?
a: They produce stomach acid for the body
They take up food from the intestine
122787.e: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes and break down cell components and particles taken in. They were discovered by the Belgian researcher Christian de Duve.
122787.m: Lysosomes are the digestive vesicles of the cell.

122788.q: What is the process called in which a cell breaks down its own damaged components in lysosomes?
122788.e: In autophagy, cell components are enclosed by a membrane and digested with lysosomes; Yoshinori Ohsumi received the Nobel Prize for this in 2016.
122788.m: In autophagy, the cell recycles its own components.

122789.q: What is the cause of lysosomal storage diseases such as Tay-Sachs disease?
a: A fault in the nuclear envelope
122789.e: If a particular breakdown enzyme is missing, undigested substances build up in the lysosomes; in Tay-Sachs these are gangliosides in nerve cells.
122789.m: In storage diseases, the lysosomes lack a breakdown enzyme.

122790.q: How is the acidic environment in the lysosome maintained?
a: By proton pumps in the membrane
122790.e: An ATP-dependent proton pump (V-ATPase) continuously transports hydrogen ions into the lysosome.
122790.m: Proton pumps keep the lysosome acidic.

122791.q: Why do lysosomal enzymes that get into the cytoplasm usually cause only little damage?
a: They are hardly active at neutral pH
They are immediately converted into ATP
122791.e: The hydrolases need an acidic environment; in the almost neutral cytoplasm (pH about 7.2) they work only weakly.
122791.m: Lysosomal enzymes only work properly in acidic conditions.

122792.q: What is the vesicle called that forms when a phagosome fuses with a lysosome?
122792.e: Phagocytes take bacteria into a phagosome; after fusion with a lysosome, the bacteria are digested in the phagolysosome.
122792.m: Phagocytes digest their prey in the phagolysosome.

122793.q: Which three types of filament make up the cytoskeleton of animal cells?
a: Microtubules, actin filaments and intermediate filaments
Microtubules, collagen fibres and elastin fibres
122793.e: The cytoskeleton consists of microtubules, actin filaments (microfilaments) and intermediate filaments.
122793.m: The cytoskeleton consists of three kinds of filament.

122794.q: Which protein are microtubules made of?
122794.e: Microtubules are hollow tubes made of dimers of alpha and beta tubulin.

122795.q: What tasks does the cytoskeleton perform?
a: It gives the cell its shape and makes movement possible
122795.e: The cytoskeleton is a network of protein fibres. It supports the cell, transports substances and makes movements such as cell division possible.
122795.m: The cytoskeleton is the scaffold and transport network of the cell.

122796.q: Which structure made of microtubules pulls the chromosomes apart during cell division?
122796.e: During mitosis, microtubules form the spindle apparatus. Its fibres attach to the chromosomes and pull the halves to the poles of the cell.
122796.m: The spindle apparatus distributes the chromosomes during cell division.

122797.q: Which protein forms the intermediate filaments in the epithelial cells of the skin?
122797.e: Keratins are typical intermediate filaments of epithelial cells and make skin, hair and nails tough.

122798.q: From which structure do most microtubules originate in animal cells?
122798.e: The centrosome with its two centrioles is the most important organising centre for microtubules in animal cells.

122799.q: Which arrangement of microtubules does a cross-section through a cilium or flagellum of eukaryotes show?
122799.e: Nine doublet microtubules surround two single central microtubules; the motor protein dynein makes the doublets slide against each other.
122799.m: Cilia have nine doublet microtubules around two central ones.

122800.q: Which protein of the cytoskeleton works together with myosin in the muscle cell?
122800.e: During muscle contraction, myosin heads pull on the actin filaments. As a result the filaments slide into each other and the muscle shortens.
122800.m: Actin and myosin make the muscle contract.

122801.q: In which order do the classic phases of mitosis take place?
122801.e: Mitosis begins with prophase, followed by metaphase, anaphase and finally telophase.
122801.m: The phases of mitosis are prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.

122802.q: In which phase of mitosis are the sister chromatids pulled to the poles of the cell?
122802.e: In anaphase, the sister chromatids are separated from each other and pulled by the spindle fibres to opposite poles.
122802.m: In anaphase, the chromatids move apart.

122803.q: To which protein structure of the chromosomes do the spindle fibres attach?
122803.e: The kinetochore is a protein complex at the constriction of the chromosome to which the microtubules of the spindle bind.
122803.m: Spindle fibres attach at the kinetochore.

122804.q: What is the division of the cytoplasm after nuclear division called?
122804.e: Nuclear division (karyokinesis) is followed by cytokinesis, in which the cell body splits into two daughter cells.
122804.m: After nuclear division, cytokinesis divides the cell body.

122805.q: In which phase of mitosis do the chromosomes condense enough to become visible under a light microscope?
122805.e: At the beginning of mitosis the chromatin condenses strongly; the chromosomes become recognisable as threads.
122805.m: In prophase, the chromosomes become visible.

122806.q: In which phase of mitosis do new nuclear envelopes form around the two sets of chromosomes?
122806.e: In telophase the chromosomes uncoil again and new nuclear envelopes and nucleoli form.
122806.m: In telophase, two new nuclei are formed.

122807.q: How is the cytoplasm divided in animal cells at the end of mitosis?
a: By the breakdown of the nucleus
122807.e: A ring of actin and myosin contracts beneath the membrane and pinches the cell in two along a cleavage furrow.
122807.m: Animal cells pinch in two when they divide.

122808.q: In which phase of the cell cycle is the DNA copied?
122808.e: In the synthesis phase (S phase) of interphase, all the DNA is replicated.
122808.m: The DNA is copied in the S phase.

122809.q: What is the state called into which many specialised cells, such as nerve cells, leave the cell cycle?
122809.e: Cells in the G0 phase no longer divide but remain metabolically active; some can re-enter the cycle.
122809.m: Resting cells are in the G0 phase.

122810.q: Which proteins rise and fall periodically in the cell cycle and activate certain kinases that control the process?
122810.e: Cyclins bind to kinases (CDKs) and so allow the transition to the next phase of the cycle; afterwards they are broken down.
122810.m: Cyclins set the rhythm of the cell cycle.

122811.q: Which protein is called the “guardian of the genome” because it stops the cell cycle when DNA is damaged?
122811.e: When DNA is damaged, p53 stops the cycle until the damage is repaired, or triggers programmed cell death; its gene is mutated in many tumours.
122811.m: The protein p53 protects the cell from dividing with damaged DNA.

122812.q: Which stage makes up most of the cell cycle in most dividing cells?
122812.e: Interphase, with the G1, S and G2 phases, usually lasts many hours, while the actual nuclear division takes only about an hour.
122812.m: The cell spends most of its time in interphase.

122813.q: What are genes called that normally slow down cell division and whose failure can contribute to cancer?
122813.e: Tumour suppressor genes inhibit division or promote repair; if both copies fail, this brake is missing.
122813.m: Tumour suppressor genes act as a brake on cell division.

122814.q: What is the limited number of divisions that normal human body cells can go through in cell culture called?
122814.e: In 1961 Leonard Hayflick showed that normal fibroblasts divide only about 40 to 60 times and then stop.
122814.m: Normal body cells cannot divide endlessly.

122815.q: Which ends of the chromosomes become shorter with every cell division in many body cells?
122815.e: DNA polymerase cannot fully copy the end of a strand; that is why, without the enzyme telomerase, the telomeres shorten with each division.
122815.m: Telomeres protect the ends of chromosomes and become shorter with age.

a: The random thermal motion of the particles
122816.e: Particles move randomly because of their thermal energy (Brownian motion); this results in a net flow from the place of higher to the place of lower concentration.
122816.m: Diffusion is based on the random movement of particles.

122817.q: What does Fick's first law state?
a: The flow of particles is proportional to the concentration gradient
The flow of particles is independent of concentration
The pressure is proportional to the temperature
122817.e: According to Adolf Fick, the steeper the concentration gradient, the more substance flows per unit of time.
122817.m: A steeper concentration gradient speeds up diffusion.

122818.q: How does a rise in temperature affect the speed of diffusion?
122818.e: At higher temperatures the particles move faster, and the diffusion coefficient increases.

122819.q: How does glucose passively enter many body cells via GLUT transport proteins?
122819.e: GLUT transporters let glucose pass through the membrane along its concentration gradient without using ATP.
122819.m: Facilitated diffusion uses transport proteins but no energy.

122820.q: Which substance can diffuse most easily straight through the lipid bilayer of a membrane?
122820.e: Small non-polar molecules such as O₂ and CO₂ dissolve in the fatty interior of the membrane; ions and large polar molecules need transport proteins.
122820.m: Small non-polar molecules pass through membranes easily.

122821.q: Why is the huge surface area of the alveoli so important for gas exchange?
a: The amount of diffusion increases with the exchange surface
A large surface raises body temperature
Active transport takes place on large surfaces
122821.e: The flow of diffusing gas is proportional to the area; many small alveoli create a surface of roughly 100 square metres.
122821.m: Large surfaces make fast gas exchange possible.

122822.q: How does the time particles need to diffuse across a distance change if the distance is doubled?
122822.e: The average diffusion time grows with the square of the distance; twice the distance means about four times the time. That is why diffusion is only efficient over short distances.
122822.m: Diffusion is only fast over short distances.

122823.q: What happens once the concentrations have evened out in diffusion?
a: Particles keep moving, but there is no net flow
122823.e: At equilibrium, the same number of particles move in both directions; the concentration therefore stays the same everywhere.
122823.m: Diffusion equilibrium is a dynamic equilibrium.

122824.q: What happens to red blood cells that are placed in distilled water?
a: They shrink into a spiky shape
122824.e: The inside of the cell is more concentrated than pure water; water flows in until the membrane tears (haemolysis).
122824.m: Red blood cells burst in pure water.

122825.q: What is it called when the protoplast pulls away from the cell wall after a plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution?
122825.e: In the hypertonic solution the vacuole loses water, the protoplast shrinks and pulls away from the rigid cell wall.
122825.m: Plant cells undergo plasmolysis in a concentrated solution.

122826.q: What is the internal pressure of a plant cell against its cell wall, which keeps herbaceous plants upright, called?
122826.e: Through osmotic uptake of water, the vacuole presses the cell contents against the cell wall; if water is lacking, the plant wilts.
122826.m: Turgor makes plant parts firm and plump.

122827.q: Which membrane proteins allow water to pass through especially quickly?
122827.e: Aquaporins are water channels; Peter Agre received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2003 for discovering them.
122827.m: Aquaporins are the water channels of the cell membrane.

122828.q: What concentration does a physiological saline solution have, which is roughly isotonic with blood?
122828.e: A solution with 0.9 g of sodium chloride per 100 ml has roughly the same osmotic value as blood plasma.
122828.m: Physiological saline contains 0.9 per cent salt.

122829.q: How does the osmotic pressure of a solution change if the concentration of dissolved particles is doubled?
122829.e: Osmotic pressure is proportional to the number of dissolved particles. Twice as many particles produce about twice the pressure.
122829.m: More dissolved particles mean more osmotic pressure.

122830.q: Why do strawberries release juice when you sprinkle them with sugar?
a: Water moves out by osmosis towards the sugar solution
The sugar dissolves the cell walls
The sugar is actively pumped into the cells
122830.e: The sugar forms a very concentrated solution on the outside; water flows out of the fruit cells.
122830.m: Sugar draws water out of fruit by osmosis.

a: It uses an ion gradient that was built up beforehand
It splits ATP directly at the transporter
It only takes place in plant cells
It works without a transport protein
122831.e: A secondary active transporter couples the movement of a substance to the backflow of ions whose gradient was built up by an ATP-driven pump.
122831.m: Secondary active transport uses the energy from ATP indirectly.

122832.q: What is transport called in which two substances are carried in the same direction at the same time?
122832.e: In symport, two substances move together in the same direction through the same transport protein.
122832.m: In symport, two substances travel together in the same direction.

122833.q: What fundamentally distinguishes active transport from diffusion?
a: It works against a concentration gradient
122833.e: Active transport can move substances from a place of lower to a place of higher concentration and needs energy for this, usually from ATP.
122833.m: Active transport needs energy and can work against the gradient.

122834.q: What is the uptake of droplets of fluid by infolding of the cell membrane called?
122834.e: In pinocytosis (“cell drinking”), the membrane pinches off small vesicles of fluid towards the inside; this vesicle transport needs energy.
122834.m: In pinocytosis, the cell drinks small amounts of fluid.

122835.q: Which medicines inhibit the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase of the parietal cells and so reduce stomach acid?
122835.e: Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole block the pump that transports hydrogen ions into the stomach.
122835.m: Proton pump inhibitors slow down acid production in the stomach.

122836.q: Which German physicist built the first electron microscope with Max Knoll from 1931 and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1986?
122836.e: Ernst Ruska developed the electron microscope with Max Knoll at the Technical University of Berlin and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986.
122836.m: Ernst Ruska is regarded as the inventor of the electron microscope.

122837.q: Which Swiss biophysicist from the University of Lausanne received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for contributions to cryo-electron microscopy?
122837.e: Jacques Dubochet developed a method of freezing samples in a flash in glass-like ice; he shared the prize with Joachim Frank and Richard Henderson.
122837.m: Jacques Dubochet made biomolecules in ice visible for the electron microscope.

122838.q: Why does an electron microscope achieve a much higher resolution than a light microscope?
a: Electrons have a much shorter wavelength
122838.e: Resolving power depends on the wavelength; fast electrons have a wavelength of only a few picometres.

122839.q: Why must there be a high vacuum in the electron microscope?
a: Air molecules would scatter the electrons
Electrons only form from light in a vacuum
122839.e: Electrons are deflected by even a few gas molecules; without a vacuum the beam would become blurred and weakened.
122839.m: Electron microscopes work in a vacuum.

122840.q: Which type of microscope produces three-dimensional-looking images of surfaces, such as the head of a fly?
a: Stereo magnifier with a light source
122840.e: The SEM scans the surface with a fine beam of electrons and analyses the electrons knocked out; this produces images that look three-dimensional.
122840.m: The scanning electron microscope shows surfaces in three dimensions.

122841.q: What is used to focus the electron beam in an electron microscope?
122841.e: Electrons are deflected by magnetic fields; coils carrying a current therefore act as electromagnetic lenses.

122842.q: Why do images from the electron microscope originally appear only in shades of grey?
a: Electrons have no colour as visible light does
The electrons are sent through colour filters
122842.e: Colours arise from different wavelengths of visible light. Electron images only show how strongly electrons are scattered; coloured images have been coloured in afterwards.
122842.m: Coloured electron microscope images are coloured in afterwards.

122843.q: Which cell structure can be clearly seen in the electron microscope but not in the light microscope?
122843.e: Ribosomes measure only around 20 to 30 nm and are therefore far below the resolution limit of the light microscope of about 200 nm.
122843.m: Ribosomes can only be seen in the electron microscope.

122844.q: Which plastids store large amounts of starch in potato tubers?
122844.e: Amyloplasts are colourless plastids that build glucose into starch grains and store them.
122844.m: Amyloplasts are the starch stores of the plant cell.

122845.q: Which plastids give ripe tomatoes and carrots their red to orange colour?
122845.e: Chromoplasts contain carotenoids such as lycopene or beta-carotene and colour fruits, roots and flowers.

122846.q: What are the reaction spaces of a eukaryotic cell that are separated by membranes called?
122846.e: Membranes divide the cell into compartments so that opposing metabolic processes such as building up and breaking down can take place at the same time.
122846.m: Membranes divide the cell into separate reaction spaces.

122847.q: What are the fine channels called that connect neighbouring plant cells through the cell wall?
122847.e: Plasmodesmata are channels lined with membrane through which the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells is connected.
122847.m: Plasmodesmata connect plant cells to each other.

122848.q: Which proteins inside the rough ER help newly made chains to find their correct shape?
122848.e: Chaperones such as BiP bind to unfolded protein chains in the ER and support their correct folding; misfolded proteins are sorted out.
122848.m: Chaperones help proteins to fold correctly.

122849.q: At which constricted point are the two sister chromatids of a chromosome joined?
122849.e: The centromere is the constriction of the chromosome; there the chromatids remain joined until they are separated.
122849.m: Sister chromatids are joined at the centromere.

122850.q: What is the result of mitosis?
a: Four cells with half a set of chromosomes
Two cells with different genetic material
One cell with a double nucleus
122850.e: In mitosis, each chromosome is distributed evenly between two nuclei. The daughter cells have the same genetic material as the parent cell. Four cells with half a set are produced in meiosis.
122850.m: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells.

122851.q: What is transport called in which two substances are carried in opposite directions at the same time?
122851.e: An antiporter exchanges substances, for example the sodium-calcium exchanger, which carries calcium out of the cell while sodium flows in.
122851.m: In antiport, two substances are exchanged for each other.

122852.q: Why do drinking solutions for diarrhoea contain a little sugar as well as salt?
a: Sugar helps the intestine take up sodium and therefore water
Sugar stops the movement of the intestine
Sugar makes the solution keep longer
122852.e: In the small intestine, glucose and sodium are taken up together by a transporter. Water follows, so the body loses less fluid.
122852.m: Sugar and salt together help the intestine to take up water.

122853.q: Which pump uses ATP to transport sodium out of the cell and potassium into the cell?
122853.e: The sodium-potassium pump carries three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in. It maintains the resting potential of the cells.
122853.m: The sodium-potassium pump works with energy from ATP.

122854.q: What disadvantage does electron microscopy have compared with light microscopy for biological samples?
a: No preparation at all is needed
122854.e: There is a vacuum in the electron microscope, and samples are fixed, sliced or frozen. Living cells in motion cannot be viewed in this way.
122854.m: You cannot see living cells in the electron microscope.

123154.q: What is the thin layer called on which epithelial cells sit and which separates them from the tissue underneath?
123154.e: The basement membrane is a thin layer of extracellular material. It anchors the epithelium and separates it from the tissue below.
123154.m: Epithelial cells sit on a basement membrane.

123155.q: Which type of epithelium forms the human epidermis?
123155.e: The epidermis consists of many layers of cells, the top ones of which become horny and flake off. This protects the skin well against friction and drying out.
123155.m: The epidermis consists of stratified keratinised squamous epithelium.

123156.q: Which epithelium lines the bladder and adapts to the strong stretching as it fills?
123156.e: Transitional epithelium (urothelium) can change its height: when the bladder is empty it looks many-layered, when full it is flatter. It is found in the urinary tract.
123156.m: The bladder is lined with stretchy transitional epithelium.

123157.q: Which property is typical of epithelial tissue?
a: It has a great deal of intercellular substance
123157.e: Epithelia have no blood vessels. They are nourished by diffusion from the well-supplied tissue underneath.
123157.m: Epithelial tissue is supplied by diffusion without its own blood vessels.

123158.q: What do the cilia of the epithelium in the airways move along?
a: Mucus with dust towards the throat
123158.e: The cilia beat in a coordinated way and push the mucus with trapped particles and germs upwards. There it is swallowed or coughed up.
123158.m: Ciliated epithelium cleans the airways by moving mucus upwards.

123159.q: Which type of epithelium lines the alveoli and allows fast gas exchange because it is so thin?
123159.e: In the alveoli the wall is made only of very flat cells. This makes the diffusion path for oxygen and carbon dioxide very short.
123159.m: Thin simple squamous epithelium makes gas exchange in the lungs easier.

123160.q: What are the cell junctions called that seal neighbouring epithelial cells so tightly that hardly any substances get through between them?
123160.e: Tight junctions (zonula occludens) form a belt around the cells and seal the space between them. In this way the lining of the intestine, for example, controls which substances are taken up.
123160.m: Tight junctions seal epithelia against uncontrolled passage of substances.

123161.q: What is a malignant tumour that starts in epithelial tissue called?
123161.e: Carcinomas arise from epithelial cells, for example in the skin, lungs or intestine. They are the most common group of malignant tumours.
123161.m: A carcinoma is a malignant tumour of epithelial tissue.

123162.q: Which protein is the most common structural protein of connective tissue and makes tendons particularly strong under tension?
123162.e: Collagen forms tear-resistant fibres found in tendons, ligaments, bones and skin. It is the most common protein in the human body.
123162.m: Collagen fibres make tendons strong under tension.

123163.q: Which cells produce the fibres and ground substance in loose connective tissue?
123163.e: Fibroblasts are the typical cells of connective tissue. They make fibre proteins and components of the ground substance and are important in wound healing.
123163.m: Fibroblasts build the fibres of connective tissue.

123164.q: What is the whole of fibres and ground substance lying between the cells in connective tissue called?
123164.e: In connective tissue, the cells lie loosely scattered in a lot of intercellular substance. This extracellular matrix determines whether the tissue is firm, elastic or soft.
123164.m: Connective tissue consists largely of extracellular matrix.

123165.q: A lack of which vitamin disturbs the formation of stable connective tissue fibres and leads to the disease scurvy?
123165.e: Vitamin C is needed for an enzyme that stabilises the fibre proteins. Without it, bleeding gums, poor wound healing and bleeding occur.
123165.m: A lack of vitamin C causes scurvy.

123166.q: What are the cells called that store fat in fatty tissue?
123166.e: Adipocytes store fat in large droplets. Fatty tissue serves as an energy store, heat insulation and padding.

123167.q: Which fatty tissue can produce heat directly by burning fat, especially in babies?
123167.e: Brown fat cells contain a great many mitochondria with the protein thermogenin. As a result, energy is released as heat instead of as ATP.

123168.q: Which fibres make sure that skin or artery walls return to their shape after being stretched?
123168.e: Elastic fibres consist mainly of elastin and can be stretched like rubber. Their amount decreases with age, which is why the skin becomes more wrinkled.
123168.m: Elastic fibres make tissue stretchy and springy.

123169.q: Which two types of cell make up nervous tissue?
123169.e: Nerve cells (neurons) conduct and process signals. Glial cells support, nourish and insulate them.
123169.m: Nervous tissue consists of nerve cells and glial cells.

123170.q: Which glial cells form the myelin sheath around axons in the peripheral nervous system?
123170.e: Schwann cells wrap themselves several times around an axon and insulate it electrically. In the brain and spinal cord, other glial cells perform this task.
123170.m: In the peripheral nervous system, Schwann cells form the myelin.

123171.q: What are the uncovered points between two sections of myelin called, where the impulse jumps from point to point?
123171.e: The action potential only arises at the bare points between the sections of myelin. This saltatory conduction is much faster than continuous conduction.
123171.m: At the nodes of Ranvier, the impulse jumps along the axon.

123172.q: Which glial cells take on the role of immune and scavenger cells in the brain?
123172.e: Microglial cells remove pathogens, dead cells and waste products. They are the resident defence cells of the central nervous system.
123172.m: Microglia are the defence cells of the brain.

123173.q: What is the point of contact called where a nerve cell passes its signal on to another cell with the help of messenger substances?
123173.e: At a chemical synapse, neurotransmitters are released into a narrow gap. They bind to receptors on the next cell and trigger a response there.
123173.m: At synapses, a signal is transmitted with neurotransmitters.

123174.q: Which muscle tissue is striated but works involuntarily?
123174.e: Like skeletal muscle, heart muscle cells show striations. However, they are not controlled voluntarily but by the heart's own system for generating impulses.
123174.m: Heart muscle is striated and works involuntarily.

123175.q: Which two proteins slide past each other when a muscle contracts?
123175.e: The myosin heads pull on the actin filaments and push them towards each other. In this way the muscle shortens without the filaments themselves becoming shorter.
123175.m: During contraction, actin and myosin slide past each other.

123176.q: Which ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and trigger muscle contraction?
123176.e: Calcium binds to troponin and so frees the binding sites on the actin. Only then can the myosin heads grab hold.

123177.q: Which substance is needed so that the myosin heads can let go of the actin again?
123177.e: Only the binding of ATP releases the connection between myosin and actin. After death there is no ATP, which is why the muscles stay stiff in rigor mortis.
123177.m: Without ATP, a muscle cannot relax again.

123178.q: How do the multinucleated skeletal muscle fibres form during development?
a: By nuclear division without cell division
123178.e: Myoblasts with a single nucleus fuse into long muscle fibres with many nuclei. Such a structure is called a syncytium.
123178.m: Skeletal muscle fibres form by the fusion of many cells.

123179.q: What are the junctions between heart muscle cells called, through which the impulse spreads quickly from cell to cell?
123179.e: Intercalated discs contain mechanical anchoring junctions and gap junctions. The impulse flows directly into the neighbouring cell through these channels.
123179.m: Intercalated discs connect heart muscle cells mechanically and electrically.

123180.q: What usually distinguishes adult stem cells from embryonic stem cells?
a: They only form cells of their own tissue
They form all cell types of the body
123180.e: Adult stem cells are usually multipotent: they renew a particular tissue, such as blood or skin. Embryonic stem cells, on the other hand, can form a great many cell types.
123180.m: Adult stem cells are usually limited to their own tissue.

123181.q: Which stem cells constantly replace all the blood cells in adults?
123181.e: Haematopoietic, that is blood-forming, stem cells produce red and white blood cells and platelets. In this way billions of new blood cells are formed every day.
123181.m: Haematopoietic stem cells are the source of all blood cells.

123182.q: Where are most blood-forming stem cells found in adults?
123182.e: In adults, blood formation takes place mainly in the red bone marrow of the pelvis, vertebrae, ribs and breastbone.
123182.m: In adults, blood is formed in the red bone marrow.

123183.q: Which disease has been treated for decades with the transplantation of blood-forming stem cells?
123183.e: In leukaemia, the diseased blood cells are destroyed and the blood system is rebuilt with healthy stem cells. The stem cells come from a donor or from the patient themselves.
123183.m: Stem cell transplants can save lives in leukaemia.

123184.q: Which two properties characterise every stem cell?
a: Self-renewal and the formation of specialised cells
123184.e: A stem cell can divide and in doing so form stem cells again. At the same time it can produce daughter cells that specialise.
123184.m: Stem cells renew themselves and supply specialised cells.

123185.q: Which cells can develop from mesenchymal stem cells?
123185.e: Mesenchymal stem cells are found, for example, in bone marrow and fatty tissue. They can develop into cells of the supporting tissues.
123185.m: Mesenchymal stem cells supply cells for bone, cartilage and fat.

123186.q: Why does the lining of the intestine need a particularly large number of stem cells?
a: Its cells are renewed every few days
123186.e: The cells of the intestinal lining are under heavy strain and are shed after a few days. Stem cells at the base of the lining constantly supply replacements.
123186.m: The lining of the intestine renews itself every few days.

123187.q: What is the special environment in a tissue called that keeps a stem cell in its stem cell state?
123187.e: In the niche, neighbouring cells and the matrix give signals that control the division and specialisation of the stem cell. If a daughter cell leaves the niche, it begins to specialise.
123187.m: The stem cell niche controls the behaviour of stem cells.

123188.q: How are blood-forming stem cells obtained from most donors today?
a: From the blood after a growth factor is given
By an operation on the liver
From a sample of the lining of the mouth
123188.e: A growth factor (G-CSF) draws the stem cells out of the bone marrow into the blood. There they are filtered out with a cell separator; less often, bone marrow is taken directly from the hip bone.
123188.m: Blood stem cells are usually collected from the donor's blood.

123189.q: What is meant by cell differentiation?
a: The specialisation of a cell for a task
The division of a cell into two identical cells
The programmed death of a cell
123189.e: In differentiation, a cell that is not very specialised develops into a particular cell type with its own shape and function, for example a nerve cell.

123190.q: Why do a liver cell and a nerve cell of the same person differ even though they have the same DNA?
a: Different genes are active in each
Only one of the two has mutations
123190.e: All body cells basically carry the same genetic material. But depending on the cell type, they switch different genes on or off.
123190.m: Cell types differ in their gene activity, not in their DNA.

123191.q: What are cells called that can develop into all cell types of the three germ layers?
123191.e: Pluripotent cells such as embryonic stem cells can form cells of all three germ layers. Multipotent cells are limited to a few cell types.
123191.m: Pluripotent cells can form a great many different cell types.

123192.q: Which researcher received the 2012 Nobel Prize in Medicine together with John Gurdon for reprogramming specialised body cells?
123192.e: In 2006 Shinya Yamanaka showed that a few genes are enough to return skin cells to a stem cell-like state. These cells are called induced pluripotent stem cells.
123192.m: Shinya Yamanaka discovered how to reprogramme body cells.

123193.q: What are proteins called that bind to DNA and control which genes are read?
123193.e: Transcription factors bind to control sections of the DNA and switch genes on or off. Certain combinations determine which cell type develops.
123193.m: Transcription factors switch genes on and off.

123194.q: Which chemical change to DNA often switches genes off permanently in specialised cells?
123194.e: Methyl groups on certain sections of DNA prevent genes from being read. Such epigenetic marks are passed on during cell division.
123194.m: DNA methylation can silence genes without changing the base sequence.

123195.q: What is the well-known image called that shows cell differentiation as a ball rolling down a slope with branching valleys?
123195.e: In 1957 the biologist Conrad Waddington described development as a ball rolling into one of several valleys. The further down it is, the more fixed the cell type.
123195.m: The epigenetic landscape illustrates how cells become committed.

123196.q: From which germ layer of the embryo does the nervous system develop?
123196.e: The outer germ layer forms the epidermis and the nervous system. The inner layer gives rise to the lining of the intestine and lungs, for example, and the middle layer to muscles and bones.
123196.m: The nervous system develops from the ectoderm.

123197.q: What is the aim of tissue engineering?
a: To make working tissue in the laboratory
123197.e: In tissue engineering, cells, carrier materials and growth factors are combined. This produces tissue intended to replace or repair damaged tissue.
123197.m: Tissue engineering grows replacement tissue from living cells.

123198.q: What is the supporting framework called on which the cells grow in tissue engineering?
123198.e: A scaffold gives the cells a three-dimensional shape. It is often made of biodegradable plastics or natural biomaterials.
123198.m: In tissue engineering, cells grow on a scaffold.

123199.q: Why are the patient's own cells preferred in tissue engineering?
123199.e: The body's own (autologous) cells are recognised by the immune system as its own. That is why no long-term medicines against rejection are needed.
123199.m: Autologous cells are not rejected by the immune system.

123200.q: Which tissue has been made from cultured cells since the 1980s, for example for people with extensive burns?
123200.e: From a small skin sample, skin cells can be multiplied in the laboratory into thin layers. These can be transferred onto large wounds.
123200.m: Cultured skin helps with severe burns.

123201.q: Which method builds up tissue structures layer by layer from cells and gel?
123201.e: In 3D bioprinting, “bio-inks” containing living cells are printed layer by layer. In this way shapes such as cartilage or blood vessels can be built up precisely.

123202.q: What is a bioreactor used for in tissue engineering?
a: It supplies growing tissue with nutrients in a controlled way
It breaks tissue down into single molecules
It stains tissue for the microscope
123202.e: In the bioreactor, temperature, oxygen, nutrients and often mechanical stimuli are regulated. This helps the cells develop properties typical of the tissue.
123202.m: A bioreactor creates ideal growing conditions for tissue.

123203.q: Which method removes cartilage cells, multiplies them in the laboratory and inserts them into a cartilage defect?
123203.e: In this procedure, healthy cartilage cells are taken from a part of the joint under little strain. After being multiplied, they fill the damage, for example in the knee.
123203.m: Cartilage damage can be treated with the patient's own cultured cartilage cells.

123204.q: What is one of the greatest difficulties in growing thick tissues and whole organs?
123204.e: Oxygen only reaches about 0.1 to 0.2 millimetres into tissue from a blood vessel by diffusion. Without a network of vessels, thick tissue dies on the inside.
123204.m: Grown organs need their own network of blood vessels.

123205.q: In which process are all the cells removed from a donor organ so that only the framework of matrix remains?
123205.e: The cells are washed out with mild detergents. The remaining framework can then be repopulated with the patient's cells.
123205.m: Decellularised organs serve as natural scaffolds.

a: A tiny organ-like tissue from cell culture
An artificial organ made of plastic
A benign tumour of an organ
A cell organelle in the cytoplasm
123206.e: Organoids are three-dimensional clusters of cells, often only a few millimetres in size. They reproduce the structure and some functions of a real organ.
123206.m: Organoids are mini-organs from the culture dish.

123207.q: From which cells are organoids usually grown?
123207.e: Organoids develop from adult stem cells of a tissue or from pluripotent stem cells. In a suitable environment the cells organise themselves.

123208.q: What can organoids from a patient's tumour tissue be used for?
123208.e: Tumour organoids can be used in the laboratory to test which medicine works. In this way treatment can be better adapted to the individual person.
123208.m: Tumour organoids help to find the right treatment.

123209.q: In which material are organoids usually embedded as they grow, to imitate the natural environment of the cells?
a: In a hydrogel made of matrix proteins
123209.e: A gel-like mixture of extracellular matrix proteins gives the cells support in three dimensions. Growth factors in the nutrient medium guide their development.
123209.m: Organoids grow in a gel that imitates the cell environment.

a: As big as a real organ
123210.e: Organoids are three-dimensional clusters of cells, often only a few millimetres in size. Without blood vessels they cannot grow larger, because nutrients do not reach the inside.
123210.m: Organoids are only a few millimetres in size.

123211.q: What are organoids called that reproduce parts of the human brain?
123211.e: Brain organoids develop layers of nerve cells like those found in early brain development. They are used to study, for example, malformations caused by the Zika virus.
123211.m: Brain organoids help us understand how the brain develops.

123212.q: What do most of today's organoids lack compared with real organs?
123212.e: Organoids usually consist of only a few cell types of an organ. Without blood vessels they stay small, and without immune cells some diseases are hard to model.
123212.m: Organoids usually lack blood vessels and immune cells.

123213.q: What advantage do human organoids have over many animal experiments?
a: They are made of human cells
They live for an unlimited time
123213.e: Medicines sometimes work differently in animals than in humans. Organoids made of human cells can partly avoid such differences.

123214.q: Organoids are seen as a possible alternative to animal experiments. What is the principle “Replace, Reduce, Refine” called, which a dedicated competence centre promotes in Switzerland?
123214.e: The 3R principle calls for animal experiments to be replaced, reduced and made gentler. In Switzerland, the Swiss 3R Competence Centre promotes such methods.
123214.m: The 3R principle aims to replace, reduce and refine animal experiments.

123215.q: What distinguishes a malignant tumour from a benign one?
a: It grows destructively into neighbouring tissue
It is always surrounded by a capsule
123215.e: Malignant tumours grow invasively, which means they break through tissue boundaries and destroy surrounding tissue. Benign tumours only push the tissue aside.
123215.m: Malignant tumours grow invasively into neighbouring tissue.

123216.q: What is a malignant tumour called that starts in connective or supporting tissue such as bone?
123216.e: Sarcomas arise from mesenchymal cells, for example from bone, cartilage, muscle or fatty tissue. They are much rarer than tumours of covering tissue.
123216.m: A sarcoma is a malignant tumour of connective or supporting tissue.

123217.q: What is a benign tumour called that arises from glandular tissue?
123217.e: Adenomas are benign growths of glandular epithelium, for example polyps in the large intestine. Some can become malignant over time.
123217.m: An adenoma is a benign tumour of a gland.

123218.q: What is the formation of new blood vessels called, by which a growing tumour supplies itself with oxygen?
123218.e: Once it reaches a size of a few millimetres, a tumour needs its own vessels. It sends out signalling substances such as VEGF that make vessels grow in.
123218.m: Tumours trigger angiogenesis to supply themselves.

123219.q: Which process do cancer cells avoid that normally makes damaged cells die in a controlled way?
123219.e: Apoptosis is programmed cell death. Cancer cells often switch off this self-destruction programme and survive despite damage to their genetic material.
123219.m: Cancer cells escape programmed cell death.

123220.q: What does the letter T stand for in the TNM classification of tumours?
a: Size and extent of the primary tumour
123220.e: T describes the original tumour, N the involvement of lymph nodes and M distant spread. Together they determine the stage and the treatment.
123220.m: The TNM classification describes how far a tumour has spread.

123221.q: Which malignant skin cancer starts in the pigment cells of the skin?
123221.e: Malignant melanoma arises from melanocytes. Heavy UV exposure and sunburn increase the risk; Switzerland has many cases compared with the rest of Europe.
123221.m: Melanoma arises from the pigment cells of the skin.

123222.q: What is the removal of a tissue sample that is examined under the microscope to identify a tumour with certainty called?
123222.e: In a biopsy, a small piece of tissue is removed. Only the examination of the cells shows for certain whether a tumour is benign or malignant.
123222.m: A biopsy provides tissue for a reliable diagnosis.

a: A secondary tumour far from the original tumour
A benign tumour with a capsule
A scar after a cancer operation
123223.e: Metastases form when cancer cells break away, travel through the body and grow again somewhere else. They consist of cells of the original tumour.
123223.m: Metastases are offshoots of a tumour in other parts of the body.

123224.q: By which two main routes do cancer cells spread through the body?
a: Through lymph vessels and blood vessels
123224.e: Cancer cells enter lymph vessels and reach lymph nodes. Through the blood vessels they reach distant organs such as the lungs, liver, bones or brain.
123224.m: Cancer cells spread through the lymph and the blood.

123225.q: What is the first lymph node in the drainage area of a tumour, which is specifically examined during operations, called?
123225.e: The sentinel lymph node is tracked down with a marker. If it is free of cancer cells, the other lymph nodes are usually not affected either.
123225.m: The sentinel lymph node shows whether a tumour has spread to the lymph nodes.

123226.q: What must cancer cells be able to do in order to form metastases?
a: Break away from the group of cells and move
123226.e: Normally cells stick firmly together. Cancer cells that spread release these connections, become mobile and enter blood or lymph vessels.
123226.m: To form metastases, cancer cells must become mobile.

123227.q: Why do some tumours spread preferentially to very particular organs?
a: Because the cancer cells find good conditions for growth there
Because these organs have no immune system
Because cancer cells from food collect there
Because these organs have no blood vessels
123227.e: The surgeon Stephen Paget compared cancer cells to seeds that only thrive in suitable soil. Certain organs offer them particularly favourable conditions.
123227.m: Metastases grow where the soil suits the cancer cells.

123228.q: Through which blood vessel do cells from a bowel tumour usually reach the liver first?
123228.e: Blood from the intestine flows first into the liver through the portal vein. That is why liver metastases are especially common in bowel cancer.
123228.m: Bowel cancer often spreads to the liver through the portal vein.

123229.q: What is the original tumour from which the secondary tumours start called?
123229.e: The primary tumour is the place where the cancer arose. Even metastases in the liver, in bowel cancer for example, consist of bowel cancer cells.
123229.m: Metastases come from the primary tumour.

123230.q: What is the actual cause of death in most cancer patients?
123230.e: A tumour that is confined to one place can often be removed by surgery. If, however, metastases have formed in vital organs, the disease is much harder to cure.
123230.m: Metastases are responsible for most cancer deaths.

123231.q: What are cancer cells called that can be detected in the blood and are looked for in a liquid biopsy, for example?
123231.e: Circulating tumour cells have broken away from the tumour and float in the blood. Detecting them can give clues about the spread and course of the disease.
123231.m: Circulating tumour cells are cancer cells in the blood.

a: A changed gene that drives cell growth excessively
A gene that stops cell division
A gene that only occurs in viruses
123232.e: Oncogenes arise by mutation from normal growth genes. Their product is permanently active and drives the cell to uncontrolled division.
123232.m: An oncogene acts like a stuck accelerator pedal for cell division.

123233.q: What is the normal, unchanged precursor of an oncogene called?
123233.e: Proto-oncogenes normally control growth and division. Only a mutation, multiplication or rearrangement turns them into oncogenes.
123233.m: A proto-oncogene can become an oncogene through mutation.

123234.q: Which tumour suppressor gene is called the “guardian of the genome” and is mutated in around half of all cancers?
123234.e: The protein p53 stops cell division when DNA is damaged or triggers cell death. If it fails, damaged cells can multiply unchecked.
123234.m: The TP53 gene protects the cell from damaged genetic material.

123235.q: Why does a mutated oncogene such as KRAS constantly drive the growth of a cell?
a: Its protein stays switched on all the time
123235.e: KRAS makes a switch protein that passes on growth signals. Because of the mutation it can no longer be switched off, much like a stuck accelerator pedal.
123235.m: Mutated oncogenes send growth signals all the time.

123236.q: What has happened in the Philadelphia chromosome, which occurs in one form of leukaemia?
a: One chromosome is present three times
123236.e: Chromosomes 9 and 22 exchange pieces. This creates a fusion gene whose protein is permanently active and makes the blood cells proliferate.
123236.m: The Philadelphia chromosome forms when two chromosomes exchange pieces.

123237.q: According to which hypothesis must both copies of a tumour suppressor gene usually fail for cancer to develop?
123237.e: In 1971 Alfred Knudson concluded from cases of retinoblastoma that two mutations are needed. If someone has already inherited a defective copy, a second hit is enough.
123237.m: Tumour suppressor genes usually need two hits.

123238.q: What is a tumour suppressor gene?
a: A gene that slows down uncontrolled cell division
A gene that drives cell growth excessively
A gene that only occurs in tumours
A gene that makes antibodies against tumours
123238.e: Tumour suppressor genes such as TP53 act like brakes on cell division. If they fail, damaged cells can multiply unchecked.
123238.m: Tumour suppressor genes are the brakes of cell division.

123239.q: What is the multiplication of a gene called, by which MYCN, for example, becomes overactive in neuroblastoma?
123239.e: In gene amplification, there are many copies of a gene. The cell then makes far too much protein, which drives growth.
123239.m: Gene amplification can turn a proto-oncogene into an oncogene.

123240.q: Why is a single mutated copy of an oncogene usually enough to have an effect?
a: Because the mutation increases the gene's function
Because the second allele is always missing
Because oncogenes lie in the mitochondria
Because the cell breaks down the gene immediately
123240.e: Oncogene mutations lead to a gain of function; the changed protein is overactive. The intact second copy cannot make up for this, so the effect is dominant.
123240.m: Oncogenes act dominantly because they increase a function.

123241.q: On which cells do classic cytostatic drugs have a particularly strong effect?
a: On cells with a lot of fat
123241.e: Cytostatic drugs disrupt DNA copying or cell division. Cancer cells often divide quickly and are therefore hit hard.
123241.m: Cytostatic drugs mainly attack cells that divide rapidly.

123242.q: Against which common side effect of chemotherapy are medicines such as ondansetron used?
123242.e: Ondansetron blocks serotonin receptors that trigger the urge to vomit. Such antiemetics make chemotherapy much more bearable.

123243.q: From the bark of which tree was the cancer drug paclitaxel originally obtained?
123243.e: Paclitaxel originally came from the bark of the Pacific yew. It prevents cancer cells from dividing. Today it is produced semi-synthetically.
123243.m: Paclitaxel originally came from the yew.

123244.q: Why do people lose their hair with many chemotherapies?
a: Hair root cells divide quickly and are damaged too
The medicines dissolve the hair chemically
The scalp is cooled during the treatment
The body needs the hair as an energy reserve
123244.e: Cytostatic drugs hit all cells that divide rapidly. Besides cancer cells, these include the cells of the hair roots. After treatment the hair usually grows back.
123244.m: Hair loss happens because hair root cells also divide quickly.

123245.q: From which chemical warfare agent were the first cytostatic drugs developed in the 1940s?
123245.e: It was observed that mustard gas greatly reduces the number of white blood cells. This led to the nitrogen mustard compounds that were used against lymphomas.
123245.m: The first chemotherapy drugs go back to mustard gas.

123246.q: What distinguishes a targeted cancer therapy such as imatinib, developed in Basel, from classic chemotherapy?
a: It specifically blocks a particular cancer protein
It is always used during surgery
It irradiates the tumour from outside
123246.e: Classic cytostatic drugs damage all cells that divide quickly. Imatinib, by contrast, specifically inhibits an overactive enzyme in leukaemia cells and so tends to spare healthy cells.
123246.m: Targeted cancer therapies attack a particular cancer protein.

123247.q: Why is chemotherapy sometimes given before a cancer operation?
a: To make the wound heal faster
123247.e: A smaller tumour can be removed more easily and more completely. Specialists call treatment before an operation neoadjuvant.
123247.m: Chemotherapy before an operation can shrink the tumour.

123248.q: What do many cytostatic drugs disrupt in cancer cells so that they can no longer divide?
123248.e: Before each division, a cell must copy its DNA. Many cytostatic drugs block this step, for example by depriving the cell of DNA building blocks.
123248.m: Cytostatic drugs prevent DNA copying before cell division.

123249.q: Why is chemotherapy usually given in cycles with breaks?
a: So that healthy tissue can recover
So that the tumour grows faster
Because otherwise the medicines go off
Because hospitals are closed at night
123249.e: Healthy dividing cells, for example in the bone marrow, are also damaged. During the breaks they can regenerate before the next cycle.
123249.m: Breaks between cycles protect healthy tissue.

123250.q: Which glial cells form an important part of the blood-brain barrier with their extensions?
123250.e: Astrocytes wrap their end feet around the blood capillaries in the brain. Together with the tightly connected vessel cells, they control which substances get into the brain.
123250.m: Astrocytes are important for the blood-brain barrier.

123251.q: At which point on a nerve cell is it decided whether an action potential is triggered?
123251.e: At the axon hillock, the incoming signals are added up. If the threshold is exceeded there, an action potential arises and travels along the axon.
123251.m: The axon hillock decides whether an action potential is triggered.

123252.q: What is the point of contact between a motor nerve fibre and a skeletal muscle fibre called?
123252.e: At the motor end plate, the nerve ending passes the impulse on to the muscle fibre. This special synapse triggers every voluntary movement.
123252.m: At the motor end plate, the nerve controls the muscle.

123253.q: Which neurotransmitter is released when a motor nerve stimulates a skeletal muscle?
123253.e: Acetylcholine binds to receptors in the muscle fibre membrane and opens ion channels. The arrow poison curare blocks these receptors and so paralyses the muscles.
123253.m: Acetylcholine transmits the signal from the nerve to the skeletal muscle.

123401.q: Which plants are typical of the Arctic tundra?
123401.e: Only low plants that can cope with cold and a short growing season grow in the tundra. Dwarf willows and dwarf birches hardly reach knee height.
123401.m: The tundra is dominated by mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs.

123542.q: Why can you not see the DNA double helix in a light microscope?
a: It is only a few nanometres thick
It is as transparent as water
123542.e: The double helix is only around 2 nanometres thick. Light microscopes only show structures from about 200 nanometres.
123542.m: The DNA double helix is too thin for the light microscope.

123543.q: Whose X-ray diffraction image (Photo 51) provided an important clue to the helical structure of DNA?
123543.e: Rosalind Franklin and her doctoral student Raymond Gosling took the famous image “Photo 51”. The typical X-shaped pattern points to a helix.
123543.m: Rosalind Franklin's Photo 51 revealed the helical shape of DNA.

123544.q: What is the “backbone” of every DNA strand made of?
123544.e: The nucleotides are linked by phosphodiester bonds between the sugar deoxyribose and phosphate groups. The bases point inwards.
123544.m: Sugar and phosphate form the backbone of DNA.

123545.q: Roughly how many base pairs make up one turn of the common B-DNA?
123545.e: In the B form of DNA, one full turn of the helix contains around 10 to 10.5 base pairs. This can be worked out from X-ray diffraction data.
123545.m: One turn of B-DNA has around ten base pairs.

123546.q: Roughly what diameter does the DNA double helix have?
123546.e: B-DNA is about 2 nanometres thick. That makes it far too thin to be visible in a light microscope.
123546.m: The DNA double helix is only around two nanometres thick.

123547.q: In which direction is natural B-DNA twisted?
123547.e: B-DNA is a right-handed helix. There is also left-handed Z-DNA, but it is rare.
123547.m: Normal DNA is a right-handed helix.

123548.q: Which bonds hold the two strands of the double helix together?
123548.e: The opposite bases are connected by hydrogen bonds. In addition, stacking forces between the bases stabilise the helix.
123548.m: Hydrogen bonds connect the two DNA strands.

123549.q: What are the two grooves of different widths on the surface of the double helix called?
123549.e: Because the sugars of the two strands do not lie exactly opposite each other, a major and a minor groove form. Many proteins bind to the DNA there.
123549.m: The double helix has a major and a minor groove.

123550.q: What is the complementary strand to 5'-ATGC-3', also written from 5' to 3'?
123550.e: The complement of ATGC is TACG, but it runs from 3' to 5'. Read in the 5' to 3' direction, this gives GCAT.
123550.m: The complementary strand is written as the complement and reversed.

123551.q: What pairs with the codon of the mRNA during translation?
a: The start codon of the DNA
123551.e: Each tRNA carries an anticodon of three bases. It pairs complementarily with the matching codon of the mRNA and so brings the correct amino acid to the ribosome.
123551.m: The anticodon of the tRNA recognises the codon of the mRNA.

123552.q: What happens to the base pairs when DNA is heated to over 90 degrees Celsius?
a: They come apart and the strands separate
123552.e: When heated, the bonds between the opposite bases break and the DNA denatures. This melting is used in PCR.
123552.m: Heat separates the two DNA strands.

123553.q: How many hydrogen bonds connect an adenine-thymine pair?
123553.e: Adenine and thymine are connected by two hydrogen bonds. Sections rich in AT can therefore be separated more easily.
123553.m: An AT pair is held together by two hydrogen bonds.

123554.e: Purines have a double-ring system; they include adenine and guanine. Cytosine and thymine are pyrimidines with only one ring.
123554.m: Adenine and guanine are purines with two rings.

123555.q: Why does every base pair consist of one purine and one pyrimidine?
a: So that the helix is the same width everywhere
So that the DNA becomes water-soluble
So that enzymes can break it down faster
So that the strands never separate
123555.e: A large purine and a small pyrimidine together always give roughly the same length. In this way the distance between the two backbones stays constant.
123555.m: Purine plus pyrimidine keeps the helix the same width.

123556.q: Which base replaces thymine in RNA?
123556.e: In RNA, the base uracil is found instead of thymine. Uracil also pairs with adenine.
123556.m: In RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine.

123557.q: What does Chargaff's rule state for double-stranded DNA?
a: Adenine and thymine occur equally often
All four bases occur equally often
Purines are twice as common as pyrimidines
Guanine is always the most common base
123557.e: Erwin Chargaff found that the proportion of adenine equals that of thymine, and that of guanine equals that of cytosine. This fits with complementary base pairing.
123557.m: According to Chargaff, there is as much adenine as thymine.

123558.q: A double-stranded DNA contains 20 per cent adenine. What is the proportion of guanine?
123558.e: Thymine also makes up 20 per cent, so together 40 per cent. The remaining 60 per cent are shared equally between guanine and cytosine, so 30 per cent each.
123558.m: The proportion of guanine can be calculated from the proportion of adenine.

123559.q: What is the type of DNA copying called in which each new double helix keeps one old strand?
123559.e: In semi-conservative replication, each parent strand serves as a template. Each daughter DNA consists of one old and one new strand.

123560.q: Which researchers proved semi-conservative replication with heavy nitrogen in 1958?
123560.e: Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl labelled bacterial DNA with the isotope 15N. The density of the DNA after each division showed the semi-conservative pattern.
123560.m: Meselson and Stahl proved semi-conservative copying.

123561.q: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA at the replication fork?
123561.e: Helicase separates the two strands by pulling the base pairs apart. For this it needs energy from ATP.

123562.q: In which direction does DNA polymerase extend a new strand?
123562.e: DNA polymerase only adds new nucleotides to the 3' end. The new strand therefore grows from 5' to 3'.
123562.m: DNA polymerases always build from 5' to 3'.

123563.q: Which enzyme makes the short RNA starter pieces for DNA polymerase?
123563.e: DNA polymerase cannot start on its own; it needs a free 3' end. Primase supplies an RNA primer for this.
123563.m: Primase lays down the starting primer.

123564.q: Which enzyme joins the Okazaki fragments into a continuous strand?
123564.e: DNA ligase closes the last gaps in the sugar-phosphate backbone. This produces a strand without gaps.
123564.m: Ligase sticks pieces of DNA together.

123565.q: Which property of many DNA polymerases lowers the error rate during replication?
123565.e: Many DNA polymerases recognise wrongly inserted nucleotides and remove them with their exonuclease activity. This checking is called proofreading.

123566.q: Which enzyme prevents the DNA ahead of the replication fork from becoming too tightly twisted?
123566.e: Unwinding creates tension ahead of the fork. Topoisomerases briefly cut the DNA and so release the overwinding.

123567.q: Where does transcription take place in cells with a nucleus?
123567.e: In eukaryotes the DNA lies in the nucleus, so it is copied there. The finished mRNA is then exported into the cytoplasm.
123567.m: In eukaryotes, transcription takes place in the nucleus.

123568.q: What is the DNA region called where RNA polymerase begins transcription?
123568.e: The promoter is a recognition sequence in front of the gene. Transcription factors and RNA polymerase bind there.

123569.q: Which well-known sequence is found in many eukaryotic promoters?
123569.e: The TATA box lies just before the starting point of many genes. It serves as a binding site for transcription factors.
123569.m: Many promoters contain a TATA box.

123570.q: What is the DNA strand called that is read as a template during transcription?
123570.e: The template strand is read. The RNA produced therefore has the sequence of the other, coding strand, only made of RNA building blocks.
123570.m: RNA polymerase reads the template strand.

123571.q: What is removed from the pre-mRNA during splicing?
123571.e: Introns are non-coding sections and are cut out. The exons are joined to form the mature mRNA.

123572.q: Which two modifications does eukaryotic mRNA receive at its ends?
123572.e: A cap of modified guanine is added to the 5' end, and a tail of many adenine nucleotides to the 3' end. Both protect the mRNA from being broken down.
123572.m: The cap and poly-A tail protect the mRNA.

123573.q: What does alternative splicing make possible?
123573.e: Depending on which exons are joined, different mature mRNAs are produced. In this way one gene can code for several versions of a protein.
123573.m: Alternative splicing makes several proteins from one gene.

123574.q: What guides a ribosome with its growing protein chain to the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
a: A signal peptide at the start of the chain
A stop codon at the end of the mRNA
The poly-A tail of the mRNA
123574.e: Proteins for membranes or for export carry a signal sequence at the start. It is recognised and the ribosome docks onto the rough ER.
123574.m: A signal peptide sends ribosomes to the rough ER.

123575.q: How large are eukaryotic ribosomes, given as a sedimentation coefficient?
123575.e: Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S, bacterial ones only 70S. The difference matters for some antibiotics.

123576.q: What is the group of three on the tRNA called that attaches to the codon of the mRNA?
123576.e: The anticodon is complementary to the codon. This ensures that the correct amino acid is built in.
123576.m: The anticodon of the tRNA recognises the codon.

123577.q: Which bond links the amino acids during translation?
123577.e: The ribosome links the carboxyl group of one amino acid to the amino group of the next. In the process, water is released.

123578.q: What are the three tRNA binding sites in the ribosome called?
123578.e: The loaded tRNA arrives at the A site, the growing chain hangs at the P site, and the empty tRNA leaves the ribosome via the E site.
123578.m: The ribosome has an A, a P and an E site.

123579.q: Which enzyme loads each tRNA with the matching amino acid?
123579.e: There is a separate aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase for each amino acid. Using ATP, it links the amino acid to the correct tRNA.
123579.m: Synthetases load tRNAs with amino acids.

123580.q: What binds to the ribosome when a stop codon is reached?
123580.e: There is no matching tRNA for stop codons. A release factor binds and releases the finished chain.

123581.q: What is an mRNA called that is read by several ribosomes at the same time?
123581.e: Several ribosomes can work one behind the other on the same mRNA. In this way many copies of a protein are made in a short time.
123581.m: A polysome is many ribosomes on one mRNA.

123582.q: What is different in bacteria compared with eukaryotes as regards transcription and translation?
a: They can take place at the same time
They only take place at night
123582.e: Bacteria have no nucleus. Ribosomes can therefore attach to the mRNA while it is still being transcribed.
123582.m: In bacteria, transcription and translation are coupled.

123583.q: Which amino acid is coded by the start codon AUG?
123583.e: AUG marks the start of translation and at the same time codes for methionine. That is why newly made proteins initially begin with methionine.
123583.m: The start codon AUG stands for methionine.

123585.q: How many stop codons does the standard code contain?
123585.e: The stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA. There is no matching tRNA for them.
123585.m: The standard code has three stop codons.

123586.q: Which codon is the usual start codon?
123586.e: The codon AUG marks the start of translation. At the same time it codes for methionine.

123587.q: For how many standard amino acids does the genetic code code?
123587.e: The sense codons are distributed among 20 canonical amino acids. In addition there are the stop codons.
123587.m: The genetic code specifies 20 amino acids.

123588.q: What does it mean that the genetic code is “degenerate”?
a: Several codons stand for the same amino acid
One codon stands for several amino acids
123588.e: Because there are more codons than amino acids, most amino acids are coded more than once. This is also called redundancy.
123588.m: Many amino acids are coded by several codons.

123589.q: What does it mean that the genetic code is almost universal?
a: Almost all living things use the same code
Every gene has the same code
The code is the same length in all proteins
123589.e: Bacteria, plants and humans translate codons almost identically. That is why a human gene can be read in bacteria; there are small differences, for example in mitochondria.
123589.m: Almost all living things use the same genetic code.

123590.q: Which circular table is used in biology lessons to read off which amino acid a codon codes for?
123590.e: In the codon wheel, a codon is read from the inside out. On the outside you find the matching amino acid or the stop signal.
123590.m: The codon wheel translates codons into amino acids.

123591.q: What is a mutation called in which a single base is exchanged for another?
123591.e: In a substitution, one base is replaced and the length of the DNA stays the same. It is a form of point mutation.
123591.m: In a substitution, one base is exchanged.

123592.q: What does the deletion of a single base in a gene usually cause?
a: A shift in the reading frame
123592.e: Because the codons are read in groups of three, all the following triplets shift. This usually produces a completely changed or shortened protein.
123592.m: If a base is missing, the reading frame shifts.

123593.q: What is a mutation called that does not change the amino acid sequence?
123593.e: Because of multiple coding, a new codon can stand for the same amino acid. The protein then stays the same.
123593.m: A silent mutation does not change the protein.

123594.q: What is created in a nonsense mutation?
123594.e: If a codon becomes a stop codon, translation breaks off too early. The protein is shortened and usually does not work.
123594.m: A nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon.

123595.q: What is a point mutation called that leads to a different amino acid being built in?
123595.e: In a missense mutation, the changed codon codes for a different amino acid. The consequences range from harmless to severe.
123595.m: A missense mutation exchanges one amino acid.

123596.q: Which DNA damage does UV radiation typically cause?
123596.e: UV light links two neighbouring thymines together. If these dimers are not repaired, mutations and skin cancer can result.
123596.m: UV radiation creates thymine dimers in DNA.

123597.q: Which type of mutation is trisomy 21?
123597.e: In a genome mutation, the number of chromosomes is changed. In trisomy 21, chromosome 21 is present three times.
123597.m: In trisomy 21, the number of chromosomes is changed.

123598.q: What are substances or radiation that trigger mutations called?
123598.e: Mutagens increase the mutation rate. Examples are ionising radiation, UV light and certain chemicals in tobacco smoke.

123599.q: What are sections of DNA called that can change their position in the genome?
123599.e: Transposons are also called jumping genes. They make up a large part of the human genome.
123599.m: Transposons can jump around in the genome.

123600.q: Roughly what percentage of the genome do two people share?
123600.e: Two people differ in only about one in every thousand building blocks. Even so, these small differences account for a great deal of variety.

123601.q: What share of the human genome codes directly for proteins?
123601.e: Only a small part of the DNA consists of exons, which code for proteins. The rest includes introns, regulatory sections and repeats.
123601.m: Only a small part of the genome codes for proteins.

123602.q: Roughly how long would all the DNA in a human body cell be if stretched out?
123602.e: A diploid cell contains around 6 billion base pairs, which stretched out gives about 2 metres. The DNA is wound around histones and highly compacted.
123602.m: The DNA of one cell is around two metres long when stretched out.

123603.q: Which cell organelles have their own small genome?
123603.e: Mitochondria have a ring-shaped DNA with a few genes. This is seen as evidence that they originated from bacteria.

123604.q: What shape is the main chromosome of most bacteria?
123604.e: Most bacteria have a closed, ring-shaped chromosome. In addition, small plasmids may be present.
123604.m: Bacteria usually have a ring-shaped chromosome.

123605.q: Some amoebae and lungfish have much more DNA than humans. What does this show?
a: Genome size and complexity are hardly related
These animals are more complex than humans
123605.e: The amount of DNA says little about how complex a living thing is. A large part of many genomes consists of repeats and non-coding sections.
123605.m: A large genome does not mean a complex living thing.

123606.q: What is the field called that studies whole genomes?
123606.e: Genomics studies the structure, function and comparison of complete genomes. Proteomics, by contrast, studies the whole set of proteins.

123607.q: In which year did the public Human Genome Project officially start?
123607.e: The project was launched in 1990, mainly by US authorities. Research centres from several countries soon took part.
123607.m: The Human Genome Project began in 1990.

123608.q: Which researcher competed with the public project with the company Celera Genomics?
123608.e: With Celera, Craig Venter relied on fast shotgun sequencing. The race sped up the whole undertaking.
123608.m: Craig Venter challenged the public project with Celera.

123609.q: Which sequencing method was mainly used in the Human Genome Project?
123609.e: Frederick Sanger's chain termination method was highly automated. Modern high-throughput methods only came later.
123609.m: The human genome was sequenced with the Sanger method.

123610.q: In which year were the first draft versions of the human genome published in scientific journals?
123610.e: The draft was publicly announced in 2000, and the publications appeared in “Nature” and “Science” in 2001.
123610.m: The draft sequence of the human genome appeared in 2001.

123611.q: Who led the public Human Genome Project in its main phase?
123611.e: James Watson led the US part at the beginning; from 1993 Francis Collins took over. Collins led the project until it was completed.
123611.m: Francis Collins led the Human Genome Project to its goal.

123612.q: Roughly how much did the Human Genome Project cost?
123612.e: The public project cost around 3 billion US dollars. Today sequencing a genome costs only a tiny fraction of that.
123612.m: The Human Genome Project cost around three billion dollars.

123613.q: What did researchers achieve with the human genome in 2022?
a: The first complete sequence without gaps
The discovery of the DNA double helix
123613.e: The 2003 sequence still had gaps, for example at the centromeres. In 2022 they were closed with new long-read methods.
123613.m: Only in 2022 was a human genome sequenced without gaps.

123614.q: Which substance did the Swiss scientist Friedrich Miescher discover in 1869?
123614.e: Miescher isolated a new substance from cell nuclei and called it nuclein. Today we know that it was mainly DNA.
123614.m: Friedrich Miescher discovered nucleic acid in 1869.

123615.q: In which city was Friedrich Miescher born?
123615.e: Friedrich Miescher was born in Basel in 1844. He came from a Basel family of doctors.

123616.q: From what material did Miescher obtain his first cell nuclei?
123616.e: He used white blood cells from the pus on used dressings from a hospital. These cells have large nuclei.
123616.m: Miescher found nuclein in white blood cells from pus.

123617.q: In which city did Miescher make his discovery?
123617.e: Miescher worked in Felix Hoppe-Seyler's laboratory at Hohentübingen Castle. There he isolated nuclein.

123618.q: Which element was strikingly abundant in nuclein and distinguished it from proteins?
123618.e: Miescher's analyses showed a high phosphorus content. This made it clear that it was not an ordinary protein.

123619.q: At which university was Miescher later professor of physiology?
123619.e: In 1872 Miescher became professor of physiology at the University of Basel. There he continued to study nuclein, among other things in salmon sperm.
123619.m: Miescher later taught at the University of Basel.

123620.q: From what did Miescher later obtain large amounts of nuclein in Basel?
123620.e: Salmon from the Rhine provided Miescher with sperm cells with very large nuclei. From these he could obtain and study a lot of nuclein.
123620.m: In Basel, Miescher studied nuclein from salmon sperm.

123621.q: In which place in the Grisons did Friedrich Miescher die in 1895?
123621.e: Miescher had tuberculosis and sought a cure in Davos. He died there in 1895.

123622.q: Which protein is often used as “gene scissors” in the CRISPR method?
123622.e: Cas9 is an endonuclease that cuts DNA at a chosen point. That is why people speak of the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors.
123622.m: Cas9 is the best-known pair of gene scissors.

123623.q: Which two researchers received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for CRISPR/Cas9?
123623.e: In 2012 Charpentier and Doudna showed that Cas9 can be programmed precisely. For this they were honoured in 2020.
123623.m: Charpentier and Doudna received the Nobel Prize for CRISPR.

123624.q: What is the CRISPR system originally used for in bacteria?
123624.e: Bacteria store pieces of virus DNA in their CRISPR section. In a new infection, Cas recognises and cuts up the virus DNA.
123624.m: CRISPR is originally an immune system of bacteria.

123625.q: What steers Cas9 to the right place on the DNA?
123625.e: The guide RNA is complementary to the target sequence. It leads Cas9 exactly there.
123625.m: A guide RNA shows Cas9 where to cut.

123626.q: What does the enzyme Cas9 do to the DNA in the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors?
a: It cuts both DNA strands at a particular point
It translates the DNA into a protein
123626.e: Cas9 is an enzyme that cuts through DNA at a precisely chosen point. The cell then repairs the cut, and in the process the gene can be changed.
123626.m: Cas9 is the blade of the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors.

123627.q: What can be achieved with the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors by cutting a gene at a chosen point?
123627.e: The cell often repairs the cut inaccurately. This produces small errors that frequently switch the gene off.
123627.m: A targeted cut with CRISPR can switch a gene off.

123628.q: What is CRISPR/Cas9 mainly used for in research today?
a: To change genes in a targeted way
To stain viruses under the microscope
123628.e: CRISPR/Cas9 is also called gene scissors. It can be used to cut and change genes at precisely chosen points.
123628.m: CRISPR/Cas9 is a pair of gene scissors for changing genes precisely.

123629.q: For which hereditary disease was the first CRISPR therapy approved in 2023?
123629.e: The therapy Casgevy was approved in 2023, first in Great Britain and the USA. It is also used to treat beta thalassaemia.
123629.m: The first approved CRISPR therapy treats a blood disease.

123630.e: Only someone who carries two changed alleles has the disease. People with one changed allele are healthy.

123631.q: Which organ is particularly affected in cystic fibrosis?
123631.e: In cystic fibrosis the body produces sticky mucus. It mainly blocks the airways and leads to frequent chest infections; digestive organs are also affected.
123631.m: Cystic fibrosis makes the mucus in the lungs sticky.

123632.e: A single changed allele is enough for the disease. It usually only appears in adulthood.

123633.q: Which organ is progressively damaged in Huntington's disease?
