123633.e: In Huntington's disease, nerve cells in the brain gradually die. This leads to involuntary movements and to changes in thinking and behaviour.
123633.m: Huntington's disease is a hereditary disease of the brain.

123634.q: What advantage do healthy carriers of a sickle cell allele have in some regions?
a: They are better protected against malaria
123634.e: Heterozygous carriers fall seriously ill with malaria less often. That is why the allele is common in malaria regions.
123634.m: The sickle cell allele partly protects carriers against malaria.

a: With a diet low in phenylalanine
123635.e: In phenylketonuria, the body cannot break down phenylalanine. A special low-protein diet started early prevents brain damage; newborns in Switzerland are tested for it.
123635.m: A diet low in phenylalanine helps with phenylketonuria.

123636.q: Both parents are healthy carriers of the same recessive disease allele. What is the risk that a child will have the disease?
123636.e: Each parent passes on the changed allele with a probability of 50 per cent. Together this gives 0.5 times 0.5, so 25 per cent.
123636.m: Two carriers have a one-in-four risk for each child.

123637.q: What is a person called who carries a recessive disease allele but is healthy?
123637.e: A carrier is heterozygous and shows no symptoms. However, they can pass the allele on.
123637.m: Healthy people with a recessive disease allele are called carriers.

123931.q: In which part of the cell does glycolysis take place?
123931.e: The enzymes of glycolysis are dissolved in the cytoplasm. That is why it can also take place in cells without mitochondria.
123931.m: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm.

123932.q: Which end product is formed from one molecule of glucose in glycolysis?
123932.e: Glucose, with six carbon atoms, is split into two C3 units and oxidised to two pyruvate molecules.
123932.m: Glycolysis makes two pyruvate from one glucose.

123933.q: How many ATP does the cell gain net from one molecule of glucose in glycolysis?
123933.e: Glycolysis uses 2 ATP at the start and later forms 4 ATP. That leaves a net 2 ATP per glucose.
123933.m: Glycolysis yields a net 2 ATP per glucose.

123934.q: What is the main purpose of converting pyruvate into lactate when oxygen is lacking?
a: It produces a lot of extra ATP
123934.e: Glycolysis needs NAD+ as an electron acceptor. Without oxygen, it is only made available again through the formation of lactate.
123934.m: Lactate formation keeps glycolysis going by recovering NAD+.

a: No, it also works without oxygen
Yes, it always needs a lot of oxygen
Yes, but only in the nucleus
123935.e: Glycolysis is anaerobic. That is why yeasts during fermentation or muscles short of oxygen can also gain energy from it.

123936.q: What happens to the pyruvate from glycolysis when there is enough oxygen?
a: It is broken down further in the mitochondria
It is stored in the nucleus
123936.e: With oxygen, pyruvate enters the mitochondria. There it is completely broken down to carbon dioxide and water via the citric acid cycle and the respiratory chain.
123936.m: With oxygen, pyruvate is broken down further in the mitochondria.

123937.q: Why do red blood cells depend entirely on glycolysis for their energy?
a: They have no contact with glucose
They do not need to transport oxygen
123937.e: Mature erythrocytes have neither a nucleus nor mitochondria. They therefore lack the citric acid cycle and the respiratory chain.
123937.m: Red blood cells only gain ATP through glycolysis.

123938.q: Where does the citric acid cycle take place in human cells?
123938.e: The enzymes of the citric acid cycle are in the matrix of the mitochondria. Only succinate dehydrogenase sits in the inner membrane.
123938.m: The citric acid cycle takes place in the matrix of the mitochondria.

123939.q: With which molecule does acetyl-CoA react at the start of the citric acid cycle to form citrate?
123939.e: Citrate synthase links the C2 unit from acetyl-CoA with the C4 molecule oxaloacetate to form citrate with six carbon atoms.
123939.m: Acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate together form citrate.

123940.q: After which biochemist is the citric acid cycle also named?
123940.e: Hans Adolf Krebs described the cycle in the 1930s. That is why it is also called the Krebs cycle.
123940.m: After Hans Krebs, the citric acid cycle is also called the Krebs cycle.

123941.q: How many molecules of carbon dioxide are released per turn of the citric acid cycle?
123941.e: In two oxidative decarboxylations, one CO2 is split off each time. This corresponds to the two carbon atoms from the acetyl-CoA fed in.
123941.m: Each turn of the citric acid cycle releases two carbon dioxide.

123942.q: Which reducing equivalents does one turn of the citric acid cycle supply?
123942.e: Three dehydrogenases transfer hydrogen to NAD+, and succinate dehydrogenase to FAD. The electrons then go into the respiratory chain.
123942.m: One turn of the citric acid cycle supplies three NADH and one FADH2.

123943.q: What are the substances NADH and FADH2 formed in the citric acid cycle used for?
a: They supply electrons for the respiratory chain
123943.e: NADH and FADH2 hand their electrons over to the respiratory chain. There most of the ATP is gained from them.
123943.m: NADH and FADH2 bring electrons to the respiratory chain.

123944.q: Which enzyme complex links glycolysis with the citric acid cycle?
123944.e: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, splitting off CO2. This step cannot be reversed.
123944.m: Pyruvate dehydrogenase turns pyruvate into acetyl-CoA.

123945.q: Why does the citric acid cycle quickly come to a standstill without oxygen, even though it does not use oxygen itself?
a: NAD+ and FAD are no longer regenerated
Citrate breaks down immediately without oxygen
123945.e: The respiratory chain only oxidises NADH and FADH2 with oxygen as the final acceptor. Without it, the cycle runs out of oxidised coenzymes.
123945.m: The citric acid cycle needs oxygen indirectly, because the respiratory chain recovers its coenzymes.

123946.q: In which structure are the complexes of the respiratory chain located?
123946.e: The enzyme complexes are built into the inner mitochondrial membrane. Its folds, the cristae, increase the surface area.
123946.m: The respiratory chain lies in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

123947.q: Which substance is the final electron acceptor of the respiratory chain?
123947.e: At complex IV the electrons are transferred to oxygen. Together with protons, this produces water.
123947.m: Oxygen takes up the electrons at the end of the respiratory chain.

123948.q: Which enzyme uses the backflow of protons into the mitochondrial matrix to make ATP?
123948.e: ATP synthase works like a tiny turbine. When protons flow back through it, it turns and joins ADP and phosphate to form ATP.
123948.m: ATP synthase makes ATP using the proton gradient.

123949.q: What do complexes I, III and IV of the respiratory chain pump across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
123949.e: The energy from electron transfer is used to pump protons into the intermembrane space. This creates an electrochemical gradient.
123949.m: The respiratory chain pumps protons out of the matrix.

123950.q: Which complex of the respiratory chain does the poison cyanide inhibit?
123950.e: Cyanide binds to cytochrome c oxidase, complex IV. The electrons can no longer be transferred to oxygen, and cellular respiration comes to a halt.
123950.m: Cyanide blocks cytochrome c oxidase and therefore cellular respiration.

123951.q: Which mobile molecule transfers electrons from complexes I and II to complex III?
123951.e: Ubiquinone, also called coenzyme Q10, is fat-soluble and moves freely in the membrane. It shuttles electrons to complex III.
123951.m: Ubiquinone transports electrons within the membrane.

123952.q: According to current estimates, roughly how many ATP does the complete oxidation of one glucose molecule yield?
123952.e: Older textbooks give 36 to 38 ATP. Because the flow of protons has been measured more precisely, the figure today is around 30 to 32 ATP.
123952.m: A completely respired glucose yields around thirty ATP.

123953.q: Which molecules supply the electrons that flow through the respiratory chain?
123953.e: NADH and FADH2 are formed mainly in the citric acid cycle. They hand their electrons to the respiratory chain, whose energy is used to make ATP.
123953.m: NADH and FADH2 feed electrons into the respiratory chain.

123954.q: Where does the beta-oxidation of fatty acids mainly take place in humans?
123954.e: The fatty acids are broken down step by step in the mitochondria. Very long-chain fatty acids are first shortened in the peroxisomes.
123954.m: Beta-oxidation takes place in the mitochondria.

123955.q: Which product of beta-oxidation is then broken down further in the citric acid cycle?
123955.e: Beta-oxidation breaks fatty acids down into acetyl-CoA. This is broken down further into carbon dioxide in the citric acid cycle of the mitochondria.
123955.m: Fatty acids produce acetyl-CoA for the citric acid cycle.

123956.q: By how many carbon atoms is a fatty acid shortened in each round of beta-oxidation?
123956.e: Each round splits off a C2 unit as acetyl-CoA. The remaining chain starts the next round.
123956.m: Beta-oxidation shortens the fatty acid by two carbon atoms per round.

123957.q: How many molecules of acetyl-CoA are produced when palmitic acid with 16 carbon atoms is broken down completely?
123957.e: 16 carbon atoms divided by 2 gives 8 acetyl-CoA. Only 7 rounds are needed for this, because the last step yields two acetyl-CoA.
123957.m: Palmitic acid is broken down into eight acetyl-CoA.

123958.q: Where do the fatty acids broken down in beta-oxidation come from?
123958.e: Fats consist of glycerol and three fatty acids. When they are split, the fatty acids enter the mitochondria and are broken down there.
123958.m: Beta-oxidation breaks down fatty acids from split fats.

123959.q: Where do the coenzymes NADH and FADH2 loaded in beta-oxidation hand over their electrons?
123959.e: NADH and FADH2 deliver their electrons to the respiratory chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane. There most of the ATP is formed with them.
123959.m: The respiratory chain uses the electrons from beta-oxidation.

123960.q: When does the body rely particularly heavily on beta-oxidation?
a: During fasting and long endurance exercise
123960.e: When carbohydrate stores are low, the body increasingly draws on its fat reserves. The fatty acids are then broken down in beta-oxidation.
123960.m: During fasting and endurance sport, the body burns more fat.

123961.q: In which organ are ketone bodies formed?
123961.e: The liver cells form ketone bodies in their mitochondria, especially during fasting. They then release them into the blood.
123961.m: Ketone bodies are formed in the liver.

123962.q: Which ketone body is given off in the breath and has a fruity smell?
123962.e: Acetone forms through the spontaneous decarboxylation of acetoacetate. It is volatile and is breathed out.
123962.m: Acetone gives the breath a fruity smell in ketosis.

123963.q: From which nutrient does the liver mainly form ketone bodies during fasting?
123963.e: During fasting, fatty acids are brought from the fatty tissue to the liver and broken down into acetyl-CoA. From this the liver builds the ketone bodies.
123963.m: Ketone bodies are made from fat.

123964.q: Why does the liver release ketone bodies into the blood during fasting?
a: As a source of energy for other organs
123964.e: The liver forms ketone bodies but cannot use them itself. In this way they are available as fuel for the heart, muscles and brain.
123964.m: The liver exports ketone bodies but does not use them itself.

123965.q: Which organ, which hardly uses fatty acids, covers a large part of its energy needs from ketone bodies during prolonged starvation?
123965.e: Fatty acids hardly cross the blood-brain barrier, but ketone bodies do. In this way the body saves glucose and spares the muscle proteins.
123965.m: During long fasting, the brain uses ketone bodies as a source of energy.

123966.q: What is the dangerous metabolic derailment called in which ketone bodies build up in the blood because of a lack of insulin?
123966.e: Without insulin, fatty acids are broken down on a massive scale and ketone bodies are formed. These acids lower the pH of the blood dangerously.
123966.m: A lack of insulin can lead to dangerous ketoacidosis.

123967.q: Which hormone situation promotes the formation of ketone bodies?
a: Little insulin and a lot of glucagon
A lot of insulin and little glucagon
A lot of insulin and a lot of glucagon
A lot of insulin after a meal
123967.e: Low insulin and high glucagon promote lipolysis and beta-oxidation in the liver. As a result, more ketone bodies are formed.
123967.m: More ketone bodies are formed when insulin is low and glucagon is high.

123968.q: Why does the body form more ketone bodies on a low-carbohydrate, ketogenic diet?
a: Without carbohydrates it breaks down more fat
Ketone bodies are found directly in vegetables
Protein is fermented into ketone bodies in the intestine
It then stores particularly large amounts of glycogen
123968.e: Without carbohydrates, the insulin level falls and the glycogen stores empty. The liver then breaks down more fatty acids and forms ketone bodies from them.
123968.m: Few carbohydrates put the body into ketosis.

123969.q: Why do people with ketoacidosis breathe very deeply and quickly?
a: To breathe out carbon dioxide and reduce the acid
Because the lungs form ketone bodies
123969.e: Carbon dioxide acts as an acid in the blood. If more of it is breathed out, the acidity falls. This deep breathing is called Kussmaul breathing.
123969.m: Kussmaul breathing is a response to metabolic acidosis.

123970.q: What does a permanently positive energy balance mean?
a: More energy is taken in than used
More energy is used than taken in
Intake and use are the same
123970.e: Excess energy is stored mainly as fat. In the long run, body weight therefore increases.
123970.m: Anyone who takes in more energy than they use gains weight.

123971.q: Which component makes up the largest part of daily energy use in adults who are not very active?
123971.e: With little exercise, the basal metabolic rate makes up around 60 to 70 per cent of total energy use. Activity and digestion share the rest.
123971.m: The basal metabolic rate is usually the biggest item in energy use.

123972.q: Which physical law forms the basis of every energy balance of the body?
123972.e: The first law states that energy is not lost but only converted. Energy taken in is used, stored or given off as heat.
123972.m: Energy is not lost in the body; it is only converted.

123973.q: A person has a basal metabolic rate of 1600 kcal and a PAL value of 1.5. What is their total energy use per day?
123973.e: Total energy use is the basal metabolic rate times the PAL value: 1600 kcal × 1.5 = 2400 kcal.
123973.m: Basal metabolic rate times PAL value gives total energy use.

123974.q: What does indirect calorimetry measure in order to determine energy use?
a: Oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide output
123974.e: From the gas exchange of breathing, you can calculate how much energy the body uses. For this the person wears a breathing mask, for example.
123974.m: Indirect calorimetry calculates energy use from the breathing gases.

123975.q: What respiratory quotient does the pure burning of carbohydrates have?
123975.e: With glucose, exactly one molecule of carbon dioxide is produced for each molecule of oxygen used. The ratio of CO2 output to O2 uptake is therefore 1.0.
123975.m: For carbohydrates, the respiratory quotient is one.

123976.q: For a week, someone takes in 500 kcal a day less than they use. How big is the energy deficit after this week?
123976.e: 7 days × 500 kcal = 3500 kcal. The body covers this deficit mainly from its energy stores.
123976.m: A daily deficit adds up over the week.

123977.q: How is the body mass index calculated?
a: Body mass in kg divided by the square of height in m
Body mass in kg divided by height in cm
Waist measurement divided by hip measurement
123977.e: The BMI has the unit kg per square metre. So the height is squared.
123977.m: For the BMI, you divide the weight by the height squared.

123978.q: What is the BMI of a person with a body mass of 72 kg and a height of 1.80 m (rounded)?
123978.e: 1.80 m × 1.80 m = 3.24 m². 72 kg ÷ 3.24 m² gives around 22.2 kg/m².
123978.m: You get the BMI by dividing the weight by the height squared.

123979.q: A person weighs 90 kg and is 1.75 m tall. Which WHO category does their BMI fall into?
123979.e: 1.75 m × 1.75 m = 3.0625 m². 90 kg ÷ 3.0625 m² gives around 29.4, which is in the range from 25 to under 30.
123979.m: A BMI between 25 and 30 counts as overweight.

123980.q: Which BMI range counts as normal weight for adults according to the WHO?
123980.e: The WHO classifies adults with a BMI of 18.5 or more and under 25 as normal weight. Above that, overweight begins.
123980.m: Normal weight is a BMI between 18.5 and 25.

123981.q: From what BMI does the WHO speak of obesity in adults?
123981.e: A BMI of 30 or more counts as obesity. This is further divided into three classes.
123981.m: A BMI of 30 or more is called obesity.

123982.q: Which Belgian scholar developed the basis of the body mass index in the 19th century?
123982.e: The statistician Adolphe Quetelet found that the weight of adults increases roughly with the square of their height. The BMI used to be called the Quetelet index.
123982.m: The BMI goes back to Adolphe Quetelet.

123983.q: What is an important weakness of the body mass index?
a: It does not distinguish between muscle and fat mass
It can only be determined in a laboratory
It is only valid for children
It does not take body weight into account
123983.e: Very muscular athletes can have a high BMI without carrying much fat. The BMI does not show how fat is distributed either.
123983.m: The BMI says nothing about muscle content or fat distribution.

123984.q: How is the BMI assessed in children and teenagers?
a: With percentiles by age and sex
With the same fixed limits as for adults
Not at all, it cannot be calculated for them
123984.e: Because body shape changes a great deal during growth, the BMI is compared with children of the same age and sex. Percentile curves are used for this.
123984.m: In children, the BMI is assessed with percentile curves.

123986.q: Which distribution of fat is considered particularly bad for health?
a: A lot of fat in the abdomen around the organs
A lot of fat on the hips and thighs
A lot of fat on the forearms
Evenly distributed fat under the skin
123986.e: Visceral belly fat is metabolically active and releases substances that promote inflammation. It increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes.
123986.m: Belly fat is particularly bad for health.

123987.q: Which metabolic disease is a common consequence of obesity?
123987.e: Being overweight promotes insulin resistance in the body's cells. This can develop into type 2 diabetes mellitus.
123987.m: Obesity increases the risk of type 2 diabetes.

123988.q: Which hormone does fatty tissue produce to tell the brain how large the fat reserves are?
123988.e: Leptin has a satiating effect in the hypothalamus. In obesity the leptin level is high, but the brain often responds to it less strongly.
123988.m: Leptin from fatty tissue tells the brain about the fat reserves.

123989.q: Which joint disease is encouraged by severe overweight, especially in the knees?
123989.e: The extra load wears down the joint cartilage faster. That is why osteoarthritis of the knee is more common in obesity.
123989.m: Being overweight strains the knee joints and promotes osteoarthritis.

123990.q: Which breathing disorder during sleep occurs more often in obesity?
123990.e: Fatty tissue on the neck can narrow the upper airways during sleep. This leads to repeated pauses in breathing.
123990.m: Obesity encourages pauses in breathing at night.

123991.q: What is the surgery called that, in severe obesity, creates a gastric bypass, for example?
123991.e: Bariatric operations make the stomach smaller or shorten the path of food. They are an option in severe obesity when other measures are not enough.
123991.m: Bariatric surgery treats severe obesity with an operation.

123992.q: What is meant by activity energy expenditure?
a: Energy use beyond the basal metabolic rate
The energy use of the brain alone
123992.e: Activity energy expenditure covers the energy for movement, work, sport and other extra effort. Together with the basal metabolic rate, it gives total energy use.
123992.m: Activity energy expenditure is energy use above the basal metabolic rate.

123993.q: What does the unit 1 MET mean?
a: Energy use at rest while sitting
The energy in one gram of fat
123993.e: 1 MET corresponds roughly to resting energy use, around 1 kcal per kg of body mass per hour. An activity of 8 MET therefore uses eight times as much.
123993.m: One MET corresponds to energy use at rest.

123994.q: A person weighing 70 kg jogs for an hour at 8 MET. Roughly how much energy do they use if 1 MET is around 1 kcal per kg per hour?
123994.e: 8 kcal per kg per hour × 70 kg × 1 h = 560 kcal.
123994.m: You estimate energy use as MET times body mass times time.

123995.q: Roughly what share of the energy is converted into mechanical work during muscle activity?
123995.e: The efficiency of the muscles is around 20 to 25 per cent. The rest is released as heat, which is why we get warm during sport.
123995.m: Muscles convert most of the energy into heat.

123996.q: What is the increased oxygen consumption after intense exercise called?
123996.e: After exercise the body has to refill stores, break down lactate and cool down. For this it uses more oxygen than at rest for a while.
123996.m: After intense sport, oxygen consumption stays raised for a while.

123997.q: Which activity has the highest activity energy expenditure per hour?
123997.e: In cross-country skiing, the arms and legs work at the same time at high intensity. Energy use is therefore very high.
123997.m: Endurance sport using many muscles uses a particularly large amount of energy.

123998.q: Which energy store supplies ATP particularly quickly in the first seconds of a sprint?
123998.e: Creatine phosphate transfers its phosphate group directly to ADP. However, the supply only lasts for a few seconds of maximum effort.
123998.m: Creatine phosphate supplies energy in the first seconds of a sprint.

123999.q: How does the activity energy expenditure of a person change if they become heavier while doing the same activity?
a: It rises because more mass has to be moved
It falls because fat saves energy
It always stays exactly the same
123999.e: When walking or climbing stairs, you have to move your own body weight. More mass needs more energy for this.
123999.m: Anyone who weighs more uses more energy for the same movement.

124000.q: Roughly what energy value does alcohol (ethanol) have?
124000.e: Ethanol supplies around 7 kcal or 29 kJ per gram. Alcoholic drinks are therefore high in energy.
124000.m: Alcohol supplies almost as much energy as fat.

124001.q: Why is the physiological energy value of protein lower than its physical energy value?
a: The nitrogen is excreted as urea, which still contains energy
Protein is not broken down in the body at all
Protein burns hotter in the body
124001.e: In a calorimeter, protein burns completely. The body, however, excretes the nitrogen as urea, which still contains energy.
124001.m: With urea, the body loses part of the energy in protein.

124002.q: Which device is used to determine the physical energy value of a food?
124002.e: The sample is burned completely in pure oxygen in the bomb calorimeter. The energy value is worked out from how much the surrounding water warms up.
124002.m: In a bomb calorimeter, the energy value is measured by burning.

124003.q: How many kilojoules are equal to one kilocalorie?
124003.e: A calorie is the heat that warms one gram of water by about one degree. One kilocalorie is equal to 4.184 kilojoules.
124003.m: One kilocalorie is just over four kilojoules.

124004.q: A snack contains 10 g of fat, 30 g of carbohydrates and 5 g of protein. Roughly how much energy does it supply (9, 4 and 4 kcal per gram)?
124004.m: You calculate the energy value by multiplying each nutrient by its value and adding them up.

124005.q: Why does fibre supply the body with only a little energy?
a: It is not digested in the small intestine
It is burned in the stomach straight away
124005.e: Our digestive enzymes cannot split fibre. Only gut bacteria in the large intestine ferment part of it, which is why it supplies only around 2 kcal per gram.
124005.m: Fibre supplies only a little energy.

124006.q: Roughly how large is diet-induced thermogenesis on a mixed diet?
a: Around 10 per cent of total energy use
Around 50 per cent of total energy use
Around 1 per cent of total energy use
Around 30 per cent of total energy use
124006.e: Digesting, absorbing and processing nutrients costs energy. On a mixed diet this is about ten per cent of daily energy use.
124006.m: Digestion uses around a tenth of the daily energy.

124007.q: Which nutrient has the strongest diet-induced thermogenesis?
124007.e: With protein, around 20 to 30 per cent of the energy taken in is used for processing it. With fat the share is smallest.
124007.m: Protein costs the most energy to process.

124008.q: How does the body quickly produce extra heat using the skeletal muscles when it is cold?
a: By widening the blood vessels in the skin
124008.e: When shivering, the muscles contract rapidly and without coordination. The energy is turned almost completely into heat.
124008.m: Shivering is a quick source of heat in the cold.

124009.q: What is the production of heat in the cold that happens without shivering called?
124009.e: In non-shivering thermogenesis, energy is released directly as heat in the metabolism. It is particularly important in newborn babies.
124009.m: The body can also produce heat without shivering.

124010.q: Which hormones increase the basal metabolic rate and therefore the body's heat production?
124010.e: Thyroxine and triiodothyronine increase the metabolic activity of many cells. People with an overactive thyroid often sweat and hardly feel cold.
124010.m: Thyroid hormones fire up the metabolism.

124011.q: What does the abbreviation NEAT stand for in the energy balance?
a: Energy used in everyday movement without sport
124011.e: NEAT means non-exercise activity thermogenesis. It includes walking, standing, climbing stairs or fidgeting.
124011.m: Everyday movement without sport also uses energy.

124012.q: Why is 2,4-dinitrophenol, which used to be sold as a slimming product, life-threatening?
a: It uncouples the respiratory chain and can cause fatal overheating
It blocks the digestion of fat in the intestine
124012.e: The substance lets protons flow back past ATP synthase. The energy is released as heat instead of as ATP, and body temperature can rise dangerously.
124012.m: Uncouplers turn energy into heat instead of ATP.

124013.q: Which region of the brain controls body temperature and therefore heat production?
124013.e: The body's temperature centre is in the hypothalamus. It compares the actual temperature with the set point and starts heat production or cooling.
124013.m: The hypothalamus is the body's thermostat.

124014.q: Which protein makes heat production possible in brown fat?
124014.e: UCP1 lets protons flow back into the mitochondrial matrix without making ATP. The energy of the gradient is thus turned directly into heat.
124014.m: Thermogenin turns brown fat into a heater.

124015.q: Why is brown fat brownish in colour?
a: It contains a great many mitochondria
It stores a lot of melanin
It contains a lot of bile pigment
It has a poor blood supply
124015.e: The numerous mitochondria contain iron-containing cytochromes. Together with the good blood supply, this produces the brownish colour.
124015.m: The many mitochondria colour brown fat.

124016.q: Where is there a particularly large amount of brown fat in newborn babies?
a: Between the shoulder blades and on the neck
In the soles of the feet
In the lens of the eye
In the bone marrow of the fingers
124016.e: Newborn babies can hardly shiver yet. The brown fat in the back and neck area therefore protects them from getting cold.
124016.m: Newborn babies keep warm with brown fat in the neck.

124017.q: How do brown fat cells differ in structure from white fat cells?
a: They contain many small fat droplets instead of one large one
They contain no fat at all
They are much bigger than white fat cells
124017.e: White fat cells have a single large fat droplet. Brown fat cells are multilocular, so the mitochondria can reach the fatty acids quickly.
124017.m: Brown fat cells have many small fat droplets.

124018.q: Through which part of the nervous system is brown fat activated in the cold?
a: Through the sympathetic nervous system with noradrenaline
Through the parasympathetic nervous system with acetylcholine
Through the motor nerves of the arms
124018.e: Cold stimuli lead to the release of noradrenaline at the brown fat cells. This starts lipolysis and switches on UCP1.
124018.m: In the cold, the sympathetic nervous system switches on brown fat.

124019.q: What are fat cells in white fat called that take on heat-producing properties because of cold?
124019.e: With prolonged cold, cells with UCP1 and many mitochondria can form in white fat. They are called beige or brite fat cells.
124019.m: White fat can partly turn beige and produce heat.

124020.q: Which imaging method made active brown fat in adults visible?
a: A normal X-ray of the lungs
124020.e: Active brown fat takes up a lot of glucose. In PET-CT with labelled glucose it therefore lights up brightly, especially after exposure to cold.
124020.m: Active brown fat shows up in PET-CT.

124021.q: What do hibernating animals such as marmots use their brown fat for in particular?
a: To warm up quickly when they wake
124021.e: When waking from hibernation, the body temperature has to rise a great deal. Brown fat supplies a lot of heat quickly for this.
124021.m: Hibernating animals heat themselves up with brown fat.

124022.q: What is produced from the pyruvate of glycolysis in the alcoholic fermentation of yeast?
124022.e: Without oxygen, yeasts convert pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide makes bread dough rise, for example.
124022.m: Yeast turns pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

124023.q: Which organ covers most of its energy needs at rest by breaking down fatty acids?
124023.e: The heart muscle is rich in mitochondria and works non-stop. At rest, most of its ATP comes from beta-oxidation.
124023.m: The heart mainly burns fatty acids.

124024.q: What is the combination of abdominal obesity, high blood pressure, unfavourable blood fats and insulin resistance called?
124024.e: When these risk factors occur together, it is called metabolic syndrome. It clearly increases the risk of heart attack and stroke.
124024.m: Metabolic syndrome combines several metabolic risk factors.

124025.q: Why does the body store energy for the long term mainly as fat rather than as glycogen?
a: Fat is stored without water and is much more energy-dense
Fat can be broken down faster than glycogen
The body cannot store glycogen at all
Fat contains more oxygen than glycogen
124025.e: Glycogen binds a lot of water and supplies little energy per gram of stored weight. Fat is compact and therefore the ideal long-term store.
124025.m: Fat is the body's most compact energy store.

124026.q: Why are the physiological and physical energy values of carbohydrates almost the same?
a: They are broken down completely to carbon dioxide and water in the body
They are not used by the body at all
They contain nitrogen, which is excreted
They do not burn in the calorimeter
124026.e: In the body, as in the calorimeter, carbohydrates end up only as carbon dioxide and water. No waste product containing energy is left over.
124026.m: Nutrients that are broken down completely give the body almost all their energy value.

124027.q: Which substance is formed at the end of the respiratory chain when oxygen takes up electrons and protons?
124027.e: At the last complex of the respiratory chain, oxygen, electrons and protons combine to form water. The carbon dioxide, by contrast, is produced earlier in the citric acid cycle.
124027.m: The respiratory chain turns oxygen into water.

124028.q: Why do many cancer cells use a particularly large amount of glucose?
a: They break down glucose heavily by glycolysis even with oxygen
They need glucose for their cell wall
They pass glucose on to healthy cells
124028.e: Many tumour cells rely heavily on glycolysis and form lactate even when there is enough oxygen. This quickly supplies energy and building blocks for their growth.
124028.m: Cancer cells often rely heavily on glycolysis even with oxygen.

124029.q: How does the basal metabolic rate usually respond to a long and severe reduction in calories?
a: It always stays exactly the same
124029.e: The body adapts to the shortage and saves energy, partly because body mass is lost. This makes further weight loss harder.
124029.m: During strict fasting, the body saves energy.

124030.q: Which SI unit of energy appears on nutrition tables next to the kilocalorie?
124030.e: The joule is the SI unit of energy. On packaging, the energy content is given in kilojoules and in kilocalories.
124030.m: The energy content of food is given in kilojoules.

124328.q: Which food group forms the broad base of the Swiss food pyramid?
124328.e: The bottom level of the pyramid shows drinks such as water and unsweetened tea. They should be consumed in the largest amounts every day.
124328.m: Unsweetened drinks form the base of the pyramid.

124329.q: Which organisation publishes the Swiss food pyramid together with the federal government?
124329.e: The pyramid comes from the Swiss Society for Nutrition (SGE) and is supported by the Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office (FSVO).
124329.m: The SGE is the specialist body behind the Swiss food pyramid.

124330.q: Roughly what amount counts as one portion of vegetables in the Swiss food pyramid?
124330.e: One portion of vegetables is around 120 grams, about a handful. This makes it easy to estimate the recommended daily portions.
124330.m: One portion of vegetables is about a handful.

124331.q: On which level of the Swiss food pyramid are potatoes and pulses found as well as cereals?
a: On the level of starchy foods
On the level of vegetables and fruit
124331.e: Cereal products, potatoes and pulses together form the group that mainly supplies starch and therefore energy.
124331.m: In the pyramid, potatoes and pulses belong to the starchy foods.

124332.q: Which kind of nuts does the Swiss food pyramid recommend for the small daily portion?
124332.e: Nuts supply unsaturated fatty acids, vitamin E and fibre. Salt or a sugar coating would reduce this benefit.
124332.m: A handful of unsalted nuts fits into a daily diet.

124333.q: Which cereal products does the Swiss food pyramid prefer?
124333.e: Wholegrain products contain more fibre, vitamins and minerals than white flour, because the outer layers of the grain are kept.
124333.m: For cereals, wholegrain is the better choice.

124334.q: How many portions of milk and dairy products are recommended each day according to the Swiss food pyramid?
124334.e: Three portions a day, such as a glass of milk, a yoghurt and a piece of cheese, cover a large part of the calcium requirement.
124334.m: Three portions of dairy products a day help the bones.

124335.q: Which principle does the shape of the food pyramid illustrate?
a: The higher the level, the smaller the recommended amount
The higher the level, the more important the food
Each level should be eaten in equal amounts
Main meals are at the top, snacks at the bottom
124335.e: The area of each level shows its share of the amount. At the bottom are the groups for large amounts, at the top those for small amounts.
124335.m: In the pyramid, the recommended amount decreases towards the top.

124336.q: Which food serves as the reference with the value 100 in the glycaemic index?
124336.e: The rise in blood sugar after glucose (dextrose) is set at 100. Other foods are compared with it.
124336.m: Glucose is the standard of the glycaemic index, with a value of 100.

124337.q: What does the glycaemic index of a food show?
a: How much it makes blood sugar rise compared with glucose
How many calories it contains per 100 grams
How much sugar it contains per portion
How quickly it is digested in the stomach
124337.e: The area under the blood sugar curve after an amount containing 50 g of usable carbohydrates is measured and compared with glucose.
124337.m: The glycaemic index describes the effect of carbohydrates on blood sugar.

124338.q: From what value is a glycaemic index usually considered high?
124338.e: The usual classification is: low up to 55, medium 56 to 69, high from 70.
124338.m: A glycaemic index of 70 or more counts as high.

124339.q: How do you calculate the glycaemic load of a portion?
a: GI times grams of carbohydrate divided by 100
GI divided by grams of carbohydrate
124339.e: The glycaemic load also takes into account the amount of carbohydrate actually eaten in a portion.
124339.m: The glycaemic load combines the GI with the amount of carbohydrate in a portion.

124340.q: A portion contains 30 g of carbohydrates and has a GI of 70. What is the glycaemic load?
124340.m: For the glycaemic load, you multiply the GI by the carbohydrates and divide by a hundred.

124341.q: Which sugar has a particularly low glycaemic index?
124341.e: Fructose (fruit sugar) is mostly converted in the liver and makes blood sugar rise only a little. Its GI is around 20.
124341.m: Fruit sugar makes blood sugar rise only a little.

124342.q: How does the glycaemic index of pasta change if it is cooked al dente instead of soft?
124342.e: With a shorter cooking time the starch is less broken down and is digested more slowly. Blood sugar therefore rises more slowly.
124342.m: Pasta cooked al dente has a lower glycaemic index.

124343.q: Which component of a meal usually lowers its effect on blood sugar?
124343.e: Fibre, fat and protein slow down stomach emptying and the uptake of glucose into the blood.
124343.m: Fibre slows down the rise in blood sugar.

124344.q: Which hormone does the pancreas release mainly after meals with a high glycaemic index?
124344.e: When blood sugar rises quickly, the beta cells of the pancreas release a lot of insulin so that the cells take up glucose.
124344.m: Insulin lowers blood sugar after eating.

124345.q: Which of these amino acids is not essential for humans?
124345.e: The body can make glycine, the simplest amino acid, itself from serine. This is not possible with lysine, leucine and valine.
124345.m: The body can make glycine itself.

124346.q: How many proteinogenic amino acids are built into proteins in humans according to the standard genetic code?
124346.e: The standard code has 20 proteinogenic amino acids. Of these, 8 are considered essential in adults, or 9 including histidine.
124346.m: Human proteins are made of twenty standard amino acids.

124347.q: What does it mean that an amino acid is essential?
a: The body cannot make it itself
The body does not need it at all
124347.e: Essential amino acids must be taken in with food because the body cannot make them. If one of them is missing, the body cannot build certain proteins.
124347.m: Essential amino acids must come from food.

124348.q: Which food group supplies a particularly large amount of plant protein?
a: Pulses such as lentils and beans
Fruit such as apples and pears
Cooking oils such as rapeseed oil
124348.e: Lentils, beans, peas and chickpeas contain a lot of protein. Together with cereals, they supply all the essential amino acids in good amounts.
124348.m: Pulses are important sources of plant protein.

124349.q: Which three essential amino acids are called branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs)?
124349.e: Leucine, isoleucine and valine have a branched side chain and are metabolised mainly in muscle.
124349.m: Leucine, isoleucine and valine are the branched-chain amino acids.

124350.q: From which essential amino acid does the body make the messenger substance serotonin?
124350.e: Tryptophan is converted via 5-hydroxytryptophan into serotonin, from which melatonin is later also formed.
124350.m: Serotonin is made from the amino acid tryptophan.

124351.q: Which essential amino acid must people with phenylketonuria strictly limit?
124351.e: In phenylketonuria, the breakdown of phenylalanine is disturbed. It builds up and, if untreated, damages the brain. Newborns are tested for it.
124351.m: Phenylketonuria requires a diet low in phenylalanine.

124352.q: Why is combining maize and beans good from a nutritional point of view?
a: Their amino acids complement each other
Maize supplies the missing vitamin B12
124352.e: Maize is low in lysine and tryptophan, while beans supply a lot of lysine. Together they give a more complete pattern of amino acids.
124352.m: Different plant proteins complement each other's amino acids.

124353.q: What characterises a saturated fatty acid chemically?
a: It has no carbon double bond
It has exactly one double bond
It contains nitrogen in the chain
124353.e: In saturated fatty acids, all the carbon atoms in the chain are bonded to the maximum number of hydrogen atoms; there are no double bonds.
124353.m: Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds.

124354.q: Which saturated fatty acid with 16 carbon atoms is common in palm oil and many animal fats?
124354.e: Palmitic acid (C16:0) is one of the most common fatty acids of all. Oleic acid and linoleic acid, by contrast, are unsaturated.
124354.m: Palmitic acid is a common saturated fatty acid with 16 carbon atoms.

124355.q: Which cooking fat contains a particularly high proportion of saturated fatty acids?
124355.e: Coconut fat consists of around 90 per cent saturated fatty acids, mainly lauric acid. That is why it is solid at room temperature.
124355.m: Coconut fat is rich in saturated fatty acids.

124356.q: Why are fats with many saturated fatty acids usually solid at room temperature?
a: The straight chains can pack closely together
They have shorter chains than oils
They have a stronger ionic charge
124356.e: Without double bonds the chains are straight and pack tightly together. This raises the melting point.
124356.m: Straight fatty acid chains pack tightly, which is why saturated fats are solid.

124357.q: According to current knowledge, which blood value does a high intake of saturated fatty acids raise in particular?
124357.e: Many saturated fatty acids increase LDL cholesterol, which is considered a risk factor for cardiovascular disease.
124357.m: A lot of saturated fat pushes LDL cholesterol up.

124358.q: What is the general molecular formula of saturated monocarboxylic acids?
124358.e: Saturated fatty acids are unbranched carboxylic acids of the form CnH2nO2, for example stearic acid C18H36O2.
124358.m: Saturated fatty acids follow the formula CnH2nO2.

124359.q: Which saturated fatty acid with 18 carbon atoms is found in large amounts in beef tallow and cocoa butter?
124359.e: Stearic acid (C18:0) is saturated. Oleic acid also has 18 carbon atoms, but one double bond.
124359.m: Stearic acid is the saturated fatty acid with 18 carbon atoms.

124360.q: According to nutrition research, which swap is more likely to lower the risk of cardiovascular disease?
a: Replacing saturated with unsaturated fatty acids
Replacing unsaturated with saturated fatty acids
124360.e: Anyone who replaces saturated fats with rapeseed or olive oil, for example, lowers their LDL cholesterol. Replacing them with sugar does not bring this benefit.
124360.m: Unsaturated plant oils are a good replacement for saturated fats.

124361.q: How does a trans fatty acid differ from the usual natural unsaturated fatty acid?
a: The double bond is in the trans configuration
124361.e: Natural unsaturated fatty acids usually have cis double bonds. In trans, the hydrogen atoms are on opposite sides and the chain stays straight.
124361.m: Trans fatty acids have a straight double bond in the trans position.

124362.q: In which industrial process were large amounts of trans fatty acids formed in the past?
124362.e: In the partial hydrogenation of plant oils, some double bonds are not saturated but rearranged. This produces trans fatty acids.
124362.m: Partially hydrogenated fats were the main source of trans fatty acids.

124363.q: How do trans fatty acids affect blood fats?
a: They raise LDL and lower HDL
They lower LDL and raise HDL
They do not affect blood fats
124363.e: Trans fatty acids worsen the ratio of LDL to HDL cholesterol in two ways and so increase the risk of heart attack.
124363.m: Trans fatty acids harm the cholesterol profile twice over.

124364.q: How has Switzerland regulated trans fatty acids in plant oils and fats since 2008?
a: With a maximum value per 100 g of fat
With a complete ban on hydrogenated fats
Not at all, only with recommendations
124364.e: Since 2008, plant oils and fats in Switzerland may contain no more than 2 grams of trans fatty acids per 100 grams of fat.
124364.m: In Switzerland, no more than two per cent trans fatty acids are allowed in fat.

124365.q: Which country was the first to introduce a legal limit for trans fatty acids?
124365.e: Denmark was the first country to limit industrial trans fatty acids, in 2003. Switzerland followed in 2008.
124365.m: Denmark led the way in limiting trans fatty acids.

124366.q: Where do trans fatty acids also occur naturally in small amounts?
a: In the milk and meat of ruminants
124366.e: Bacteria in the rumen of cows, sheep and goats form trans fatty acids. That is why butter and beef contain small amounts.
124366.m: Milk fat from ruminants also contains a little trans fat.

124367.q: Which organisation has set the goal of banishing industrial trans fatty acids from food worldwide?
124367.e: The World Health Organization (WHO) calls on countries to eliminate industrially produced trans fatty acids, for example through limits.
124367.m: The WHO wants to remove industrial trans fatty acids from all food.

124368.q: Which foods typically contained a lot of trans fatty acids before the limits were introduced?
a: Fried foods and puff pastry made with hydrogenated fats
124368.e: Partially hydrogenated fats were used for frying oils, puff pastry, biscuits and margarines because they kept for a long time and were easy to shape.
124368.m: Pastries and fried foods used to be typical sources of trans fat.

124369.e: The body needs micronutrients only in small amounts, and they supply no energy. Carbohydrates, fats and protein are macronutrients.
124369.m: Vitamins and minerals are micronutrients without energy content.

124370.q: According to the WHO, which micronutrient deficiency is the most common worldwide?
124370.e: Iron deficiency affects a great many people worldwide, especially children and women, and is the most common cause of anaemia.
124370.m: Iron deficiency is the most widespread nutrient deficiency in the world.

124371.q: Which vitamin do people on a vegan diet usually need to take as a supplement?
124371.e: Vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal foods, as it is made by microorganisms. Vegans therefore need a supplement.
124371.m: On a vegan diet, vitamin B12 is needed as a supplement.

124372.q: Which vitamin does the body need for blood clotting?
124372.e: Vitamin K is needed for making several clotting factors in the liver. That is why newborns are given it as a precaution.
124372.m: Without vitamin K, blood does not clot well.

124373.q: Which disease is caused by a severe lack of vitamin B1 (thiamine)?
124373.e: Beriberi used to occur mainly where people ate almost nothing but polished white rice, because thiamine is in the husk.
124373.m: Beriberi is the result of thiamine deficiency.

124374.q: For which function is the trace element iron mainly needed in the blood?
124374.e: Iron forms the centre of the haem group in the haemoglobin of the red blood cells and binds oxygen there.

124375.q: What is a micronutrient deficiency called that exists despite enough calories?
124375.e: The term “hidden hunger” describes people who get enough to fill them up but too few vitamins or minerals such as iron, iodine or vitamin A.
124375.m: Hidden hunger is a lack of micronutrients despite a full plate.

124376.q: Which B vitamin is important for closing the neural tube in early embryonic development?
124376.e: Folic acid (vitamin B9) is needed for cell division. A deficiency increases the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida.
124376.m: Folic acid is essential for cell division in the embryo.

124377.q: Why is vitamin D not really a typical vitamin?
a: The body can make it itself with sunlight
It is only needed in the brain
124377.e: Vitamins normally have to be taken in with food. However, the skin makes vitamin D itself with sunlight, which is why it acts more like a hormone.
124377.m: The body can make vitamin D itself with sunlight.

124378.q: Which radiation does the skin need to make vitamin D?
124378.e: UVB radiation converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin into a precursor of vitamin D3.
124378.m: The skin needs UVB light to make vitamin D.

124379.q: Why does the skin hardly make any vitamin D in Switzerland in winter?
a: The sun is too low, so too little UVB arrives
The air is too dry in winter
The days are longer in winter
124379.e: When the sun is low, the path through the atmosphere is long and the ozone layer filters out most of the UVB.
124379.m: In the Swiss winter, the UVB light is hardly enough for vitamin D.

124380.q: Which disease do children get from a severe lack of vitamin D?
124380.e: Without enough vitamin D, too little calcium is built into the bones. They stay soft and become deformed. Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C, night blindness by a lack of vitamin A.
124380.m: A severe lack of vitamin D causes rickets in children.

124381.q: In which organ is the active hormone form calcitriol made?
124381.e: The liver first forms calcidiol, which the kidney then converts into active calcitriol.
124381.m: The kidney activates vitamin D into the hormone calcitriol.

124382.q: What task does vitamin D perform in the intestine?
a: It promotes the uptake of calcium
124382.e: Calcitriol increases the production of transport proteins that bring calcium from the intestine into the blood.
124382.m: Vitamin D makes sure calcium from food is taken up.

124383.q: Which food is one of the few good natural sources of vitamin D?
124383.e: Oily fish such as herring, salmon or mackerel contain significant amounts of vitamin D. Most other foods supply very little.
124383.m: Oily sea fish supplies natural vitamin D.

124384.q: A supplement contains 20 micrograms of vitamin D. How many international units (IU) is that if 1 µg is 40 IU?
124384.m: One microgram of vitamin D equals forty international units.

124385.q: Which group of people routinely receives vitamin D drops from birth in Switzerland?
a: Women pregnant for the first time
124385.e: Breast milk contains little vitamin D and babies should not be in strong sun. That is why a daily dose of vitamin D is recommended for babies.
124385.m: Babies in Switzerland are given vitamin D drops as a precaution.

124386.q: Which disease was the introduction of iodised table salt in Switzerland mainly meant to fight?
124386.e: A lack of iodine leads to an enlarged thyroid (goitre, struma). Goitre used to be very widespread in the Alpine region.
124386.m: Iodised salt has made goitre almost disappear in Switzerland.

124387.q: In which decade was iodised table salt introduced in Switzerland?
124387.e: In the 1920s Switzerland was one of the first countries with iodised table salt. The canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden led the way.
124387.m: Switzerland has been iodising its salt for around a hundred years.

124388.q: Why can the supply of iodine become low despite iodised household salt?
a: Many processed foods are made with non-iodised salt
Iodine evaporates immediately when the packet is opened
Iodised salt is banned in Switzerland
The body stores iodine for decades
124388.e: We take in a large part of our salt through bread, cheese and ready meals. If non-iodised salt is used there, iodine intake falls.
124388.m: For enough iodine, bakeries and industry should also use iodised salt.

124389.q: Roughly how much iodine does iodised table salt contain in Switzerland?
124389.e: The iodine content is around 25 milligrams per kilogram of salt. With a few grams of salt a day, part of the iodine requirement is covered in this way.
124389.m: Even a tiny amount of iodine in salt clearly improves the supply.

124390.q: Why are the soils in the Alpine region particularly low in iodine?
a: Glaciers and rain have washed the iodine out
The Alps are made of pure granite without salts
Cows take all the iodine out of the soil
The thin air breaks down iodine
124390.e: After the Ice Ages, meltwater and rain washed the easily dissolved iodine out of the soils. Plants and animals therefore contain little of it.
124390.m: Washed-out Alpine soils supply little iodine.

124391.q: Which severe developmental disorder can a serious lack of iodine during pregnancy cause in the child?
124391.e: Missing thyroid hormones disturb the growth of the brain and body. Cretinism used to be common in the Alpine region.
124391.m: A lack of iodine before birth can seriously damage brain development.

124392.q: Which company produces table salt in Switzerland and is responsible for iodising it?
124392.e: Swiss Saltworks extracts salt at Schweizerhalle, Riburg and Bex, among other places, and supplies iodised table salt.
124392.m: Swiss Saltworks supplies the country with iodised salt.

124393.q: In what form is iodine added to table salt?
a: As potassium iodide or potassium iodate
As tincture of iodine with alcohol
124393.e: Iodine is added as a potassium salt, because in this form it is stable, tasteless and easy to dose.
124393.m: Table salt is enriched with potassium compounds of iodine.

124394.q: What is fluoridated table salt for?
124394.e: Fluoride hardens tooth enamel and inhibits the bacteria that cause decay. Fluoridated salt therefore works against tooth decay through the diet.
124394.m: Fluoride in salt protects teeth against decay.

124395.q: Which compound forms in tooth enamel when fluoride is built in?
124395.e: Fluoride replaces hydroxide ions in hydroxyapatite. The fluorapatite produced is more resistant to acid.
124395.m: Fluorapatite makes tooth enamel more resistant to acid.

124396.q: In which decade was fluoridated table salt introduced in Switzerland?
124396.e: In 1955 the canton of Zurich became the first authority in the world to allow the sale of fluoridated table salt. The other cantons followed later.
124396.m: Switzerland was a pioneer of fluoridated table salt.

124397.q: Roughly how much fluoride does fluoridated table salt contain in Switzerland?
124397.e: The content is around 250 milligrams of fluoride per kilogram of salt, that is 0.025 per cent.
124397.m: Fluoridated salt contains only a tiny amount of fluoride.

124398.q: Which city fluoridated its drinking water instead of salt for decades?
124398.e: For decades Basel added fluoride to its drinking water. In 2003 the canton switched to fluoridated salt.
124398.m: Basel fluoridated its drinking water until 2003.

124399.q: What can too high an intake of fluoride cause while the teeth are developing?
a: Bleeding gums from a vitamin deficiency
124399.e: Too much fluoride while the enamel is forming leads to fluorosis: white to brownish spots on the permanent teeth.
124399.m: Too much fluoride in children can cause spots on the teeth.

124400.q: How can you tell in the shop whether table salt contains fluoride?
a: From the note “with fluoride” or “fluoridated” on the packet
From the green colour of the salt
124400.e: Fluoridated salt looks and tastes like ordinary salt. Only the label on the packet shows the additive.
124400.m: Whether salt is fluoridated is written on the packaging.

124401.q: What effect does fluoride have in addition to hardening tooth enamel?
a: It promotes the remineralisation of early damage
124401.e: Fluoride helps to put calcium and phosphate back into damaged areas of enamel and inhibits the metabolism of decay bacteria.
124401.m: Fluoride helps to repair early enamel damage.

124402.q: How many levels does the Nutri-Score scale have?
124402.e: The scale goes from A (dark green) via B, C and D to E (red).
124402.m: The Nutri-Score has five levels from A to E.

124403.q: In which country was the Nutri-Score developed and first introduced?
124403.e: The Nutri-Score comes from French nutrition researchers and was first introduced in France as a voluntary label.
124403.m: The Nutri-Score originally comes from France.

124404.q: Is the Nutri-Score compulsory for food in Switzerland?
124404.e: In Switzerland, manufacturers may use the Nutri-Score voluntarily. The FSVO supports it as a guide.
124404.m: In Switzerland, the Nutri-Score is a voluntary label.

124405.q: Which component gives positive points for a better rating in the Nutri-Score?
124405.e: Fibre, protein and the shares of fruit, vegetables and pulses improve the rating. Energy, sugar, saturated fats and salt make it worse.

124406.q: On which reference amount is the Nutri-Score calculated?
124406.e: Because all products refer to 100 g or 100 ml, they can be compared regardless of portion size.
124406.m: The Nutri-Score always refers to 100 grams or 100 millilitres.

124407.q: What is the Nutri-Score most useful for?
a: Comparing similar products in one category
124407.e: The Nutri-Score helps, for example, when comparing different breakfast cereals. It does not judge whether a food fits into a balanced diet.
124407.m: The Nutri-Score works best for comparing products of the same kind.

124408.q: What colour is grade A on the Nutri-Score?
124408.e: A is dark green and stands for the best nutritional composition. E is red.
124408.m: A dark green A is the best Nutri-Score grade.

124409.q: Which criticism of the Nutri-Score is often made?
a: It does not take into account the degree of processing or additives
It can only be read in English
It only applies to fresh fruit
124409.e: The algorithm is based on nutritional values. How heavily a product is processed or which additives it contains is not included.
124409.m: The Nutri-Score says nothing about the degree of processing.

124410.q: What does the biological value of a dietary protein show?
a: How much body protein can be made from it
How many calories the protein supplies
How quickly the protein is digested
How much fat is in the food
124410.e: The more similar the amino acid pattern is to the body's own protein, the more body protein can be built from 100 g of dietary protein.
124410.m: Biological value measures how well dietary protein becomes body protein.

124411.q: Which food serves as the reference with a biological value of 100?
124411.e: The whole hen's egg was set as the reference with a value of 100 because of its favourable amino acid pattern.
124411.m: The egg is the reference for biological value.

124412.q: Which combination reaches one of the highest known biological values, around 136?
124412.e: Potatoes and egg in a ratio of about 35 to 65 complement each other so well that they exceed the value of egg alone. So rösti with a fried egg is a protein-rich combination.
124412.m: Potatoes with egg make a particularly high-quality protein combination.

124413.q: What mainly determines the biological value of a protein?
124413.e: The essential amino acid that is in shortest supply relative to need limits the building of body protein.
124413.m: The scarcest essential amino acid limits the biological value.

124414.q: A dietary protein has a biological value of 80. In theory, how much body protein can be built from 50 g of it?
124414.e: A value of 80 means 80 g of body protein per 100 g of dietary protein. 50 g × 0.8 = 40 g.
124414.m: The biological value shows what percentage can become body protein.

124415.q: Why does gelatine have a very low biological value?
a: It lacks the essential amino acid tryptophan
It is not digested in the stomach
124415.e: Gelatine made from collagen contains practically no tryptophan. Without this essential amino acid, the body can hardly build body protein from it.

124416.q: What do modern measures of protein quality such as DIAAS take into account in addition to the amino acid pattern?
a: How well the amino acids are digested
How much fat the food contains
124416.e: A protein is only as useful as the amount the body can absorb from it in the small intestine. That is why DIAAS includes the digestibility of each essential amino acid.
124416.m: Digestibility also counts for protein quality.

124417.q: Why is the combination of milk and cereals, for example in Bircher muesli, a good one?
a: Milk protein supplies the lysine that cereals lack
Cereals greatly increase the calcium content of milk
124417.e: Milk protein is rich in lysine and so makes up for the weakness of cereal protein.
124417.m: Milk and cereals together make high-quality protein.

124418.q: What does the 16:8 method mean in intermittent fasting?
a: Fasting for 16 hours, eating for 8 hours
Fasting for 16 days, eating for 8 days
16 grams of fat, 8 grams of sugar
124418.e: With 16:8, you eat nothing for 16 hours every day. The meals fall within a window of 8 hours.
124418.m: With 16:8, you only eat within eight hours a day.

124419.q: Someone fasting with the 16:8 method eats their last meal at 7 pm. When is the earliest they may have their first meal the next day?
124419.e: 7 pm plus 16 hours gives 11 am the next day.
124419.m: For the fasting window, you count the hours from the last meal.

124420.q: What does the 5:2 method mean in intermittent fasting?
a: Eating normally on 5 days, greatly reduced on 2 days
Eating for 5 hours, fasting for 2 hours
124420.e: On two non-consecutive days a week, you eat only about 500 to 600 kcal, and normally on the other five days.
124420.m: With 5:2, you partly fast on two days of the week.

124421.q: What is the cellular recycling process called that is stepped up during fasting?
124421.e: In autophagy, cells break down their own components and reuse them. Yoshinori Ohsumi received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for researching it.
124421.m: Autophagy is the self-recycling of cell components.

124422.q: Which energy sources does the liver increasingly make from fatty acids during prolonged fasting?
124422.e: When the glycogen stores are used up, ketone bodies such as acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate are formed from fatty acids; the brain can also use them.
124422.m: During fasting, the liver makes ketone bodies from fat.

124423.q: What have studies shown so far about weight loss through intermittent fasting?
a: It is similar to that from an equal reduction in calories
It is always twice as large as with any diet
It is completely independent of the number of calories
124423.e: Many comparative studies find that intermittent fasting brings about a similar amount of weight loss to a classic reduction in calories. The energy balance remains decisive.
124423.m: Even with intermittent fasting, the energy balance is what counts for losing weight.

124424.q: Which hormone level typically drops clearly during the fasting phases?
124424.e: Without food, blood sugar stays low and the release of insulin falls. Glucagon, by contrast, rises.
124424.m: During fasting phases, the insulin level is low.

124425.q: Which group of people should only try intermittent fasting after consulting a doctor?
a: People with diabetes who take medication
Adults with a healthy body weight
124425.e: With medicines that lower blood sugar, longer fasting can lead to dangerously low blood sugar. Children and people with eating disorders should not fast either.
124425.m: Anyone taking diabetes medication should only fast under medical supervision.

124426.q: Which mineral is present in the largest amount in the human body?
124426.e: An adult contains around one kilogram of calcium, almost all of it in bones and teeth. Iron, zinc and iodine are trace elements with only a few grams or less.
124426.m: Calcium is the most common mineral in the body.

124427.q: What is the form of intermittent fasting called in which you alternately eat for one day and fast for one day?
124427.e: In alternate-day fasting, eating days and fasting days alternate. Therapeutic fasting, by contrast, lasts several days in a row.
124427.m: In alternate-day fasting, eating days and fasting days alternate.

124720.q: In which unit is relative VO2max usually given?
a: ml per minute per kg of body weight
Litres per kg of body weight
124720.e: So that people of different weights can be compared, oxygen uptake is divided by body weight. This gives the unit ml/(min·kg).
124720.m: Relative VO2max is given in millilitres per minute per kilogram.

124721.q: An athlete weighs 70 kg and has an absolute VO2max of 4.2 l/min. What is her relative VO2max?
124721.m: For relative VO2max, you divide absolute VO2max by body weight.

124722.q: Which athletes typically reach the highest relative VO2max values?
124722.e: Cross-country skiing uses a very large amount of muscle mass over a long time. Top athletes in this sport therefore reach exceptionally high values of oxygen uptake.
124722.m: Endurance athletes such as cross-country skiers have particularly high VO2max values.

124723.q: Which factor mainly limits VO2max in healthy, trained people?
a: The pumping capacity of the heart
The strength of the breathing muscles
124723.e: In healthy people, the main limit is the transport of oxygen by the cardiovascular system. Cardiac output determines how much oxygen-rich blood reaches the muscles.
124723.m: VO2max is limited mainly by the performance of the heart.

124724.q: Which adaptation of the heart through endurance training increases VO2max?
124724.e: Endurance training enlarges the heart and its stroke volume. As a result it pumps more oxygen-rich blood into the muscles per minute, and VO2max rises.
124724.m: Endurance training increases stroke volume and therefore VO2max.

124725.q: How does VO2max typically change with increasing age in adulthood?
124725.e: From young adulthood, VO2max slowly falls, partly because the maximum heart rate decreases. Regular endurance training can slow down this decline.

124726.q: Which field test estimates endurance capacity from the distance you can run in 12 minutes?
124726.e: In the Cooper test, you run as far as possible in 12 minutes. VO2max can be roughly estimated from the distance.
124726.m: The Cooper test measures the distance run in 12 minutes.

124727.q: Which method is used to measure VO2max directly?
124727.e: In spiroergometry, you breathe into a mask during an exercise test. A device analyses the breathing gases and so measures oxygen uptake directly.
124727.m: Spiroergometry measures oxygen uptake through the breathing gases.

124728.q: What does the anaerobic threshold describe?
a: The highest workload at which blood lactate stays steady
The point at which breathing stops completely
The workload at maximum heart rate
The lowest workload at which you sweat
124728.e: At the anaerobic threshold, the production and breakdown of lactate are only just balanced. If the workload is increased further, lactate in the blood keeps rising.
124728.m: At the anaerobic threshold, lactate production and breakdown are only just in balance.

124729.q: What is measured in a stepwise lactate test to determine the anaerobic threshold?
a: The lactate concentration in the blood
The blood sugar in the urine
The cholesterol level in the blood
124729.e: At each stage of the test, a drop of blood is usually taken from the earlobe. The threshold can be read from the course of the lactate values.
124729.m: The anaerobic threshold is often determined from blood lactate.

124730.q: Which form of training improves the anaerobic threshold in a particularly targeted way?
a: Longer runs at a pace just at the threshold
Short maximum sprints of five seconds
Pure strength training with heavy weights
124730.e: In threshold training, you run for 20 to 40 minutes at a pace that is just possible without lactate rising. In this way the body learns to break down more lactate.
124730.m: Training close to the threshold pushes the threshold upwards.

124731.q: What happens during a workload clearly above the anaerobic threshold?
124731.e: Above the threshold, more lactate is produced than broken down. It builds up, and the workload can only be kept up for a limited time.
124731.m: Above the anaerobic threshold, lactate builds up in the blood.

124732.q: Roughly how long can a well-trained person keep up a workload at the anaerobic threshold?
124732.e: At the threshold the workload is high, but the metabolism is still in balance. Trained people can therefore keep it up for roughly half an hour to an hour.
124732.m: A workload at the anaerobic threshold can be kept up for about half an hour to an hour.

124733.q: How does targeted endurance training affect the anaerobic threshold?
a: It shifts towards a higher performance
It shifts towards a lower performance
124733.e: Through training, the body can break down more lactate and supply more energy aerobically. That is why the threshold is afterwards at a higher speed or power.
124733.m: Endurance training shifts the anaerobic threshold towards higher performance.

124734.q: Which test tries to determine the anaerobic threshold from a kink in the heart rate curve?
124734.e: The Italian Francesco Conconi described a kink after which the heart rate no longer rises in a straight line with speed. The method is scientifically disputed, because the kink does not appear in everyone.
124734.m: The Conconi test looks for the threshold from a kink in the pulse curve.

124735.q: How does breathing change when you raise the workload clearly above the threshold?
124735.e: More acid in the blood is buffered by breathing out more carbon dioxide. That is why breathing rises more steeply than the workload, which is used as the ventilatory threshold.
124735.m: Above the threshold, breathing rises disproportionately.

124736.q: What is the threshold called that is determined by breathing gas analysis instead of blood samples?
124736.e: In spiroergometry, the ventilatory thresholds can be recognised from changes in breathing and carbon dioxide output. No blood lactate measurement is needed for this.
124736.m: The ventilatory threshold is determined from the breathing gases.

a: Performance rises above the starting level after recovery
The body replaces muscle with fat
Heart rate rises above its maximum during training
124737.e: After exercise the body not only recovers but builds its reserves up a little above the previous level. This raised level is called supercompensation.
124737.m: In supercompensation, performance rises above the starting level after recovery.

124738.q: In which order do the phases take place in the supercompensation model?
124738.e: First, performance falls because of the load. Then the body recovers and rises briefly above the starting level.
124738.m: Load and fatigue are followed by recovery and supercompensation.

124739.q: According to the model, what happens if the next training stimulus comes far too late?
a: Performance falls back to the starting level
124739.e: Supercompensation only lasts for a limited time. If no new stimulus comes, the gain is lost again.
124739.m: If the next stimulus comes too late, the training gain is lost again.

124740.q: According to the model, what happens if new strong stimuli are always applied before recovery?
124740.e: If you train again before the body has recovered, the fatigue adds up. Performance then decreases instead of increasing.
124740.m: Breaks that are too short between hard training sessions lower performance.

124741.q: Which energy store is often given as an example of supercompensation?
124741.e: After being emptied by long endurance exercise and followed by a carbohydrate-rich diet, the glycogen stores fill up beyond their previous level. This is considered a well-documented example of supercompensation.
124741.m: Muscle glycogen is a textbook example of supercompensation.

124742.q: Why is the supercompensation model considered highly simplified?
a: Different body systems recover at different speeds
The body cannot recover after training at all
Training has no effect on performance
124742.e: Energy stores, muscle structures, tendons and the nervous system take different amounts of time to recover. A single curve cannot show this accurately.
124742.m: The supercompensation model is a simplification because systems recover at different speeds.

124743.q: According to the stimulus threshold rule, which stimuli trigger an adaptation of the body?
124743.e: Below-threshold stimuli cause no adaptation, and stimuli that are too strong can do harm. Only stimuli that are strong enough, above the threshold, produce a training effect.
124743.m: Only training stimuli above the threshold cause adaptation.

124744.q: Why must the training load be increased over time?
a: Familiar stimuli become too weak after adaptation
Otherwise the body forgets the technique
Otherwise the risk of injury rises sharply
Otherwise the pulse would stay too high permanently
124744.e: After adaptation, the same stimulus is no longer big enough for the body. That is why the principle of progressive overload calls for new, slightly higher stimuli.
124744.m: Further progress needs gradually increasing loads.

124745.q: Which nutritional strategy before a marathon makes deliberate use of supercompensation?
124745.e: In carb-loading, a lot of carbohydrates are eaten in the days before the competition and training is reduced. As a result the stores are particularly full on race day.
124745.m: Carb-loading fills up the carbohydrate stores particularly well before a competition.

a: Planned alternation of effort and recovery
Continuous effort at the same pace
124746.e: In interval training, phases of effort and breaks follow each other according to a fixed plan. In this way you can train at high intensities for longer in total.
124746.m: Interval training alternates between effort and recovery according to a plan.

124747.q: In the interval method, what is the incomplete break called after which you already start the next effort?
124747.e: In the rewarding break, you only recover partly, usually until the pulse has fallen to a certain value. The first part of recovery is the fastest and is therefore the most worthwhile.
124747.m: In the interval method, you take incomplete, rewarding breaks.

124748.q: A Tabata protocol consists of 8 rounds, each with 20 seconds of effort and 10 seconds of rest. How long does it last in total?
124748.e: One round lasts 20 + 10 = 30 seconds. 8 × 30 seconds gives 240 seconds, which is 4 minutes.
124748.m: A classic Tabata workout lasts four minutes.

124749.q: What is true of intensive interval training compared with extensive interval training?
124749.e: Extensive interval training works with medium intensity and many repetitions. Intensive interval training uses higher intensities with fewer repetitions.
124749.m: Intensive interval training means higher intensity with fewer repetitions.

124750.q: What does the abbreviation HIIT stand for?
124750.e: HIIT stands for high-intensity interval training. Short, very hard efforts alternate with recovery phases.
124750.m: HIIT stands for high-intensity interval training.

124751.q: How does the repetition method differ from the interval method?
a: By having no breaks at all
By training only on a bike
124751.e: In the repetition method, you recover almost completely before the next effort. This allows each repetition to be done at very high intensity.
124751.m: The repetition method works with complete breaks.

124752.q: In classic interval training, how can you tell that the rewarding break is over?
124752.e: In the Freiburg interval training method, the next effort starts when the pulse has fallen to about 120 to 130 beats per minute.
124752.m: The pulse shows when the rewarding break is over.

124753.q: What is the Swedish “speed play” called, in which changes of pace across country are freely chosen?
124753.e: Fartlek means speed play in Swedish. You change the pace playfully depending on the terrain and how you feel.
124753.m: Fartlek is playful running training with free changes of pace.

a: The intervals first get longer and then shorter again
All intervals are exactly the same length
You only run uphill and never downhill
The breaks are always longer than the effort
124754.e: One example is 200, 400, 600, 400, 200 metres. The length of the sections rises and falls again like a pyramid.
124754.m: In pyramid intervals, the lengths of the sections rise and fall again.

a: A hormone of the adrenal gland
124755.e: Lactate is formed when glucose is broken down and a lot of energy has to be supplied quickly. It is the anion, or salt, of lactic acid.
124755.m: Lactate is the salt of lactic acid.

124756.q: Where is a small blood sample usually taken in a lactate test in sport?
124756.e: A drop of capillary blood is enough to measure lactate. It is usually taken from the earlobe or the fingertip.
124756.m: A drop of blood from the earlobe is enough for the lactate test.

124757.q: How is a typical stepwise lactate test set up?
a: The workload increases in steps, with a measurement after each step
You run once as fast as possible and measure afterwards
You only measure at rest before breakfast
The workload decreases in steps until you stop
124757.e: On the treadmill or bike ergometer, the workload is raised in fixed steps. Lactate is measured after each step, and this gives the lactate performance curve.
124757.m: In the stepwise lactate test, the workload is increased step by step.

124759.q: Which lactate value is often called the aerobic threshold?
124759.e: At the aerobic threshold, lactate begins to rise above the resting value for the first time. Many models assume a value of around 2 mmol/l for this.
124759.m: The aerobic threshold is often at about 2 mmol/l of lactate.

124760.q: What does a shift to the right of the lactate performance curve between two tests show?
a: A fault in the measuring device
124760.e: A shift to the right means that the same lactate value is only reached at a higher speed. So the body works more economically at the same performance.
124760.m: A lactate curve shifted to the right shows better endurance.

124761.q: Why is a lactate test repeated several times over a season?
a: To check progress and adjust training zones
To fill the muscles with lactate
124761.e: If the lactate performance curve changes, the right training intensities change too. Repeated tests show the success of training and allow the training zones to be set again.
124761.m: Repeated lactate tests make training progress visible.

124762.q: What can happen in a lactate test if the glycogen stores are empty beforehand?
a: The lactate values come out lower and suggest better fitness
The lactate values rise extremely high
The test cannot be carried out at all
