125591.e: Die Dargebotene Hand can be reached on 143 and is mainly for adults. The number 145 belongs to Tox Info, 118 to the fire brigade.
125591.m: Die Dargebotene Hand has the number 143.

125592.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland for the ambulance service when a life is in acute danger?
125592.e: In a medical emergency such as an acute danger to life, you call the ambulance service on 144. The 147 helpline is for talking about worries, and 145 is the number of Tox Info.
125592.m: When a life is in acute danger, you dial 144.

125593.q: Which American psychiatrist is regarded as the founder of cognitive therapy?
125593.e: Aaron T. Beck first developed cognitive therapy for depression. He showed how negative thought patterns influence feelings.
125593.m: Aaron T. Beck founded cognitive therapy.

125594.q: Who developed rational emotive behaviour therapy?
125594.e: Albert Ellis believed that irrational beliefs cause distressing feelings. His method is one of the roots of cognitive behavioural therapy.
125594.m: Albert Ellis developed rational emotive behaviour therapy.

125595.q: What does Beck's cognitive triad refer to?
a: A negative view of yourself, the world and the future
125595.e: Beck described a negative view of oneself, one's surroundings and the future in depression. The therapy examines these thoughts together.
125595.m: The cognitive triad is a negative view of yourself, the world and the future.

125596.q: What is the thinking error called in which you conclude the worst possible outcome from a small problem?
125596.e: In catastrophising, one mistake immediately becomes total failure. Therapy helps to find more realistic thoughts.
125596.m: Catastrophising turns small things into disasters.

125597.q: What does the “B” stand for in Albert Ellis's ABC model?
125597.e: A is the activating event, B the belief and C the consequence. It is not the event alone but how it is judged that determines the feeling.
125597.m: In the ABC model, how an event is judged determines the feeling.

125598.q: What is the technique called in which unhelpful thoughts are recognised, checked and replaced with more helpful ones?
125598.e: In cognitive restructuring, you look for evidence for and against a thought. This leads to more balanced views.

125599.q: What is the aim of behavioural activation in depression?
a: Staying in bed as much as possible
125599.e: Depressed people often withdraw, which lowers their mood further. Planned, positive activities break this cycle.
125599.m: Behavioural activation gets mood going again through activity.

125600.q: What is the thinking error called in which only extremes such as “perfect” or “total failure” are seen?
125600.e: In black-and-white thinking, there are no shades in between. Anyone who is not perfect then sees themselves straight away as a failure.
125600.m: Black-and-white thinking has no shades in between.

125601.q: Which skill do people practise in many modern behavioural therapies by perceiving the moment consciously and without judging it?
125601.e: Mindfulness is a core element of newer methods such as Marsha Linehan's dialectical behaviour therapy. You learn to notice thoughts and feelings without reacting to them straight away.
125601.m: Mindfulness means experiencing the moment consciously and without judging.

a: The interaction between mind and body
125602.e: The term is made up of the Greek “psyche” (soul) and “soma” (body). Psychosomatics studies how mental factors influence physical complaints and the other way round.
125602.m: Psychosomatics studies the interplay between mind and body.

125603.q: Which model explains illness as the interplay of biological, psychological and social factors?
125603.e: The biopsychosocial model was made known by the psychiatrist George Engel. It adds the mind and the environment to the purely biological view.
125603.m: The biopsychosocial model connects body, mind and social environment.

125604.q: Which hormone does the adrenal cortex release in larger amounts during lasting stress?
125604.e: Cortisol provides energy and helps to cope with strain. If it stays high for a long time, it can weaken the immune system and disturb sleep.
125604.m: Cortisol is an important stress hormone.

a: Physical complaints without a sufficient physical cause being found
A broken bone after a fall
A heart disease present from birth
125605.e: Those affected really suffer from pain or other complaints, but the examinations do not explain them sufficiently. The complaints are not imagined.
125605.m: In somatoform disorders, real complaints have no sufficient physical cause.

125606.q: Which complaint is particularly often partly caused by stress and tension?
125606.e: Under stress, the neck and head muscles tense up. This can trigger a pressing headache.

125607.q: What is the effect called that arises solely from positive expectations of a treatment?
125607.e: Just expecting a remedy to help can measurably relieve complaints. Placebo means “I shall please” in Latin.
125607.m: The placebo effect comes from positive expectations.

125608.q: What is the effect called in which negative expectations cause or worsen complaints?
125608.e: People who expect side effects, for example, feel them more often, even with a dummy pill. Nocebo means “I shall harm” in Latin.
125608.m: Negative expectations can trigger complaints through the nocebo effect.

125609.q: Which researcher shaped the modern concept of stress with the “general adaptation syndrome”?
125609.e: Hans Selye described how the body reacts to lasting strain in phases: alarm, resistance and exhaustion. He made the term stress known in medicine.
125609.m: Hans Selye shaped the modern understanding of stress.

125907.q: Where do you stick the AED pads on adults in the standard position?
a: Below the right collarbone and on the left side of the chest
Both pads next to each other on the breastbone
One on the stomach and one on the lower back
One pad on each upper arm
125907.e: This way the current flows diagonally through the heart. The devices also show the position on the pads with a picture.
125907.m: The AED pads place the heart between them.

125908.q: In ventricular fibrillation without defibrillation, roughly how does the chance of survival change per minute?
a: It falls by about 7 to 10 per cent
It stays the same for the first 10 minutes
It falls by about 50 per cent
125908.e: Without treatment, the chance of survival drops considerably every minute. Chest compressions slow this loss but do not replace the shock.
125908.m: In ventricular fibrillation, every minute until the first shock counts.

125909.q: What do you pay attention to when sticking AED pads on a person with an implanted pacemaker?
a: Do not stick the pad directly over the device
Switch off the pacemaker first with a magnet
Do not use the AED at all
Stick the pads on the back
125909.e: A pacemaker usually lies below the left or right collarbone and can be felt as a bulge. The pad is stuck next to it, a few centimetres away.
125909.m: A pacemaker is no reason not to use the AED.

125910.q: What should you do if a person's chest is wet before you stick on the AED pads?
a: Moisten the pads with water as well
Choose a shock with double the energy
Stick the pads on the clothes
125910.e: On wet skin the pads stick poorly and the current can flow away over the surface. A quick dry is enough.
125910.m: The AED pads always go on dry, bare skin.

125911.q: Why must nobody touch the person while the AED is analysing and delivering a shock?
a: Movements disturb the analysis and the current can hit the helpers
Because otherwise the battery runs flat
Because otherwise the device changes language
Because the pads would then fall off
125911.e: The AED must be able to measure the heart rhythm without disturbance. During the shock, the current could also jump to the helpers.
125911.m: During analysis and shock, nobody touches the person.

125912.q: What do helpers do immediately after an AED shock?
a: Carry on with chest compressions at once
Feel for the pulse for one minute
Put the person in the recovery position
125912.e: Even after a successful shock, the heart often does not yet pump enough. That is why compressions continue straight away until the device announces the next analysis.
125912.m: After the shock, compressions continue without a break.

125913.q: How should gasping breaths in an unconscious person be interpreted?
a: As a sign of cardiac arrest
As a sign of normal recovery
As a sign of deep sleep
125913.e: Gasping consists of rare, slow breaths without effective gas exchange. It does not count as normal breathing, so you start resuscitation immediately.
125913.m: Gasping is not normal breathing and calls for immediate chest compressions.

125914.q: According to the ERC guidelines, with how many rescue breaths do you begin resuscitating a child?
125914.e: In children, cardiac arrest is usually the result of a lack of oxygen. That is why they first receive oxygen through five rescue breaths.
125914.m: In children, resuscitation starts with five rescue breaths.

125915.q: Which medicine does the ambulance service give as standard during resuscitation?
125915.e: Adrenaline narrows the blood vessels and so increases the pressure with which blood flows to the heart and brain. It is injected into a vein or into the bone.
125915.m: Adrenaline is the most important medicine in resuscitation.

125916.q: What is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in adults?
125916.e: Narrowed coronary arteries and heart attacks often lead to ventricular fibrillation. This rhythm suddenly stops the heart's pumping.
125916.m: Sudden cardiac death is usually caused by a disease of the coronary arteries.

125917.q: In the classic chain of rescue, which link comes directly after the emergency call?
125917.e: Several minutes often pass between the alarm and the arrival of the professionals. Laypeople bridge this time with first aid.
125917.m: After the emergency call, helpers give first aid until the ambulance service arrives.

125918.q: How many links does the European Resuscitation Council's chain of survival have?
125918.e: The links are early recognition and emergency call, early chest compressions, early defibrillation and further treatment by professionals. Each link increases the chance of survival.
125918.m: The chain of survival in cardiac arrest has four links.

a: Several injuries at the same time, of which one or their combination is life-threatening
A single minor injury on several days
A chronic disease of several organs
125919.e: In polytrauma, several regions of the body or organ systems are injured. What matters is that the injuries together threaten life.
125919.m: Polytrauma is a life-threatening multiple injury.

125920.q: Where does the ambulance service in Switzerland take polytrauma patients whenever possible?
a: Always to the nearest regional hospital
125920.e: Severely injured people are treated in a few large centres where all specialities are available around the clock. A longer transport, for example by helicopter, is accepted for this.
125920.m: Severely injured people belong in a trauma centre.

125921.q: Which three conditions form the so-called lethal triad in a severely injured patient?
a: Hypothermia, acidosis and a clotting disorder
High blood pressure, diabetes and being overweight
125921.e: Hypothermia and acidification of the blood make blood clotting worse. As a result the patient bleeds more, which makes the other two conditions even worse.
125921.m: Hypothermia, acidosis and clotting disorders make each other worse in severely injured people.

125922.q: What does the term “golden hour” mean in trauma care?
a: The first hour after the accident, in which quick treatment achieves a particularly great deal
The hour before sunset with good visibility for helicopters
The time when operations are cheapest
The first hour of rest after an operation
125922.e: The term stresses that severely injured people should reach a suitable hospital as quickly as possible. The exact length is more of a guiding idea than a fixed limit.
125922.m: For severely injured people, the time until final treatment is what counts most.

125923.q: What does the “B” stand for in the ABCDE approach of emergency medicine?
125923.e: The approach checks, in order, the airway, breathing, circulation, neurological state and the undressed body. What kills fastest is treated first.
125923.m: In the ABCDE approach, breathing comes straight after the airway.

125924.q: Why does the ambulance service put a pelvic binder on an accident victim?
a: To reduce internal bleeding if a broken pelvis is suspected
To support the spine when lifting
125924.e: With an unstable pelvic fracture, a lot of blood can be lost inside the pelvis. The binder presses the bones together and reduces the space for bleeding.
125924.m: A pelvic binder stabilises the pelvis and slows internal bleeding.

125925.q: What is the aim of “damage control surgery” in severely injured people?
a: First only control bleeding and contamination, with the final repair following later
Fully repair all injuries at once in one long operation
125925.e: A long operation would overwhelm the weakened body. After a short emergency operation, the patient is stabilised in intensive care and the surgery is completed later.
125925.m: In severely injured people, life is saved first with a short operation, and everything is repaired later.

125926.q: How do you position a person with anaphylaxis who is mainly short of breath but conscious?
a: Sitting or with the upper body raised
Head down with the feet raised
125926.e: Breathing is easier when sitting, because the breathing muscles work better. If the circulation is weak, however, you lay the person flat.
125926.m: If someone is short of breath, let them sit upright.

125927.q: In an allergic reaction, which signs point to life-threatening anaphylaxis?
a: Shortness of breath and circulatory weakness
Slight redness at the sting site
125927.e: In anaphylaxis, not only the skin but also the airways and circulation are affected. Then an immediate call to 144 is needed.
125927.m: Shortness of breath and circulation problems turn an allergy into an emergency.

125928.q: In which period is the chance of survival highest for avalanche victims who are completely buried?
a: On the day after the avalanche
125928.e: Most buried people survive the first few minutes. After that the survival curve drops steeply, because many run out of air.
125928.m: In an avalanche, quick rescue in the first few minutes is what counts.

125929.q: What do most avalanche victims who are recovered dead after a short time die of?
125929.e: Once it stops moving, the snow packs down like concrete and blocks the mouth and nose. Without an air space, a lack of oxygen sets in quickly.
125929.m: The greatest danger under an avalanche is suffocation.

125930.q: Why do all avalanche transceivers send on the same frequency?
a: So that every device can locate every other one
So that they use less power
So that they do not interfere with mobile phones
So that they can also be used as radios
125930.e: All avalanche transceivers work internationally on 457 kilohertz. This way, any device can find a buried person, no matter which brand they are wearing.
125930.m: All avalanche transceivers work on the same frequency.

125931.q: Which emergency equipment is standard on ski tours away from secured pistes?
a: Avalanche transceiver, avalanche shovel and avalanche probe
Foil blanket, mobile phone and map
125931.e: With the transceiver you locate the buried person, with the probe you confirm their position and with the shovel you dig them out. If any one of these is missing, the rescue takes much longer.
125931.m: Transceiver, shovel and probe always belong together.

125932.q: Why is rescue by companions so crucial in avalanche accidents?
a: Because it is much faster than an organised rescue on the spot
Because it is cheaper than a helicopter mission
Because rescue services are not allowed to fly into the mountains
Because only companions know the victims
125932.e: Even a helicopter usually needs much longer for the alarm and the flight than the first critical minutes. The companions are already there.
125932.m: In avalanches, it is often the companions who save the lives of those buried.

125933.q: What do you uncover as early as possible when recovering an avalanche victim?
a: The head with the mouth and nose
125933.e: As soon as the airway is clear, the person can breathe. During the rescue, you also look out for a possible air pocket in front of the face.
125933.m: With avalanche victims, the head and airway are uncovered first.

125934.q: Below which core body temperature is it called hypothermia?
125934.e: The normal core temperature is about 37 degrees. If it falls below 35 degrees, a person is considered hypothermic.
125934.m: Hypothermia begins below a core temperature of 35 degrees.

125935.q: According to the Swiss staging system, what characterises stage I hypothermia?
125935.e: In the first stage, the person is awake and shivers strongly. Shivering produces heat and is a protective mechanism.
125935.m: Someone who is shivering strongly and thinking clearly is mildly hypothermic.

125936.q: Below roughly which core temperature does shivering usually stop?
125936.e: As the body cools further, the energy reserves run out and the muscles no longer work effectively. A lack of shivering is therefore a warning sign.
125936.m: If a hypothermic person stops shivering, it becomes dangerous.

125937.q: Why do you move a severely hypothermic person as gently as possible and keep them horizontal?
a: Because otherwise ventricular fibrillation can be triggered
Because otherwise they fall asleep immediately
125937.e: The cold heart is very easily irritated. Jerky movements and cold blood from the limbs can trigger a dangerous rhythm.
125937.m: Hypothermic people are kept still and lying flat.

125938.q: What does the saying “Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead” mean?
a: That you keep resuscitating hypothermic people without signs of life
That the dead must always be warmed up
That you only resuscitate in summer
125938.e: Cold greatly reduces the brain's need for oxygen. That is why even people with a long cardiac arrest in deep hypothermia have a chance of survival.
125938.m: In severe hypothermia, resuscitation is not given up too soon.

125939.q: How is a deeply hypothermic person in cardiac arrest most effectively rewarmed in hospital?
a: With a heart-lung machine or ECMO
With warm tea through a stomach tube
With infrared lamps on the skin
125939.e: In extracorporeal rewarming, the blood is warmed outside the body and enriched with oxygen. At the same time, the machine takes over the pumping work of the heart.
125939.m: In hypothermia with cardiac arrest, a heart-lung machine helps.

125940.q: Why do small children cool down faster than adults?
a: Because their body surface is larger in relation to their volume
Because their heart beats more slowly
125940.e: The body loses heat through its surface, while heat is produced and stored in its volume. A small body has relatively a lot of surface and therefore loses heat quickly.
125940.m: Small children need especially good protection from the cold.

125941.q: Why does alcohol increase the risk of hypothermia?
a: Because it widens the blood vessels in the skin, so more heat is lost
Because it heats the body up strongly from inside
125941.e: The feeling of warmth on the skin is deceptive, because heat flows out through the widened vessels. Alcohol also clouds your judgement of the danger.
125941.m: Alcohol only seems to warm you and in fact encourages cooling down.

125942.q: Which language does the word “triage” come from?
125942.e: The verb “trier” means to sort or select. In German medical services it is also called “Sichtung”.
125942.m: Triage means sorting patients by urgency.

125943.q: Which of Napoleon's military surgeons is regarded as the founder of modern triage?
125943.e: Larrey had the wounded treated according to how serious their injuries were and not according to rank. He also introduced fast transport carts for the wounded.
125943.m: Modern triage goes back to Napoleon's surgeon Larrey.

125944.q: What does the colour red mean in triage after a major incident?
125944.e: People marked red are acutely life-threateningly injured but have a good chance of survival with immediate help. Yellow stands for urgent cases, green for minor ones.
125944.m: In triage, red means treat immediately.

125945.q: In the START system, which category do all people who can walk on their own receive?
125945.e: People who can walk usually have no immediately life-threatening injury. They are sent to a gathering point and assessed more closely later.
125945.m: In the START system, people who can walk are first considered slightly injured.

125946.q: After a major incident, an injured person is breathing more than 30 times a minute. Which category do you put them in under the START system?
125946.e: Very fast breathing shows a serious disturbance of breathing or circulation. Such people need help immediately.
125946.m: If an injured person breathes very fast, they must be treated immediately.

125947.q: Above which capillary refill time is a person considered critical in the START system?
125947.e: You press on a fingernail bed and measure how quickly it turns pink again. Slow refilling points to shock.
125947.m: A slow return of colour to the nail bed points to shock.

125948.q: What does the Manchester Triage System in the emergency department set for each level of urgency?
a: A maximum waiting time until first seeing a doctor
125948.e: The system divides patients into five colour levels. Red means immediately, blue may wait the longest.
125948.m: The Manchester Triage System works with five colour levels.

125949.q: What does the German abbreviation MANV stand for in emergency services?
125949.e: A mass casualty incident occurs when there are more injured people than available rescue resources. Triage then becomes the central task of the first emergency teams.
125949.m: In a mass casualty incident, triage is essential.

125950.q: In which city is Tox Info Suisse based?
125950.e: The centre works closely with the University of Zurich. From there it gives advice to the whole of Switzerland.
125950.m: Tox Info Suisse is based in Zurich.

125951.q: When can the Tox Info Suisse emergency number be reached?
a: Only on weekdays during office hours
125951.e: Poisonings happen at any time of day. That is why experts answer the calls without a break.
125951.m: Tox Info Suisse can be reached day and night.

125952.q: Which age group among children is most often affected in poisoning enquiries to Tox Info Suisse?
125952.e: Toddlers explore their surroundings with their mouths. That is why they often swallow household products, parts of plants or medicines.
125952.m: Medicines and cleaning products should be kept out of reach of toddlers.

125953.q: What should you not do if a child has swallowed a corrosive cleaning product?
125953.e: When vomiting, the corrosive liquid would damage the oesophagus a second time. It could also get into the lungs.
125953.m: After swallowing cleaning products, never make someone vomit yourself.

125954.q: Which group of products is most often involved in enquiries to Tox Info Suisse?
125954.e: Medicines are found in almost every household and get mixed up, taken in too high a dose or found by children. Household products come next.
125954.m: Most poisoning enquiries are about medicines.

125955.q: What should you have ready if possible when calling Tox Info Suisse?
125955.e: The packaging shows the name and the ingredients. This lets the expert assess the risk accurately.
125955.m: In a poisoning, keep the product's packaging ready.

125956.q: Which remedy is used in many poisonings to bind toxic substances in the gut?
125956.e: Activated charcoal has a huge inner surface to which many substances stick. An expert decides whether it makes sense to use it.
125956.m: Activated charcoal binds many poisons before they enter the blood.

125957.q: How is the Swiss Samaritan Association organised at grassroots level?
125957.e: The clubs work largely on a voluntary basis and are grouped into cantonal associations. They offer courses and first aid services in their region.
125957.m: Samaritan work depends on local clubs with volunteers.

125958.q: Which course must people in Switzerland have attended before applying for a learner's permit for driving a car?
a: The first aid for children course
125958.e: The emergency first aid course teaches how to behave at the scene of an accident, positioning and chest compressions. Providers include the Samaritan clubs.
125958.m: Anyone who wants to learn to drive first attends the emergency first aid course.

125959.q: What role does the Interverband für Rettungswesen (IVR) play in Switzerland?
a: It is the umbrella association for rescue services
It is the police emergency call centre
It is a private ambulance company
It is the Federal Office for Civil Protection
125959.e: In the IVR, organisations and experts from the rescue services work together. It campaigns for a uniform quality of rescue.
125959.m: The IVR is the umbrella association of Swiss rescue services.

125960.q: What is the Interverband für Rettungswesen called in French?
125960.e: The French abbreviation is IAS. In French-speaking Switzerland the association is known by this name.
125960.m: In French-speaking Switzerland, the IVR is called Interassociation de sauvetage.

125961.q: What does the IVR award to ambulance services that meet its quality guidelines?
125961.e: Ambulance services are checked for equipment, staff and procedures. The recognition shows that they meet the Swiss-wide standards.
125961.m: Ambulance services recognised by the IVR meet uniform quality standards.

125962.q: Besides ambulance services, which facilities are also recognised according to IVR guidelines?
125962.e: The emergency call centres take calls, send out rescue resources and guide laypeople over the phone. Uniform quality requirements apply to them too.
125962.m: The 144 emergency call centres also follow Swiss-wide guidelines.

125963.q: At which level of education are paramedics trained in Switzerland?
a: At a college of higher education (Höhere Fachschule)
125963.e: The qualification is called qualified paramedic HF. The training combines college and practical work in the ambulance service.
125963.m: In Switzerland, paramedics are trained at colleges of higher education.

125964.q: Which qualification do patient transport attendants earn in Switzerland?
a: A federal diploma of higher vocational education
A course certificate from the employer
125964.e: The professional examination leads to the federal diploma. Patient transport attendants mainly work on planned and less urgent patient transports.
125964.m: Patient transport attendants qualify with a federal diploma.

125965.q: Which target for response time do the IVR guidelines set for ambulance services?
a: On the scene within 15 minutes in 90 per cent of call-outs
On the scene within 2 minutes in all call-outs
Within 1 hour in 50 per cent of call-outs
125965.e: The response time is the time it takes for the ambulance service to reach the scene. It is an important figure for planning ambulance stations.
125965.m: Ambulance services should reach most emergencies within a quarter of an hour.

125966.q: When is a tourniquet used in first aid?
a: For life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg that cannot be stopped any other way
For every small cut on a finger
For a bruise without a wound
125966.e: A tourniquet stops the blood flow to the whole limb. It is the right tool when pressure and a pressure bandage are not enough or there is no time for them.
125966.m: A tourniquet is meant for life-threatening bleeding from arms and legs.

125967.q: Where is a tourniquet applied when the wound is known?
a: A few centimetres above the wound, towards the body, not over a joint
Below the wound, towards the hand or foot
125967.e: Above the wound, it cuts off the supply to the bleeding site. Over a joint, the blood vessel cannot be reliably compressed.
125967.m: The tourniquet goes above the wound and never on a joint.

125968.q: What must always be written down after applying a tourniquet?
a: The skin colour of the helper
125968.e: How long the limb has been tied off is important for treatment in hospital. The time is often written directly on the tourniquet or on the person's forehead.
125968.m: With a tourniquet, the time is always written down.

125969.q: What is the turning rod called that is used to tighten a modern tourniquet?
125969.e: Turning the rod tightens the band so much that the artery is compressed. The rod is then secured in a holder.
125969.m: A tourniquet is tightened with a turning rod called a windlass.

125970.q: Who is allowed to loosen a tourniquet once it has been applied?
a: Anyone, as soon as the bleeding has stopped
Nobody, it stays on until healing is complete
125970.e: When it is loosened, the bleeding can start again and toxic substances from the limb get into the circulation. That is why professionals decide.
125970.m: Only professionals loosen a tourniquet once it has been applied.

125971.q: Where do you apply a tourniquet if the exact source of bleeding cannot be seen?
a: As high up the limb as possible, close to the body
Exactly in the middle of the limb
125971.e: Following the principle “high and tight”, this covers all possible bleeding sites below it. Later, professionals can place the tourniquet more precisely.
125971.m: If the source of bleeding is unclear, the tourniquet goes high and tight on the limb.

125972.q: How can you tell that a tourniquet is tight enough?
a: The bleeding stops and no pulse can be felt below it
The skin below turns red and warm
The injured person feels no pain
The band can still be moved easily
125972.e: A tourniquet that is too loose only traps blood in the veins and can even make the bleeding worse. It must completely cut off the flow through the arteries.
125972.m: A tourniquet is only right when the bleeding really stops.

125973.q: Why is a thin cord unsuitable as an improvised tourniquet?
a: It cuts in and damages skin and nerves
125973.e: A narrow band puts the pressure on a small area. It injures the tissue underneath and often still does not fully compress the artery.
125973.m: A tourniquet needs a wide band, not a thin cord.

125974.q: Roughly how long is a correctly applied tourniquet considered acceptable without serious damage being expected?
125974.e: After that, the risk of muscle and nerve damage rises considerably. That is why quick transport to hospital is important.
125974.m: A tourniquet is only a stopgap until treatment in hospital.

125975.q: With which heart finding does an AED not deliver a shock?
125975.e: In asystole, there is no electrical activity at all that a shock could reorganise. Only chest compressions and medicines help here.
125975.m: A flat line cannot be treated with an electric shock.

125976.q: What do you do with a medicine patch that is stuck where an AED pad needs to go?
a: Remove it and wipe the skin
Stick the pad directly over it
125976.e: A patch under the pad can block the flow of current and cause burns. It only takes seconds to pull it off.
125976.m: No patch may be stuck under an AED pad.

125977.q: What do special child pads or a child mode on an AED do?
a: They extend the analysis time to ten minutes
They switch off the voice prompts
They deliver several shocks at the same time
125977.e: Children need a smaller amount of current than adults. If there are no child pads, the adult pads are used anyway.
125977.m: On a child, an AED may be used with reduced energy.

125978.q: How often should several helpers ideally take turns doing chest compressions?
125978.e: Chest compressions are tiring, and the depth of the compressions drops unnoticed as you tire. The changeover should happen with as short a pause as possible.
125978.m: Helpers take turns regularly during chest compressions.

125979.q: What is the longest that checking an unconscious person's breathing should take?
125979.e: You tilt the head back and look, listen and feel for breathing movements, breathing sounds and airflow. If you are unsure, you start chest compressions.
125979.m: Checking breathing takes no longer than ten seconds.

125980.q: Roughly what proportion of normal heart output does good chest compression achieve?
a: About a quarter to a third
125980.e: Chest compressions only partly replace the heart's pumping. But this is enough to supply the brain and heart with some oxygen for a while.
125980.m: Chest compressions keep an emergency circulation going until the heart beats again.

125981.q: During resuscitation, how can you tell that the heart is beating on its own again?
a: A pulse and normal breathing return
125981.e: When the heart beats by itself again, a pulse can be felt and the person often starts breathing normally again. Experts call this return of spontaneous circulation.
125981.m: When pulse and breathing return, the heart is beating on its own again.

125982.q: After successful resuscitation, what is deliberately avoided in intensive care during the first few days?
125982.e: A raised body temperature makes brain damage after a lack of oxygen worse. That is why the temperature is monitored and carefully controlled.
125982.m: After resuscitation, a controlled body temperature protects the brain.

125983.q: What does the classic chain of rescue start with?
a: The arrival of the emergency doctor
125983.e: Immediate measures include securing the scene of the accident, rescuing people from the danger zone and chest compressions. They are carried out by the first people on the scene.
125983.m: The chain of rescue begins with the people who are first at the scene.

125984.q: What is it called when the emergency call centre guides laypeople through chest compressions over the phone?
125984.e: The dispatcher counts out the rhythm and gives instructions. As a result, many more laypeople start resuscitation.
125984.m: In cardiac arrest, the emergency call centre helps with resuscitation over the phone.

125985.q: What is the job of first responders, who are alerted by smartphone app in many cantons?
a: They start resuscitation before the ambulance service arrives
They replace the emergency doctor in hospital
They direct traffic at the scene of the accident
125985.e: Volunteers trained in resuscitation who are nearby are called out at the same time as the ambulance service. They are often on the scene faster.
125985.m: In cardiac arrest, first responders bridge the time until the ambulance service arrives.

125986.q: At least how far away do you set up the warning triangle on Swiss motorways?
125986.e: Because of the high speeds, vehicles behind need a long braking distance. On other roads, 50 metres is usually enough.
125986.m: On the motorway, the warning triangle stands at least 100 metres before the accident.

125987.q: What is the top priority for helpers at the scene of an accident?
125987.e: Anyone who puts themselves in danger can become an additional victim and can no longer help anyone. That is why you first secure the scene and watch out for traffic, fire or electricity.
125987.m: Anyone who helps protects themselves first.

125988.q: Which grip do you use to quickly pull an unconscious person out of a danger zone, for example out of a car?
125988.e: You reach under the armpits, grab one of the person's forearms and pull them out of the danger zone on your own thighs. The grip is named after the Austrian Franz Rautek.
125988.m: With the Rautek manoeuvre, even a weaker person can rescue someone who is unconscious.

125989.q: What do you do with an unconscious motorcyclist wearing a full-face helmet?
a: Just close the visor with tape
Bend the head with the helmet sharply forwards
125989.e: With the helmet on, the airway cannot be checked and kept clear. If possible two people remove it, stabilising the head and neck at the same time.
125989.m: If a motorcyclist is unconscious, the helmet is removed.

125990.q: Which life-threatening chest injury is relieved in an emergency with a needle?
125990.e: In a tension pneumothorax, air collects under pressure in the chest and squeezes the lungs and heart. The needle lets the air escape and buys time until a drain is inserted.
125990.m: A tension pneumothorax must be relieved immediately.

125991.q: Where do you inject an adrenaline auto-injector in anaphylaxis?
a: Into the outer side of the thigh
Into a vein on the back of the hand
Under the skin of the stomach
Into the crook of the arm
125991.e: The large thigh muscle has a good blood supply and is easy to reach. In an emergency you can even inject through trousers.
125991.m: The adrenaline pen is placed on the outer thigh.

125992.q: What do you do if anaphylaxis does not improve about 5 minutes after the first dose of adrenaline?
a: Give a second dose of adrenaline
Give the person a glass of milk
Leave the person to rest alone
125992.e: That is why many people with allergies carry two auto-injectors. The second dose is given into the other thigh.
125992.m: If the first dose of adrenaline does not help, a second one follows.

125993.q: What is anaphylaxis called that only occurs when someone does sport after eating a particular food?
125993.e: Only the combination of the food and physical exertion triggers the reaction. A well-known trigger is wheat.
125993.m: Some types of anaphylaxis also need physical exertion as a trigger.

125994.q: Which foods particularly often trigger anaphylaxis in children?
125994.e: Nuts are among the most common triggers of severe allergic reactions. Even tiny traces can be enough.
125994.m: Nuts are common triggers of anaphylaxis.

125995.q: Why does a person in anaphylactic shock quickly need a lot of intravenous fluid?
a: Because fluid leaks out of the leaky blood vessels into the tissue
Because they have too much salt in their blood
Because otherwise the adrenaline will not dissolve
125995.e: Messenger substances make the vessel walls leaky and widen the vessels. As a result, the circulation suddenly lacks a lot of volume.
125995.m: In anaphylaxis, the circulation loses fluid to the tissue.

125996.q: After the bite of which animal can alpha-gal syndrome, an allergy to red meat, develop?
125996.e: The bite sensitises the body to the sugar alpha-gal, which is also found in mammal meat. The reaction typically only occurs hours after eating.
125996.m: A tick bite can trigger a delayed allergy to red meat.

125997.q: Why is adrenaline for anaphylaxis injected into the muscle and not under the skin?
a: Because it gets into the blood faster from the muscle
Because it turns into crystals under the skin
Because the skin contains no blood
Because it costs less that way
125997.e: Muscles have a good blood supply, while adrenaline under the skin narrows the vessels there and so slows down its own absorption. That is why injecting into the muscle is standard.
125997.m: Adrenaline for anaphylaxis goes into the muscle.

125998.q: Which number do you dial in a poisoning if the person is unconscious or breathing badly?
125998.e: When life is in danger, the ambulance service is needed immediately. If necessary, the emergency call centre can consult Tox Info Suisse itself.
125998.m: In a life-threatening poisoning, you call the ambulance service first.

125999.q: Which events do many Samaritan clubs organise together with the Swiss Red Cross blood donation service?
125999.e: The clubs provide helpers for registering, looking after and feeding the donors. This way, blood is collected regularly in many municipalities.
125999.m: Samaritan clubs help with many blood donation drives.

126000.q: What aim has the Samaritan movement pursued since its beginnings in the 19th century?
a: Laypeople should be able to give first aid in accidents
Only doctors should be allowed to treat injured people
Hospitals should be replaced by clubs
Injured people should only be cared for by the army
126000.e: The Samaritan movement wants ordinary people to be able to help properly in accidents until professionals arrive. The name goes back to the parable of the Good Samaritan.

126001.q: Which course do Samaritan clubs offer in which you practise chest compressions and defibrillation?
126001.e: BLS stands for Basic Life Support, the basic measures of resuscitation. Because knowledge fades, regular refresher courses are recommended.
126001.m: In a BLS-AED course you learn how to help in cardiac arrest.

126002.q: What is the maximum age of the emergency first aid course certificate when applying for a learner's permit?
126002.e: If the course was longer ago, it has to be repeated. This is so that the knowledge is still reasonably fresh when you start driving.
126002.m: An emergency first aid course that is too old must be repeated before the learner's permit.

126003.q: In triage after a major incident, what does the category blue mean?
a: Expectant treatment, because there is hardly any chance of survival under the circumstances
Immediate treatment because of danger to life
Slightly injured and able to walk
126003.e: This difficult category is only used when there are not enough resources for everyone. Those affected are looked after and reassessed when capacity becomes free.
126003.m: The category blue is only given when rescue resources are lacking.

126114.q: The fruits of which plant served as George de Mestral's model?
126114.e: Burdock fruits have lots of tiny hooks and get caught in fur and clothes. This is how animals spread their seeds.
126114.m: Burdock was the model for Velcro.

126120.q: Which two parts does a Velcro fastener consist of?
126120.e: One strip has tiny hooks, the other soft loops. When pressed together they hook into each other; when pulled apart they come undone again.
126120.m: A Velcro fastener consists of hooks and loops.

126163.e: Urban gardening means growing vegetables, herbs and flowers in cities. It is often done together with others on waste ground, roofs or in backyards.
126163.m: Urban gardening is gardening in the city.

126179.q: Which winter road treatment is especially harmful to city trees along roads?
126179.e: Road salt gets into the soil with meltwater and damages roots and leaves. The trees then take up water and nutrients less well.
126179.m: Road salt harms the roots of city trees.

126297.q: Which federal law regulates compulsory health insurance in Switzerland?
126297.e: The Federal Health Insurance Act (KVG) sets out who must be insured and which services basic insurance pays for.
126297.m: Basic insurance is based on the Health Insurance Act.

126298.q: Since which year has health insurance been compulsory throughout Switzerland?
126298.e: The Health Insurance Act was accepted in a popular vote in 1994 and came into force on 1 January 1996. Since then, everyone living in Switzerland must be insured.
126298.m: Basic insurance has been compulsory for everyone since 1996.

126299.q: Within what period must a person take out health insurance after moving to Switzerland?
126299.e: Anyone moving to Switzerland must take out insurance within three months. The insurance then applies retroactively from the date of arrival.
126299.m: After moving here, you have three months to get insured.

126300.q: What are health insurers not allowed to do in basic insurance?
a: Reject a person because of previous illnesses
Set different premiums for premium regions
126300.e: In basic insurance, there is an obligation to accept: every insurer must accept every person regardless of age and state of health.
126300.m: In basic insurance, every insurer must accept everyone.

126301.q: Which of these does the basic insurance premium not depend on?
126301.e: Basic insurance has per-person premiums: all adults with the same insurer, in the same model and in the same region pay the same, no matter how much they earn.
126301.m: Health insurance premiums are per-person premiums and do not depend on salary.

126302.q: Which law governs supplementary insurance, where insurers may ask health questions and reject applications?
126302.e: Supplementary insurance, such as a semi-private hospital ward, consists of private law contracts under the Insurance Contract Act. There is no obligation to accept there.
126302.m: Supplementary insurance is voluntary and may reject applications.

126303.q: What does the billing system “tiers garant” mean?
a: The patient pays the bill and gets the money back from the insurer
The insurer pays the bill directly to the doctor
The canton of residence pays the whole bill
The employer pays the bill and deducts it from the salary
126303.e: In the tiers garant system, the insured person owes the bill and then has it refunded by the insurer.
126303.m: In the tiers garant system, you pay first yourself and are then reimbursed.

126304.q: Who can exclude accident cover from basic insurance and so save on premiums?
a: Employees who work at least 8 hours a week for the same employer
126304.e: Anyone who works at least 8 hours a week for the same employer is also insured against non-occupational accidents under the Accident Insurance Act. Double cover is then unnecessary.
126304.m: Anyone insured against accidents through their employer can suspend the accident cover of their health insurance.

126305.q: Which service does basic insurance usually not pay for?
a: Ordinary dental treatment such as fillings
A stay in the general ward of a hospital
Medicines prescribed by a doctor and covered by insurance
126305.e: Basic insurance only pays for dental treatment in exceptional cases, for example when it is caused by a serious illness. Normal dental care must be paid for yourself or through supplementary insurance.
126305.m: Basic insurance does not pay for normal dental treatment.

126306.q: What is the standard annual deductible for adults in basic insurance?
126306.e: The standard, which means the lowest, deductible for adults is 300 francs a year. You can choose higher deductibles voluntarily.
126306.m: The lowest deductible for adults is 300 francs.

126307.q: What is the highest deductible adults can choose in basic insurance?
126307.e: Adults can choose between 300, 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000 and 2,500 francs. The highest level brings the biggest premium discount.
126307.m: The highest deductible for adults is 2,500 francs.

126308.q: What is the standard deductible for children up to the age of 18?
126308.e: By law there is no standard deductible for children. However, parents can choose an optional deductible voluntarily.
126308.m: Unless one is chosen, children have no deductible.

126309.q: What is the highest optional deductible for children?
126309.e: For children you can choose optional deductibles in steps of a hundred, from 100 to 600 francs.
126309.m: For children, a deductible of up to 600 francs is possible.

126310.q: How does choosing a higher deductible affect the monthly premium?
a: The premium is set again by the canton
126310.e: Anyone who pays more of the costs themselves takes pressure off the insurer. In return, it gives a discount on the premium.
126310.m: A higher deductible lowers the premium but increases your own risk.

126311.q: A person has a deductible of 2,500 francs and doctor's costs of 1,800 francs for the whole year. How much does basic insurance pay?
126311.e: The costs of 1,800 francs are below the deductible of 2,500 francs. The person therefore pays everything themselves and the insurance pays nothing.
126311.m: Until the deductible is reached, you pay everything yourself.

126312.q: For what period does the deductible apply?
a: For each individual visit to the doctor
For one quarter of a year
126312.e: The deductible is calculated per calendar year. On 1 January it starts again at zero.
126312.m: The deductible starts again every year on 1 January.

126313.q: Which deductible levels apply to young adults aged 19 to 25?
a: Their own levels between 50 and 500 francs
126313.e: Young adults often pay lower premiums than older adults but have the same deductible levels of 300 to 2,500 francs.
126313.m: From the age of 19, the adult deductibles apply.

126314.q: For whom is a high deductible typically worth it?
a: For healthy people with low health costs
For people with a chronic illness
For people with expensive long-term medicines
For people who are often in hospital
126314.e: People who rarely go to the doctor benefit from the premium discount and hardly ever use up the high deductible. With high costs, however, you end up paying more.
126314.m: A high deductible is mainly worth it for healthy people.

126315.q: What percentage of the costs above the deductible do insured people usually pay as their share?
126315.e: Once the deductible has been reached, you pay 10 per cent of the further costs, up to an annual maximum.
126315.m: The normal co-payment is ten per cent.

126316.q: What is the maximum annual co-payment for adults?
126316.e: For adults, the 10 per cent co-payment is limited to 700 francs a year.
126316.m: Adults pay at most 700 francs co-payment per year.

126317.q: What is the maximum annual co-payment for children?
126317.e: For children, the co-payment is limited to half the amount for adults, which is 350 francs a year.
126317.m: For children, the co-payment is limited to 350 francs.

126318.q: Deductible 300 francs, treatment costs for the year 1,500 francs. How much does the insured person pay themselves in total?
126318.e: First comes the 300 francs deductible. Of the remaining 1,200 francs, you pay 10 per cent, which is 120 francs. Together that makes 420 francs.
126318.m: First comes the deductible, then the co-payment on the rest.

126319.q: Deductible 300 francs, treatment costs for the year 20,000 francs. How much does an adult pay themselves in total?
126319.e: 300 francs deductible plus 10 per cent of 19,700 francs would be 1,970 francs co-payment. But this is limited to 700 francs, so the total is 300 + 700 = 1,000 francs.
126319.m: The upper limit on the co-payment protects against very high costs.

126320.q: Deductible 1,000 francs, treatment costs for the year 3,000 francs. How much does the adult pay themselves?
126320.e: 1,000 francs deductible plus 10 per cent of the remaining 2,000 francs, which is 200 francs. Total 1,200 francs.
126320.m: You calculate the deductible plus ten per cent of the remaining costs.

126321.q: What is the maximum annual cost share for an adult with a deductible of 2,500 francs (deductible plus co-payment)?
126321.e: On top of the 2,500 francs deductible comes a co-payment of at most 700 francs. That makes 3,200 francs.
126321.m: With the highest deductible, in the worst case you pay 3,200 francs yourself.

126322.q: Since 2024, which co-payment usually applies if you get an original medicine even though a cheaper generic is available?
126322.e: To encourage the use of cheaper generics, the increased co-payment for overpriced original medicines was raised to 40 per cent. There are exceptions if the original is medically necessary.
126322.m: Anyone who chooses the expensive original without a medical reason pays more themselves.

126323.q: Which contribution do adults pay for a hospital stay in addition to the deductible and co-payment?
126323.e: The hospital contribution takes into account the food costs saved at home. Children and young adults in education are exempt from it.
126323.m: For every day in hospital, adults pay a small contribution towards their meals.

126324.q: What does the abbreviation IPV stand for in the Swiss health system?
126324.e: With the individual premium reduction, the state supports insured people of modest means.
126324.m: The IPV helps people on low incomes to pay their premiums.

126325.q: Who finances the individual premium reduction?
126325.e: The Confederation makes a contribution to the cantons, and the cantons add their own funds.
126325.m: The Confederation and the cantons pay for the premium reduction together.

126326.q: Who decides who is entitled to a premium reduction and how much it is?
a: The Federal Council, the same for everyone
126326.e: The cantons set the income limits and amounts themselves. That is why the rules differ greatly from canton to canton.
126326.m: Each canton regulates the premium reduction itself.

126327.q: For which groups does the Health Insurance Act require a particularly large premium reduction?
a: Children and young adults in education
126327.e: For lower and middle incomes, the cantons must reduce the premiums for children and young adults in education particularly strongly. This is to ease the burden on families.
126327.m: Families on low and middle incomes receive a large premium reduction for their children.

126328.q: How is the premium reduction usually paid out?
a: In cash at the municipal office counter
As a bonus on top of the salary
As a credit at the doctor's
126328.e: The canton transfers the amount directly to the health insurer. The insured person then pays a lower premium bill.
126328.m: The premium reduction directly lowers the premium bill.

126329.q: Which popular initiative, which wanted to limit premiums to at most 10 per cent of disposable income, did voters reject in 2024?
a: The initiative for a single health insurance fund
126329.e: The Premium Relief Initiative was rejected in June 2024. Instead, an indirect counter-proposal comes into force that obliges the cantons to make minimum contributions.
126329.m: Limiting premiums to ten per cent of income was rejected in 2024.

126330.q: What does the size of the federal contribution to the premium reduction depend on?
a: The tax rate of the municipalities
126330.e: The Confederation pays a fixed share of the gross costs of compulsory health insurance. If health costs rise, its contribution rises too.
126330.m: The federal contribution to the premium reduction grows with health costs.

126331.q: What does the Federal Office of Public Health check before basic insurance pays for a new medicine?
a: Whether it is effective, appropriate and cost-effective
Whether it is made in Switzerland
Whether it is available without a prescription
126331.e: A medicine is only added to the list of pharmaceutical specialities if it is effective, appropriate and cost-effective. Only then does basic insurance pay.
126331.m: Basic insurance only pays for effective, appropriate and cost-effective medicines.

126332.q: What must the Federal Office of Public Health approve every year before it applies?
a: The hospital bills of the cantons
126332.e: The health insurers submit their premiums for the following year to the Federal Office of Public Health. It checks them and announces the approved premiums every autumn.
126332.m: The new health insurance premiums are approved by the Federal Office of Public Health every autumn.

126333.q: Which law regulates, among other things, the duty to report certain infectious diseases?
126333.e: The Epidemics Act regulates protection against infectious diseases. Doctors and laboratories report certain diseases to the Federal Office of Public Health and the canton.
126333.m: Infectious diseases are reported and monitored under the Epidemics Act.

126334.q: In which region does the Federal Office of Public Health have its headquarters?
126334.e: The Federal Office of Public Health is based in Liebefeld near Bern, close to the rest of the federal administration.
126334.m: The Federal Office of Public Health is based near Bern.

126335.q: Which task also belongs to the Federal Office of Public Health?
a: Radiation protection, for example from radon in buildings
126335.e: The Federal Office of Public Health is responsible for radiation protection in Switzerland. This includes information about the radioactive gas radon, which can occur in cellars and living spaces.
126335.m: Protection from radiation such as radon is also a task of the Federal Office of Public Health.

126336.q: What is the official federal premium calculator called, which lets you compare health insurance premiums?
126336.e: On Priminfo, the Federal Office of Public Health publishes all approved basic insurance premiums. This lets you compare offers neutrally.
126336.m: With Priminfo you can compare the premiums of all health insurers.

126337.q: Which insurance is compulsory for all residents of Switzerland?
a: Supplementary insurance for a private room
126337.e: Basic insurance under the Health Insurance Act is compulsory for everyone living in Switzerland. Supplementary insurance is voluntary.
126337.m: Basic insurance is compulsory in Switzerland.

126338.q: What is the main task of Swissmedic?
126338.e: Swissmedic is the Swiss authority that approves and supervises medicines and medical devices. It checks safety, effectiveness and quality.
126338.m: Swissmedic approves and monitors therapeutic products.

126339.q: Why does a new medicine need approval before it may be sold in Switzerland?
a: Its safety, effectiveness and quality must be checked
So that the price is as high as possible
So that it may be advertised
So that it is only used in hospitals
126339.e: Before approval, Swissmedic examines the manufacturer's studies. Only if the benefits outweigh the risks may the medicine be sold.
126339.m: Medicines need approval before they are sold.

126340.q: Which law is Swissmedic's work mainly based on?
126340.e: The Therapeutic Products Act regulates the approval, manufacture, supply and monitoring of medicines and medical devices.
126340.m: Swissmedic works on the basis of the Therapeutic Products Act.

126341.q: What is meant by pharmacovigilance, one of Swissmedic's tasks?
a: Monitoring undesirable effects of medicines after approval
126341.e: Rare side effects can still occur after approval. Professionals and patients report suspected cases, and Swissmedic evaluates them.
126341.m: Even approved medicines continue to be monitored for side effects.

126342.q: Which task is not one of Swissmedic's?
a: Setting the prices of medicines covered by health insurance
126342.e: Swissmedic checks safety, effectiveness and quality. The price and whether insurance pays are decided by the Federal Office of Public Health instead.
126342.m: Swissmedic checks the safety of a medicine, not its price.

126343.q: What does dispensing category E mean for medicines?
a: Freely available for sale, even outside pharmacies
Can be supplied only once on a doctor's prescription
Only after expert advice in a pharmacy
Can only be used in hospital
126343.e: Medicines in category E, such as certain throat lozenges, may be sold in shops without expert advice.
126343.m: Medicines in category E are freely available.

126344.q: What does Swissmedic regularly warn about when medicines are ordered from unknown online shops abroad?
a: Delivery times that are too long
126344.e: Many medicines ordered online are fakes with the wrong dose or dangerous ingredients. Customs often stop such parcels.
126344.m: Medicines from dubious online shops can be fake and dangerous.

126345.q: How many university hospitals are there in Switzerland?
126345.e: The five university hospitals are in Zurich, Bern, Basel, Lausanne and Geneva.

126346.q: Which university does the CHUV work with in medical teaching and research?
126346.e: The Faculty of Biology and Medicine of the University of Lausanne trains its medical students together with the CHUV.
126346.m: Every university hospital works closely with a medical faculty.

126347.q: In which city is the CHUV university hospital?
126347.e: CHUV stands for Centre hospitalier universitaire vaudois. It is the university hospital of the canton of Vaud in Lausanne.
126347.m: The CHUV is the university hospital in Lausanne.

126348.q: In which city are the HUG (Hôpitaux universitaires de Genève)?
126348.e: The HUG are the university hospital of the canton of Geneva and one of the largest hospital groups in Switzerland.
126348.m: The HUG are the university hospital of Geneva.

126349.q: What are the three main tasks of university hospitals?
126349.e: University hospitals treat patients, train doctors together with the universities and carry out medical research.
126349.m: University hospitals combine treatment, training and research.

126350.q: Why are very complex operations such as organ transplants concentrated in a few centres in Switzerland?
a: Because high case numbers ensure experience and quality
Because small hospitals have no doctors
Because the Confederation wants to close all other hospitals
Because only university hospitals have electricity
126350.e: The cantons coordinate highly specialised medicine together. Those who perform an operation often have more routine, and expensive infrastructure is not built several times over.
126350.m: Rare, complex operations are concentrated in a few experienced centres.

126351.q: Who runs the University Hospital Zurich?
126351.e: The University Hospital Zurich is an independent public institution of the canton of Zurich. For teaching, it works with the University of Zurich.
126351.m: In Switzerland, university hospitals belong to the cantons.

126352.q: Which of these hospitals is not a university hospital?
126352.e: St Gallen Cantonal Hospital is a large central hospital and does train doctors, but it is not one of the five university hospitals.
126352.m: Not every large hospital is a university hospital.

126353.q: What is the guiding role that the GP takes on in the family doctor model called?
126353.e: In gatekeeping, the GP decides whether and where a patient is referred. This is meant to avoid unnecessary duplicate examinations.
126353.m: In the family doctor model, the GP is the guide through the health system.

126354.q: In which alternative insurance model do you first have to call a telephone advice service before seeing a doctor?
126354.e: In the Telmed model, a medical professional clarifies over the phone whether and where treatment is needed.
126354.m: In the Telmed model, you first call the advice service.

126355.q: In which model do you first go to a health centre with doctors employed there?
126355.e: HMO stands for Health Maintenance Organization. The first treatment takes place in a particular group practice.
126355.m: In the HMO model, a group practice is the first point of contact.

126356.q: What advantage do insured people get if they choose the family doctor model?
126356.e: Because coordinated treatment is usually cheaper, insurers offer a lower premium than in the standard model.
126356.m: People insured in the family doctor model pay a lower premium.

126357.q: In the family doctor model, in which situation may you go straight to another place without first contacting your GP?
a: If you personally know a specialist
126357.e: In an emergency, quick treatment comes first. However, you usually have to inform your GP or the insurer afterwards.
126357.m: In an emergency you may get help straight away, even in the family doctor model.

126358.q: What can happen in the family doctor model if you go straight to a specialist without a referral?
a: The insurer can refuse to pay the costs
126358.e: Anyone who repeatedly breaks the model's rules risks the insurer not paying the bill or moving them back into the more expensive standard model.
126358.m: Anyone who ignores the rules of the family doctor model may be left with the costs.

126359.q: Which proposal to promote integrated care networks did voters clearly reject in 2012?
126359.e: The revision of the Health Insurance Act on managed care aimed to promote care networks with a lower co-payment. It was clearly defeated at the ballot box in June 2012.
126359.m: The managed care bill was rejected at the ballot box in 2012.

126360.q: What did the people and the cantons add to the Federal Constitution in 2014 that strengthens family medicine?
a: An article on basic medical care
A ban on alternative insurance models
A duty to have an annual health check
126360.e: The federal decree on basic medical care obliges the Confederation and the cantons to promote good basic care, including family medicine.
126360.m: Since 2014, basic medical care has been in the Federal Constitution.

126361.q: Which services did the Tarmed tariff apply to?
126361.e: Tarmed set out how doctors' practices and hospital outpatient departments charge for their outpatient services.
126361.m: Tarmed was the tariff for outpatient medical services.

126362.q: Why was the Tarmed doctors' tariff replaced by a new tariff?
a: It was considered outdated and many services were wrongly valued
Visits to the doctor became free
126362.e: Tarmed dated from the 1990s and no longer reflected modern medicine properly. From 2026 it was replaced by TARDOC and outpatient flat rates.
126362.m: Tarmed was replaced because of outdated valuations.

126363.q: A service is valued at 40 tax points and the tax point value is 0.95 francs. How much does the service cost?
126363.e: You multiply the tax points by the tax point value: 40 times 0.95 francs makes 38 francs.
126363.m: The price of a service is the tax points times the tax point value.

126364.q: What is true of the tax point value in Tarmed?
a: It varies by canton and contract
It is the same throughout Switzerland
126364.e: The number of tax points is the same across Switzerland, but the tax point value is agreed regionally between the tariff partners. That is why the same service does not cost the same everywhere.
126364.m: The tax point value differs between cantons.

126365.q: Which new doctors' tariff replaced Tarmed from 2026, together with outpatient flat rates?
126365.e: Tarmed was considered outdated. The Federal Council therefore approved TARDOC and outpatient flat rates as its successors.
126365.m: Since 2026, TARDOC and outpatient flat rates have replaced the old Tarmed.

126366.q: Which tariff system applies to stays in acute care in hospitals?
a: SwissDRG with flat rates per case
126366.e: Since 2012, acute hospital stays have been charged with flat rates per case. For each case of treatment there is a fixed amount depending on the diagnosis.
126366.m: Hospital stays are charged with flat rates per case under SwissDRG.

126393.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland for the ambulance emergency line when an ambulance needs to go to hospital?
126393.e: 144 is the number for the ambulance emergency line. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 143 the helpline Dargebotene Hand.
126393.m: In Switzerland you dial 144 for an ambulance.

127571.q: What do people do in bionics?
a: Count the stars in the sky
127571.e: In bionics, researchers look closely at how animals and plants solve problems. Then they use these ideas for new technology.

127573.q: Which plant was the model for Velcro?
127573.e: Burdock burrs easily get caught on clothes and fur. Velcro holds in exactly the same way.
127573.m: Velcro was copied from the burdock.

127574.q: Which country did the inventor of Velcro come from?
127574.e: The engineer George de Mestral came from the canton of Vaud. He had his invention protected in the middle of the 20th century.
127574.m: Velcro was invented by a Swiss man.

127575.q: Where did the inventor of Velcro discover lots of burrs?
127575.e: After a walk, lots of burrs were stuck in his dog's fur. He looked at them closely under the microscope.
127575.m: A walk with the dog gave him the idea for Velcro.

127576.q: What does a burr have on its spines?
127576.e: The spines of the burr end in little hooks. With them, they catch in fur or fabric.
127576.m: A burr holds on with tiny hooks.

127577.q: What does the second side of a Velcro fastener have, which the hooks catch in?
127577.e: One side of the Velcro has hooks, the other lots of soft loops. If you press them together, they catch on each other.
127577.m: Hooks and loops hold Velcro together.

127578.q: What does a bionics expert do first?
127578.e: First you have to understand how an animal or plant does something. Only then can you turn the idea into technology.
127578.m: People who work in bionics observe nature first.

127579.q: What does water do on a lotus leaf?
127579.e: The lotus leaf is water-repellent. Drops of water simply roll over it.
127579.m: Water rolls off a lotus leaf in beads.

127580.q: What do the rolling water drops take with them from the lotus leaf?
127580.e: The rolling drops collect dust and dirt and carry them away. This makes the leaf clean.
127580.m: Water drops wash the lotus leaf clean.

127581.q: What is it called when a leaf keeps itself clean?
127581.e: With the lotus, rain is enough to make the leaf clean again. This is called self-cleaning.
127581.m: The lotus leaf can clean itself.

127582.q: What does the surface of a lotus leaf have when you magnify it a lot?
127582.e: Under the microscope you can see lots of tiny bumps. Drops only touch them in a few places.
127582.m: Tiny bumps make the lotus leaf water-repellent.

127583.q: What else is the lotus leaf covered with?
127583.e: A fine layer of wax repels water. Together with the bumps, this creates the lotus effect.
127583.m: Fine wax helps the lotus leaf repel water.

127584.q: Where does the lotus plant grow?
127584.e: The lotus is a water plant and grows in ponds and lakes. Its large leaves lie on the water or stick up above it.
127584.m: The lotus is a water plant.

127585.q: Which product uses the lotus effect?
127585.e: There are outdoor wall paints with a surface like a lotus leaf. Rain washes the dirt off the wall of the house.
127585.m: Some house paints stay clean thanks to the lotus effect.

127586.q: What colour is the flower of the lotus plant often?
127586.e: The large flowers of the lotus are often pink, sometimes white too. They stick up high above the water.
127586.m: The lotus often has large pink flowers.

127587.q: What shape is a water drop on a lotus leaf?
127587.e: Because the leaf repels the water, the drop pulls together almost into a ball. That way it can roll off easily.
127587.m: On a lotus leaf, drops become almost perfectly round.

127588.q: What does shark skin feel like when you stroke it from the tail to the head?
127588.e: A shark's skin is covered in tiny hard scales. That is why it feels rough when you stroke it the wrong way.
127588.m: Stroked the wrong way, shark skin is rough.

127589.q: What is the surface of shark skin made of?
127589.e: A shark's scales look like little teeth. That is why they are called skin teeth.
127589.m: A shark has tiny teeth on its skin.

127590.q: What do the fine grooves on shark skin help with?
a: Gliding through the water more easily
127590.e: The grooves on the skin teeth guide the water and reduce drag. So the shark swims using less strength.
127590.m: Shark skin helps the shark glide easily through the water.

127591.q: Which sportswear was made with shark skin as a model?
127591.e: Swimsuits with a surface like shark skin were meant to reduce drag in the water. The idea was to swim faster.
127591.m: There were swimsuits modelled on shark skin.

127592.q: What is a ship's paint modelled on shark skin meant to prevent?
a: Mussels and algae growing on it
127592.e: Hardly any algae or mussels settle on the skin of sharks. People want to achieve that for ships too.
127592.m: Shark skin stays free of mussels and algae.

127593.q: Which vehicles are given a film like shark skin to save fuel?
127593.e: A film with tiny grooves reduces air resistance. So aeroplanes need slightly less fuel.
127593.m: Shark-skin film helps aeroplanes save fuel.

127594.q: Which animal group do sharks belong to?
127594.e: Sharks breathe with gills and spend their whole life in water. They are fish.

127595.q: Where can a gecko even walk?
127595.e: Geckos cling so well that they can walk upside down on the ceiling. Even smooth panes of glass are no problem for them.
127595.m: A gecko can walk upside down on the ceiling.

127596.q: What does a gecko have on the underside of its toes?
127596.e: On the toes there are millions of tiny hairs. They get so close to the wall that they stick to it.
127596.m: Fine hairs let the gecko stick to walls.

127597.q: What does a gecko NOT need to stick to a pane of glass?
127597.e: The gecko sticks without any glue. It is only the tiny hairs on its toes that hold it on.
127597.m: A gecko sticks without any glue.

127598.q: Which animal group does the gecko belong to?
127598.e: Geckos are lizards and so they are reptiles. They have scaly skin.

127599.q: What have researchers developed with the gecko as a model?
a: Sticky tape that can be removed again
Glasses that see in the dark
127599.e: Modelled on gecko toes, there are sticky strips without glue. You can remove them and use them again.
127599.m: Gecko tape sticks and can be removed again.

127600.q: When are many geckos out and about?
127600.e: Many types of gecko hunt insects at night. During the day they hide.
127600.m: Many geckos are active at night.

127601.q: How does a gecko get its foot off the wall again?
127601.e: The gecko peels its toes off from the tip like sticky tape. That way it frees its foot very easily.
127601.m: A gecko peels off its toes to let go.

127602.q: What can a gecko shed when in danger?
127602.e: If an enemy grabs the gecko by the tail, it sheds it and escapes. The tail then grows back.
127602.m: A gecko can shed its tail.

127603.q: What does a spider build its web from?
127603.e: The spider makes its threads itself. The material is called spider silk.
127603.m: Spider webs are made of spider silk.

127604.q: Where on the spider are the threads made?
a: On the back part of the body
127604.e: At the end of the back part of its body, the spider has spinnerets. The silk comes out there.
127604.m: The spider spins its threads at the back of its body.

127605.q: A spider's thread is very thin. Does that make it weak?
127605.e: Spider silk is amazingly strong. For its thickness, it can take more than a steel wire of the same thinness.
127605.m: Spider silk is thin but very strong.

127606.q: What can a spider's thread do especially well without breaking?
127606.e: Spider silk is very stretchy. So the web catches a flying insect without tearing.
127606.m: Spider threads are stretchy and do not break easily.

127607.q: What is spider silk made of?
127607.e: Spider silk is made of proteins. Researchers are trying to produce these proteins artificially.
127607.m: Spider silk is made of protein.

127608.q: What would people like to use artificial spider silk for, for example?
127608.e: Spider silk is strong and the body accepts it well. So it could be used in medicine, for example for stitches.
127608.m: Artificial spider silk could help in medicine.

127609.q: Why doesn't a spider get stuck in its own web?
a: It walks on threads that are not sticky
It washes the web with water
127609.e: Not all the threads in the web are sticky. The spider walks mainly on the dry threads.
127609.m: The spider knows the dry threads in its web.

127610.q: What does a spider catch with its web?
127610.e: Flies, mosquitoes and other insects get caught in the web. The spider then eats them.
127610.m: Spiders catch insects in their webs.

127611.e: Many types of termite build large mounds. A whole colony lives inside.

127612.q: What do termites build their mounds from?
127612.e: Termites mix soil with their saliva. When the mixture dries, it becomes rock hard.
127612.m: Termite mounds are built from soil and saliva.

127613.q: What provides fresh air in a termite mound?
127613.e: Air flows through the mound through many tunnels and shafts. This keeps it pleasant inside.
127613.m: Tunnels and channels air the termite mound.

127614.q: On which continent is there a well-known office building that is aired like a termite mound?
127614.e: In Zimbabwe, a large building was built that airs itself on the model of termite mounds. That is why it needs much less energy for ventilation and cooling.
127614.m: A building in Africa airs itself like a termite mound.

127615.q: What does a building designed like a termite mound save?
127615.e: The air is cooled without big machines. That is why the building needs much less electricity.

127616.e: Termites like warmth. Most kinds live in the tropics and other warm areas.
127616.m: Termites live mainly in warm countries.

127617.q: How high can termite mounds get?
127617.e: Some termite mounds are taller than an adult. They can be several metres high.
127617.m: Termite mounds can be several metres high.

127618.e: Many termites eat wood and other plant parts. That is why they can also damage wooden houses.

127619.e: The boxfish has an angular body. It looks like a little box.
127619.m: The boxfish is square like a box.

127620.q: What surrounds the body of the boxfish?
127620.e: The boxfish lives inside a shell of bony plates. Only its fins, eyes and mouth stick out.
127620.m: The boxfish wears a hard shell.

127621.q: What was built with the boxfish as a model?
127621.e: A car maker built a test car in the shape of the boxfish. It was meant to have little air resistance.
127621.m: A car was modelled on the boxfish.

127622.q: What does the boxfish mainly swim with?
a: Its whole body like a snake
A jet of water like a squid
127622.e: The hard shell can hardly bend. That is why the boxfish moves mainly with its small fins.
127622.m: The boxfish swims with its fins.

a: In the sea near coral reefs
127623.e: Boxfish live in warm seas. They are often found near coral reefs.
127623.m: The boxfish lives in the sea near corals.

127624.q: What does the young yellow boxfish look like?
127624.e: The young yellow boxfish is bright yellow and has black spots. The colour warns enemies.
127624.m: The young yellow boxfish is yellow with black spots.

127625.q: What can the boxfish release when in danger?
127625.e: The boxfish can release poison through its skin. This protects it from enemies.
127625.m: The boxfish protects itself with poison.

127626.q: What did engineers learn from the boxfish's shell?
a: How to build light but strong
How to build as heavy as possible
How to build only with glass
How to build only round parts
127626.e: The boxfish's shell is light and yet very strong. This is also useful for cars and machines.
127626.m: The boxfish shows how to build light and strong.

127627.q: Which vehicle was given a nose modelled on the kingfisher's beak?
127627.e: Engineers in Japan shaped the front of a high-speed train like a kingfisher's beak. The kingfisher was a good model for this.
127627.m: A Japanese high-speed train has a nose like a kingfisher.

127628.q: What problem did the high-speed train in Japan used to have when leaving a tunnel?
127628.e: The train pushed the air in the tunnel along in front of it. When it came out, there was a loud bang.
127628.m: The new train nose helped against the bang at the tunnel.

127629.q: How does the kingfisher dive into the water?
127629.e: The kingfisher's beak is shaped so that it slides into the water with almost no splash. That is why it was a good model.
127629.m: The kingfisher dives in with almost no splash.

127630.q: What does the kingfisher mainly eat?
127630.e: The kingfisher sits on a branch over the water. When it sees a small fish, it plunges in.

127631.q: What colour is the kingfisher's back?
127631.e: The kingfisher has a bright blue back and an orange breast. It is one of the most colourful birds in Switzerland.
127631.m: The kingfisher has a bright blue back.

127632.q: Where can you watch kingfishers in Switzerland?
127632.e: The kingfisher needs clear water with small fish. That is why it lives by water.
